"You're in a mood," she said. "A good one. It's disturbing. Did something happen?"
"I played golf with a man who chipped in from the fringe."
"That's it?"
"He said he'd never be able to explain it to anyone."
She looked at me for a bit. "Okay," she said. "I'll take it. I'll take Wednesday golf man. Bring him round."

I told her he was only a guest, a day ticket, some work thing in the area, and she said that was a shame, and I said yes, and meant it more than I expected to. I'd driven home with the window down and Buddy asleep in the back, giddy, like a kid who's been picked for a team by the one who's good.
He'd asked about the dog first. I kept coming back to that. Everybody asks about the dog eventually. He asked before he asked my name.

The other thing I kept coming back to was smaller and more like me. It was the payroll. I've watched that bank's systems for eleven years and I could not have told you, honestly, what would run on the Monday.
So on Thursday morning, before the coffee, I went and found the binder.

chapters.title: Utrecht, 1993
chapters.what: Three small additions the plan needs: the two lunches (the children's schooling, the colleagues who declined), the word "seats", and the closing note now ends on Verhoef's death in 1995 on a canal road in place of the grandson. American spelling. Source: v6/05.
blocks: Wim Koster waited until the corridor was empty before he closed his office door, which was a thing he had never done in eleven years as head of department, and he noticed himself doing it, and he did it anyway.

The paper was on his desk. Thirty-one pages, double-spaced, with the figures stapled at the back the way Verhoef always did it, because Verhoef believed the argument should stand without the pictures. Two rooms, shielded, forty meters apart. Two people who had sat together for twenty minutes beforehand and were then separated. A light flashed in one room. Something moved, a little, in the other. Not much. Verhoef had the decency to say not much in the abstract, which was more than most people managed. The effect was small and it was there, and it was there on four runs out of five, and the fifth run was the one Verhoef had written about at the greatest length, because he was that kind of scientist, and because he was a friend.
The telephone had a long cord. Koster carried it to the window.
"It's Wim," he said. "From the department. You said to call if."

"Yes." The voice on the other end was pleasant and belonged to a man he had met twice, over lunch, and whose surname he could never afterward remember, which he had come to understand was deliberate. At the first lunch the man had asked about the children's schooling and seemed to know the answer. At the second he had mentioned, with regret, two colleagues at other universities who had not found time for lunch, and whose departments were smaller now. "Go ahead."

"There's a paper. A colleague. He's submitted it, I'm the internal reader." Koster looked at the bicycles in the rack below, the chained wheels, the one with no saddle that had been there since September. "It's good. That's the problem. It's careful."
"What's it about?"
Koster told him. The rooms. The light. The movement. He heard himself make it sound smaller than it was, and he heard the other man hear that, and neither of them remarked on it.
"Recall," the man said, after a moment. It was not a question. It was the sound of a word being placed in a column.
"He doesn't call it that."
"No. He wouldn't." A pause with paper in it. "Is he the sort who corrects himself in public, your colleague?"

Koster thought about Verhoef at the Christmas drinks, telling a room full of people that his own best-known result from 1987 was probably an artifact of the cabling, laughing at himself, buying the next round. "Yes."

"That's worse," the man said, mildly. "All right. Here's what we'd like. Not the paper; the paper's nothing, the paper's four runs in a cupboard. The category. Does your department have a line for instrumentation?"
"Of course."
"Then it's instrumentation. Cable artifacts, shielding, that family. File it there. Review it there. Let it be read by people who read that line. It'll find its level."
"It isn't instrumentation."

"No," the man agreed. "But it will be. That's all we ever do, Wim. We don't change what a thing is. We change where it's kept." He sounded, briefly, as though he were quoting somebody. "You're not being asked to lie about anything. You're being asked to shelve."

Koster had been going to say something about Verhoef, about the fifth run and the length of the discussion of it, about what it was like to watch a careful man be careful. He found that he was looking at the bicycle with no saddle instead.
"And the other matter," he said.
"The seats. Yes. That's confirmed. Yourself, Marianne, the two children." The voice did something small and warm. "You asked about your mother."
"I did."
"It's a budgeting thing, Wim. I'm sorry. The allocation is the allocation. I did ask."
"I understand."
"I know you do. That's why we talk to you." A chair creaked, four hundred kilometers away, in a room Koster would never see. "You'll let me know when it's filed."
"Good man."

Koster put the telephone back on the desk and stood for a while with his hand on it, as though it might ring again and take it back. It didn't. He opened the door. The corridor was still empty. He walked down it, past the noticeboard with the Christmas drinks and the seminar on superconductivity, and he knocked on Verhoef's door, and when Verhoef looked up with that face, that hopeful ruined face of a man who has handed over the best thing he has ever done, Koster said, "It's very good, Anton. Really. I've got some thoughts on the shielding section," and Verhoef said, "I knew you would," and smiled, and pulled out the chair.

They talked for two hours. Koster was kind the whole time. It cost him nothing. That was the part he would think about, years later, in a chair of his own, when he'd stopped being able to remember the foundation man's name and had never once stopped being able to remember the bicycle.
The paper was reclassified in March. It was not published. Verhoef retired early and kept his copy. He died in 1995, in a car, on a canal road.

chapters.title: Leave it
chapters.what: Now starts from Julian's payroll question: James compares the recovery plan's inventory with what actually runs and finds one job more. The dealer's letter is a reply to his own (a copy for sale, the Deventer buyer, the postscript), and continuity asks for "the person who reads things" three weeks on. Source: v6/06.
blocks: The binder turned out to be a file, four hundred pages long, and nobody had opened it in nineteen months. I know because files keep a list of who opens them, and I looked. That's the kind of thing I look at.

It answered Julian's question on page nine. If the building burns down, payroll is done on Monday from a recovery site in a business park, by people who get there on a bus. Fine. The part that concerned me was an appendix at the back: the inventory. Every scheduled job the bank would need to bring back, in order, each with a name, an owner and a reason.

My job, in one sentence, is to look at screens that look at other things. Ten thousand systems, every night, breathing, and my programs count the breaths and put the counts on a wall. Green is fine. Amber is a meeting. Red is my phone at four in the morning. But green doesn't mean nothing's wrong. Green means nothing's wrong that we decided to look for. So I don't look at the colors. I look at the list under the colors, all the little jobs that run on timers, the housekeeping. In a company our size it's a few thousand lines long and nobody reads it, the way nobody reads the ingredients.
So I had two lists of the same thing. What the plan says we run, and what we run. I did what I do with two copies of anything. I put them side by side.
They matched for three thousand eight hundred and twelve lines. The scheduler had three thousand eight hundred and thirteen.
The extra one was called rcl-agg.

Seven characters, which is the kind of name you give something when you're in a hurry or when you don't want it read. No owner. The owner field is mandatory. You literally cannot save the form without it, and it was blank. No ticket. No description. It ran every night at fourteen minutes past two, for about nine seconds, and sent roughly forty kilobytes of something to an address. When I looked the address up at ten in the morning it didn't exist. As far as I could tell it existed for nine seconds a night.
I took a screenshot. I screenshot things. It's the Record's fault.

Then I did the obvious checks, and they took me a week, because I do them properly and because I was hoping one of them would make it go away. Who created it, and when? There was no history. The first entry in the history of rcl-agg was rcl-agg, already running, as if it had been there before the list was. The other offices: same job, same minute, same forty kilobytes. The backups, as far back as the backups go, which is a long way, because the man who set them up was paranoid in the useful way. It was in all of them. Every night. Fourteen minutes past two. Nine seconds.
I'd been sleeping badly since the sentence. I don't know whether that's why I saw it. I'd like to think I'd have seen it anyway.
On the Friday I put it in the stand-up.
<hr />

Stand-up is fifteen minutes in a glass box, standing, so that nobody gets comfortable enough to talk. Pieter runs it. Pieter is my manager, and a decent man in the specific way that managers are decent, which is that he'll defend you to the end of the earth about anything that doesn't cost him anything.
There were nine people in the box. I went last. I always go last. The persona likes to see the room first.
"There's a job with no owner," I said. "I want to know why."
"Which job?"
I told him.

Something happened in Pieter's face. I don't want to make it bigger than it was. It was the size of a man remembering an appointment. He looked at his screen, and for about as long as it takes to find a card in your wallet he said nothing at all.
"That one's old," he said. "It's a diagnostic artifact. From the migration."
"Which migration?"
"The big one. Before your time." He was still looking at his screen. "Leave it."
"It sends data somewhere."

"It sends diagnostics somewhere. It's been fine for years. Leave it, James, honestly. We've got the payments thing and the Antwerp thing and I'd rather have you on either of those than on a timer from the Stone Age." He smiled, and it was a real smile, and the meeting moved on. Frank caught my eye across the box and made a little skull with his hand, which is our thing now, apparently. I've decided to find it charming.

Here's the problem. The big migration wasn't before my time. I did the big migration, a lot of it, two years before Pieter joined. There wasn't a rcl-agg in it. I'd have known. I read the ingredients.

I didn't say that. It wasn't courage and it wasn't cunning. Pieter had said leave it in the tone you use for something that's already been decided, and I've spent thirty years learning that when my memory and the paperwork disagree, I'm the error. So I nodded, and went back to my desk, and felt the thing I'd felt in the kitchen with the two books. Only this time I was feeling it about a person.

Because people who don't know what a thing is say I'll look into it. Pieter hadn't said that. He'd gone quiet, and then he'd come back with a whole sentence, with a cause in it and a date and an instruction. Nobody has that sentence lying around about a seven-character job. Either he'd needed the pause to remember it, or he'd needed the pause to decide to use it, and I sat at my desk until seven with the list open and couldn't work out which I liked less.
<hr />
Ana was in the kitchen with the dogs when I got home, and the dogs were in the kitchen with Ana's dinner, strategically.
"You're late."
"Payments thing."

"Mm." She was reading something on her phone, and she lifted it without looking at me, the way she lifts it when she wants me to see that she's not looking. "You've got a letter. Actual paper. It's on the side."

It was a good envelope, the kind with a lining, and my name was on it in a hand I didn't know. Of the three dealers I'd written to, one never answered and one had sent me four words, not in stock, sorry. The third was a shop in Groningen with a website from 2004, and he'd answered an email with a fountain pen.

Dear Mr. Klippe, it began, and I stood in my kitchen feeling oddly caught, as if I'd been spotted in a shop I'd told everyone I didn't go to. It was the first time I'd seen my name written down by somebody who had anything to do with the book.

He had a copy. The second impression, Leiden, 1931, sound, a little foxed. The price was three hundred and forty euros, which he was aware was a great deal for a book nobody read. They had become hard to find and he couldn't tell me why. He'd last sold one in 2011, to a university man in Deventer who had been very particular about the impression. If I wanted it, I could send the money and he'd send the book.

Then a postscript, in slightly different ink, as though he'd come back to the letter after a cup of tea. I would gently say that this title attracts a certain kind of inquiry, and that I have found, over forty years, that it is wisest to be plain about one's reasons.
I read that twice. Then I read it to Buddy, who was under the table in case of a chicken event.
"'Plain about one's reasons,'" I said. "What does that mean?"
"It means he thinks you're a nutter," said Ana, not looking up. "What's the book?"
"The one with the two copies."
"The one you measured."
"The one I measured."
She put the phone down then. "And a man in a shop in, where?"
"Groningen."
"A man in a shop in Groningen has written to you on nice paper to tell you to be careful."
"To be plain."
"That's what careful sounds like in a shop." She picked the phone back up. "Did you know Mora ate half a sponge today? Just so we're all plain about our reasons."

I laughed. She has better lines than I do and always has. Mine are built and hers just arrive. I sat down and ate with them, and told her a did-you-know about the Ethiopian calendar being seven years behind everybody else's, because they counted the start of things differently and never saw a reason to stop. She said that was a good one, and asked if that meant she was thirty-one in Ethiopia, and I said it did, and she said she'd think about moving.
It was a good evening. There were a lot of good evenings and I was there for all of them.
<hr />
At one in the morning I was at the kitchen table with the laptop, because of course I was.

I wasn't thinking about Tresidder. I was thinking about Pieter's face, and the pause, and a thing I'd read years ago and filed under interesting-wrong: that the easiest way to hide something is to give it a boring name and a boring reason and put it on a list nobody reads.
Two options, I told the dog, who was asleep and did not care.

One. It's exactly what Pieter said. An old diagnostic job that somebody forgot to document, sending its little report into the void every night, like a dog waiting at a door for a man who isn't coming home. Sad, boring, common as dirt. I've seen fifty of them.
Two. Somebody knows exactly what it is, and has told Pieter what to say.
I'm a reasonable man. I gave option one eighty-five percent, out of habit, and then I looked at that number and thought about where I'd last used it.

Then I did a small thing, the kind you can walk back from. I opened a ticket. Low priority, plain language. Unowned scheduled job rcl-agg: request owner and purpose for the inventory. It came back as number 41790. I assigned it to nobody, which is how you assign a thing to the system itself, and left it in the queue where the dull tickets go to be ignored for a year.
Before I went up I sent the man in Groningen his three hundred and forty euros. I hadn't told Ana the price. I'd noticed myself not telling her.
<hr />
Three weeks later Pieter stopped at my desk on his way to something else and said, "Continuity want you. The program. They asked for the person who reads things."
I said thank you. It's what you say. I was on the stairs before I noticed that I hadn't asked who they were, or who had told them that I read things.

By then I knew a few things Pieter didn't know I knew, because I hadn't left it. I'd said my eleven words in a glass box and been told to leave it by a man whose one sentence about it was false, and I know exactly one honest way to find out what a job is when the paperwork won't tell you. You don't open it and you don't stop it. You stand next to it while it runs, and you watch what comes out.
I'd started that same Friday night.

chapters.title: The payload
chapters.what: His number is already on the first capture as "asked (job)"; he then finds an older row, "wrote (dealer)", from before the stand-up, posts the question he deleted in the spring as a test input, and gets a third row the next night. He leaves with two questions: who reported a letter, and is the edit a one-off. Source: v7/10.
blocks: There's a thing engineers do when someone tells them to leave something alone, and it isn't disobedience. Pieter would call it disobedience and he'd be wrong, and the difference is the only defense I've got.

If a job runs on your systems and you don't know what it does, you don't open it. Opening it is a decision. You don't stop it, you don't change it, you don't touch it. You stand next to it while it runs and you watch what comes out. I've done that a thousand times to things I was allowed to look at, and nobody ever called it anything but Tuesday.

So on the night of the stand-up I set an alarm for ten past two, and went downstairs in my socks, and opened the laptop on the kitchen table, where the two copies of page 118 still lived in their folder.
Buddy came and lay across my feet. He does that when I'm up at the wrong time. He doesn't ask why. He just makes sure that if I get up to do something stupid, I'll have to move a dog first.

What I did will satisfy nobody. The technical people will find it too vague and everyone else will find it too much. I watched the door the job sends things through, and when it sent something, I kept a copy. I didn't break anything. I didn't log in as anyone I'm not. The data went where it always goes. It also went into a file on my laptop called, I'm embarrassed to say, nothing.txt, because if Ana came down for water I wanted the screen to tell the truth.

Fourteen minutes past two. Nine seconds. Forty-one kilobytes, which is nothing. A photo of the dogs is a hundred times that. Forty-one kilobytes is about what a person could read in the time it takes to make coffee.

I opened it expecting noise. Diagnostics look like noise: timestamps, hexadecimal, the digestive sounds of a system talking to itself. Pieter had said diagnostic artifact, and the part of me that has spent thirty years losing arguments with paperwork expected to find exactly that and go back to bed the fool.
It was a list.
<hr />

A hundred and thirteen lines. Each line was a date, then an employee number, the eight digits we all have on the back of our badges, then two words in lowercase, like a note somebody writes to himself. I'll leave the dates off.
40217733 posted (forum) 40193058 wrote (dealer) 40221904 asked (hr) 40188120 searched (archive) 40209417 recalled (family)
I read all hundred and thirteen with Buddy on my feet. Then I read them again, and the second time I wasn't reading the numbers. I was reading the verbs.
Posted. Wrote. Asked. Searched. Requested. Raised.

Every one of them was a thing a person does with words, to somebody else, on purpose. Nobody on the list had thought anything. You can't put a thought in a file. Every line was a moment when somebody in my company had stopped, and typed, or picked up a pen, or opened their mouth in a meeting, and put a question where it could be read. The thing in brackets was where.

There was one verb I couldn't place. Recalled. Seven lines of it, with (family) or (colleague) or (hr) after it. I work for a bank. In a bank a recall is a payment you sent by mistake and want back, and there's a whole team for it, with a form. So I decided it was a product term that had wandered into the wrong file, and I moved on. That's how good I am at this.
The dates went back thirty days. New lines go at the bottom. Whoever wrote the thing that writes it was tidy. So I scrolled to the bottom, and the last line had that day's date on it, and it was:
40176502 asked (job)
My number is 40176502. I know it the way you know your own phone number, because I've typed it into a hundred forms.

I didn't panic. I didn't feel watched, not yet. That came later, in a different room. What I felt, at my kitchen table with my own badge number on a list I wasn't supposed to have, was the cold, almost pleasant thing I get at work when a system finally tells me what it is. Because it had, in two words. Nobody on the list had broken a rule. The job didn't count what you did or what you knew or what you thought at four in the morning on a kitchen floor. It counted whether you'd turned it into words and handed the words to someone. I'd said eleven of them in a glass box that morning, and by a quarter past two the next morning there I was, with a reason beside my number that was exactly true.
I looked at the bracket. Not (forum), not (hr). Somebody had a category for people who asked about the thing itself. I was the only one in it.
<hr />
That would have been enough for one night. I'd like to say I went to bed.
What I did was the thing I should have done first. You don't scroll for your own number. You search for it, because scrolling finds what you expect and searching finds what's there.
Two results.
The second was the one I'd just read. The first was most of a page higher up, dated the Monday of the week before. Eleven days before I opened my mouth in stand-up.
40176502 wrote (dealer)
I sat there for a while. Buddy's weight on my feet was the only thing in the kitchen I was sure of.

I'd written to three dealers on that Monday. From this table, on this laptop, from my own email address, with a dog under the chair. I hadn't mentioned it at work. I hadn't mentioned it to Ana until a letter came. There is no system in that bank that knows I own a book, and I should know, because I watch them.

So the job wasn't only reading the bank. Whatever made this list could be told things from outside. And somebody outside, on a Monday in June, had told it that an employee with my number had written to a dealer.

Years ago I read about a technician in San Francisco, an ordinary one, the kind of man who reads the wiring diagrams because somebody has to, who found a locked room on the sixth floor of his own building where the internet was being copied through a splitter to a government agency. He found it because he read the documents nobody read. I'd always liked that story, the way you like stories about people who are a bit like you, from a safe distance. I didn't like it that night. That night I thought about what happened to him after, which was lawyers, and a long time of being called a crank, and then being right, which as far as I can tell didn't help.
I closed the laptop. I didn't delete nothing.txt. I renamed it, which is the kind of brave I am.
<hr />
I had one capture and a theory, and one capture isn't much.

At work, when you want to know what a monitor is really watching, you don't read its manual. You feed it something and see whether it shows up. A test input. It has to be something only you sent, at a time only you know, so that if it comes out the other end there's no arguing about where it came from.
I spent most of Saturday pretending I didn't know what my test input was.

In the spring I'd typed a question into a thread on a forum, looked at it for five minutes, and deleted it. I'd had ten reasons. The real one was that people who post questions like that get a label and the label doesn't come off, and I'd been lurking on that forum for twelve years under a name that's a joke only I understand, posting the safe kind of did-you-know, precisely so that I'd never have one.
Nobody at the bank knows that name. Ana doesn't know that name.

At eleven that night, with Ana asleep and Mora upstairs in my place on the bed, which she takes the second I leave it and defends like a tenant with rights, I logged in at the kitchen table and typed it again. Same thread. Same words.
Has anyone here had an NDE and is willing to talk about it?

I looked at it for a good deal less than five minutes this time, because this time it wasn't a confession. It was a test input, and I'm a professional. Then I posted it, and it turned out to be a confession anyway. There it sat, under my name, where anyone could see me looking. Fuck.
By one o'clock it had three replies. One was kind. One said it was all the pineal gland. One was a link to a retreat in Portugal.
At fourteen minutes past two I kept a copy of what went through the door.
A hundred and fourteen lines. I searched.
40176502 wrote (dealer) 40176502 asked (job) 40176502 posted (forum)
Three hours and fourteen minutes, from my kitchen to their list. A forum name I've never typed on a bank machine, tied to my badge number before I'd gone to bed.
<hr />
Here is what I had by Sunday morning, and what I'd paid for it.

I had three rows. I printed them on the home printer, the three lines and nothing else, and put the sheet in the folder with page 118. The first row had cost me nothing I knew about. The second had cost me eleven words. The third had cost me the one thing I'd been careful about for twelve years, and I'd handed it over myself, on purpose, to find out whether they'd take it. They took it. So the bank, or whoever the bank sends its forty-one kilobytes to, now knew what I call myself when I think nobody's looking, and what I ask about.

I knew what the list counted. I didn't know what it was for. A list of people who ask is a strange thing to want. It isn't thieves or leakers. It's the curious, a hundred-odd of them in one bank, counted nightly. Either that's the most pointless piece of software ever written or it's one gear of something.
And I had two questions, which is one more than I can usually carry.

The first was the letter. Three people on earth knew I'd written about that book, and all three sold books for a living. One never answered, one sent me four words, and one had told me, on good paper, to be plain about my reasons.

The second was the book itself. Nobody counts a man for buying a novel. If writing to a shop about one dull title from 1931 was worth a row, then that title mattered to somebody, and all I had to show for it was one changed sentence in one copy, found on a kitchen floor at four in the morning. Before I asked anybody anything I needed to know whether it was my copy or the whole run, and whether it was only this book.
The first question needed a drive. The second only needed a ruler, and the copy from Groningen was paid for and on its way.

I got into bed. Mora moved over by one dog's width, which is her maximum concession. Ana was asleep on her side with her hand under her cheek. I lay there next to her and didn't tell her, and I already knew that not telling her was going to be a bigger problem than the list.

chapters.title: The control case
chapters.what: (Structure 01 marks it Keep, but the copied v6 draft predates canon). The third copy now comes from Groningen, expensive, with the lie to Ana about the price; the thin book's last page holds a library reference, the second of December and "Ask" in place of coordinates and an April date; the ending points at the dealer. All other prose kept. Source: v6/07.
blocks: One hit is a story. Two hits is a coincidence. You don't have anything until you've tried to make it go away and it won't.

That's not wisdom. That's the job. Somebody calls at four in the morning and says the system is dying, and the first thing you do, before you look at the system, is find out whether it's the system or the thing that's watching the system. Half the time the patient is fine and the monitor is broken. People hate that answer. It's the correct answer about half the time.

So before I let myself believe a word of what the kitchen floor had told me, I had to try to kill it. Properly. In writing. I had a new reason to hurry, too. Somebody was counting people who wrote to shops about this book, and I'd have liked very much for the book to turn out to be nothing.
<hr />
The first thing was the other copy.

Second impression, 1931, the Leiden printing. It ought to be cheap. It was printed for the continent and the continent didn't want it. It came from Groningen in a padded envelope, wrapped in brown paper by somebody who had been wrapping books for forty years, and it had cost three hundred and forty euros.

Ana saw the parcel and asked how much. I said forty. It was the first number that sounded like a book. That's a long way outside the small honest-marriage margin, and I knew it while I was saying it, and I said it anyway and felt like shit for most of the evening.
Then I took it into the kitchen and laid it next to the other two and opened all three to page 118.
Blemish, top margin: present. Two typos: present. Arisen among the first. And the two further in, where the professor's pencil had sent me: the same.

So it wasn't my copy. It was the run. Every second impression ever sold said the new sentences. Whoever did it had done it once and let the presses do the rest, and that's a very particular kind of patience, and I wrote that down.
The second thing was the one I didn't want to do, which is why it came second. I needed a control.

The professor's crate had eleven other books in it, and nine of those I either owned or could get. If somebody had been quietly reaching into the plates of dead men's books, then a man who'd kept a first impression of Tresidder on purpose might have kept others on purpose too, and if I checked them and found more edits, I'd have a pattern, and if I checked them and found nothing, I'd have one strange book and a bad week. Either answer was fine. That's what a control is: the test where you're happy to lose.

It took three weekends. Ana called it the Summer of the Ruler. I did it the only way it can be done, which is page against page with a finger on each line, and I will say this for it: there's a kind of peace in it. Four hours with two copies of a survey of calendar systems is four hours in which nobody is dying.

Nothing. Nine books, nothing. Typos corrected between printings, the honest kind, with the little line on the copyright page to say so. One binding variant. A map re-engraved because the first one was ugly. The ordinary, decent drift of printed things.
And I was relieved, which surprised me. I'd wanted it to be nothing. Nothing is the result I know how to live with.

Then I put the nine back on the shelf and looked at the two I hadn't checked, because I couldn't. The thin one with no title. And the paperback of Blindsight read half to death, which I'd picked up and put down a dozen times by then because of four words in pencil beside a paragraph near the end. Not nobody. Not you. The professor's hand, underlined twice. I didn't know what it meant. I knew what it was like: it was like a man arguing with a book he'd lost the argument to.
<hr />
I should say something here about the window, because it comes back later and I don't want it to arrive like a stranger.

Years ago, before Ana, a friend's garden, a summer, the kind of evening where somebody produces a bag and says it's natural. I was twenty-six and I'd read everything and I thought I knew what I was in for. I'm not going to describe it, partly because I can't and partly because every description I've ever read makes it sound like a film and it was nothing like a film. I'll say this much. For about an hour, the question I've been asking my whole life, the one under the other ones, stopped being a question. It wasn't answered. It was irrelevant, the way the colour of a door is irrelevant once the door's open. And then it came back, around midnight, the way a question does, and sat down in its usual chair, and I lay on my friend's lawn and understood that I'd been shown a window and not a way in, and that I'd spend the rest of my life being very careful never to confuse the two.
I filed it. Fourteen years, filed. I'm mentioning it now because when I finally opened the thin book, the first thing I felt was that lawn.
<hr />

It was a Sunday. Ana was at her mother's. Mora was doing the thing where she lies in the doorway so that nobody can enter or leave without a negotiation, and Buddy was on the blanket, and I took the thin book down for what must have been the fifteenth time, and this time I opened it.

Not a book. A notebook, bound to look like one; the professor had had it done, or his grandfather had, because there were two hands in it. The first hand was older, the ink gone brown, careful, upright, the hand of a man who'd learned to write before biros. The second was the professor's, the one from the margins, the no, just no hand. The old hand had filled the first eleven pages. The professor had filled the next thirty. The last page was in a third version of the professor's hand, shakier, the hand of a man writing from a chair he didn't get out of much.
No title. No introduction. No thesis. Just entries, numbered, in a format that somebody had decided on in the nineteen-fifties and that nobody had changed since:
Source. Page. Printing A → Printing B. Before. After.
That's it. That's the whole discipline. Forty-one times.

I didn't go through all of them that Sunday. I read the first ten entries with my heart going harder than it had any business going, and they were all books I'd never heard of, printed before the war, in English and German and once in Dutch, and in every one a sentence had gone in one printing and come out another with its middle changed, and in every one the typos were untouched, and in every one the author was dead or gone or had publicly, carefully, taken it back.
Then I got to eleven.
Tresidder, H. M. Waters Before Memory. 1926. p. 118. 1st imp. → 2nd imp. (Leiden, 1931). "transmitted to the early" → "arisen among the first."
In the old hand. The brown ink. The grandfather's.
I put the book down on the table and sat back and looked at it from a distance, the way you look at a thing you've just understood is older than you.

My sentence. Mine. The one I'd found on a kitchen floor with a wet rope on my chest at four in the morning, sure I was the only man alive who'd ever read page 118 twice. Found, and written down, in a notebook, by a man who'd been dead for fifty years, and then kept, and added to, by his grandson, who'd bought a second impression in 2011 from a dealer in Groningen specifically so that he'd have one that did say the new sentence, to hold against the one his grandfather had kept that didn't.

I hadn't found anything. I'd been handed it. Twelve books, "because twelve sounds better," and the thin one at the bottom, and the first impression two spines above it. I was the thirtieth man to walk past that sentence and the third to stop.
Two options, I told Buddy, because he was there.

One: the crate was an accident. A man died, his daughter kept the furniture, a dealer with a beard bought the books by the meter and a man with a hobby happened to be the one kneeling on the cobblestones that Sunday. It happens. It's the ordinary way that old things find new idiots.
Two: it wasn't.

I didn't like two. I liked it less than I'd liked anything in the whole business so far, because two meant I wasn't hunting. Two meant I was being fed. And I sat there and gave it fifteen percent, and I'd like to tell you I was being generous.
Then I turned to the last page.

Three things, in the shaky hand. A reference, the kind a library gives you: a letter, four digits, a slash, two more digits. I didn't recognize the format, and I've stood in a lot of libraries. A date, circled three times. And under it one word, the only word in the whole book that wasn't a citation:
Ask.

The date was the second of December. It was July. I checked what little I had: the dealer's letter, with its university man in Deventer who was particular about impressions, and a death notice I'd found online for a retired reader in comparative religion, of Deventer, who had died at home in March.

So he'd written down a day that was nine months off, and a place I couldn't identify, and one instruction. And then he'd died with the appointment still ahead of him, and his books had gone to a market by the crate, and the appointment had gone with them.
<hr />
Ana came home at six with her mother's leftovers and found me at the table with the thin book closed in front of me and my hands flat on either side of it like a man keeping a lid on something.
"You've got the face."
"I know."
"Is this the measuring thing?"
"It's the measuring thing."
She put the leftovers in the fridge. She let Mora out. She came back and stood behind me and put her chin on top of my head, which she does, and looked down at the closed book.
"Are you going to tell me?"
"Yes," I said. "Not all of it. Not yet. I don't have it in a shape yet. But yes."
I felt her nod. "Okay, Mulder."
She went up to change. I sat there a while longer.

Here's what I didn't tell her, and it was a bigger thing than the price of a book. The professor hadn't just found what I'd found. He'd found forty more. He'd been doing it for thirty years, with his grandfather's notebook, quietly, and nobody had laughed at him, because he'd never told anyone. And then he'd written down a date and a word and died before the date came.
I'd spent three weekends trying to kill the thing, and three hundred and forty euros, and one lie. I'd failed. That was the control case.

What I had in its place was a day in December, which was a long way off, and one living person who touched both ends of this. The same man had sold the professor his 1931 copy and sold me mine. He was also, I was fairly sure by then, the (dealer) in my row.
He'd told me to be plain about my reasons. I thought I'd better go and do it in person.

chapters.title: Groningen
chapters.what: Moved before "The week it vanished", so the vanished job and Frank's blank are gone from it. James now goes because of the "wrote (dealer)" row, says why before he asks, and shows the dealer the printed rows; the dealer was told "conservation", chooses to stop telephoning, and James names what that may cost him. Source: v7/14.
blocks: The letter had been on the fridge for five weeks, under a magnet shaped like a lemon, which is where things go in our house to be dealt with by someone else.

I'd dealt with half of it. I'd bought the man's book. What I hadn't dealt with was the postscript, the one about being plain about one's reasons, which Ana had translated on the night it came. "That's what careful sounds like in a shop."

Five weeks is how long it took me to hear it properly. Five weeks, three rows with my badge number on them, and a notebook in two dead men's handwriting with my sentence at number eleven. By then I'd done the arithmetic on who could have told anyone about a letter. One dealer who never answered. One who sent four words. And one who'd sold the professor his 1931 copy in 2011, and sold me mine in June, and told me in a different ink to be plain. He was the only person alive, as far as I knew, who touched both the book and my row.
I could have written to him again. But I'd seen what happens to things I write to him.

So on the Saturday I told Ana I was going to look at a bookshop, which was true, and she said take Buddy, he likes the car, which was also true, and I drove two hours north with an old dog asleep on the back seat and the folder on the passenger seat under my phone, like a ticket.
<hr />

Groningen is a nice town and the shop was in the nice part of it, down a street with bicycles leaning on everything. It was exactly what you want a shop like that to be: narrow, deep, smelling of paper and radiator, with a bell on the door that had clearly been chosen for its sound. It was July, and I don't leave a dog in a car in July, so Buddy came in with me, slowly, paying for the step.
The dealer was in the back. He was older than I'd expected, and smaller, with reading glasses pushed up into white hair and a cardigan that had been expensive once.
I'd had two hours to think about how to be plain. It's not my best register. I've got charm for three minutes and deflection for the rest of the evening, and neither was any use here.
"My name is James Klippe," I said. "I bought the Tresidder from you in June."
"The second impression." He took the glasses down. "I hope it arrived well."
"It did. I haven't come about the book. I've come to ask you who you told about my letter. And I'd like to tell you why I'm asking before you answer, because you advised me to."

His face did something I'd only seen once before, on Pieter, in a glass box. Then it did something Pieter's hadn't. It looked relieved, the way you're relieved when the dentist finally calls your name.
He looked past me at the door, and then at me.
"May I ask," he said, "who sent you?"
"Nobody. I came on my own. Well." I looked down. "With him."

Buddy had found the one patch of sun on the floorboards and was lowering himself into it in stages, with the grunt. The dealer watched the whole operation. I think the dog did more for me than the sentence did. Whoever he'd been expecting, they don't arrive with a twelve-year-old who needs a minute to lie down.
"I wondered when," he said, mostly to himself. He went and turned the sign on the door to closed, and came back. "You'd better sit down, then. Bring him through. He'll want the rug."
<hr />

There was a customer's chair by the desk. I sat in it, and Buddy relocated under the desk, and between the dealer and me was a ledger, an actual ledger with a cloth spine. I went first, because I'd said I would.

I told him the dull version, which is the true one. That I collect differences between printings. That I'd found one sentence in his Tresidder that didn't match the first impression, and wanted a third copy to check whether it was my copy or the whole run. That I'd written to three shops on a Monday night from my kitchen. And that my employer, a bank, runs something every night that makes a list.
Then I took the sheet out of the folder and put it on his desk. Three lines, a number, two words each.
"That's my staff number. The top line has the date of the Monday I wrote to you. I didn't tell anyone at work. I only know it's there because I went looking, for a different reason."
He put the glasses back on. He read the top line for a long time, for two words.
"Dealer," he said.
"I think the brackets are you."
He put his hand flat on the ledger while he talked, the way you'd steady a boat.

He'd sold the professor the 1931 printing in 2011. A dry book nobody wanted, from a house clearance. He remembered it because the professor had been so pleased, and the professor was not a man who showed pleasure. A few weeks after, two people had come to the shop. Polite people, a man and a woman, well dressed, with a card from a foundation that looked after archives. They'd been interested in the professor's purchase. They'd asked, very reasonably, whether the shop might let them know if anyone else ever asked for that title. Not the book, I was to understand. They had the book. The title. They said certain editions were followed for conservation. A kindness to old books, the woman had called it. They'd left a telephone number. They had not threatened him, and he wanted me to be clear on that. He'd thought it slightly odd and entirely harmless, and written the number inside the back cover of the ledger, and in all the years since nobody had asked for that title.

"And then you wrote to me," he said. He turned the ledger around. There was a line in it, in a neat old hand, on a Monday in June. My name, and the title of the book. "I telephoned that morning. Before I'd answered you."
"What did they say?"

"Thank you." He looked at his hands. "The same woman, I think. Older. She said it was very helpful and that the foundation appreciated it. I took it that they might make you an offer for the professor's copy, if you had it. That is what I would have meant." He paused. "I wrote the postscript because I thought, if they do come, he should be careful what he says about why he wants the book. Dealers get strange about provenance. That is all I thought it was."
"Conservation."
"And when I walked in just now, you asked who sent me."
He didn't answer that. He didn't need to. He'd thought the polite people had come back to ask what else he knew, and he'd been ready to turn the sign and tell them.
<hr />

I wasn't angry. I'd expected to be. I sat in a customer's chair looking at a small old man in a good cardigan who had made one phone call in all that time, and what I felt was what I feel at work, in the worst outages, when you find the line of config that did it and it was written by somebody decent who was doing what the ticket said.
So I did what I do at work. I told him what the thing he'd touched actually does.

I said the number in his ledger wasn't a conservation department, or wasn't only one. I said I didn't know what it was. I said that within a day of his call, a bank he'd never heard of had my name on a nightly list of people who ask questions, next to a hundred others, and that the list goes somewhere I can't find. I said that when I asked at work what the list was, I was told to leave it, and my question went on the list too. I said the professor had found the same sentence I'd found, and forty others, and had died in March with an appointment written in a notebook that he didn't live to keep.

"You didn't do anything wrong," I said. "I need you to hear that. You answered a question, because somebody asked it nicely and gave you a reason. As far as I can tell that's all anybody does for them."
He was quiet for a long time. The radiator ticked. Under the desk Buddy sighed, the long one.

"He asked me once," the dealer said. "The professor. Years after. Whether anyone had been in asking about him." He looked at the ledger. "I said no. Which was true, by then. They had only come the once." He put his glasses on, and took them off again. "I have thought about that answer more than I'd like, since March."
"I'm not here to ask you to do anything."
"No. I see that." He closed the ledger. "I don't believe I shall telephone again."
I'd like to say I just took that and thanked him. But I'd been plain for forty minutes and it seemed a bad moment to stop.
"If you stop, they may notice that too. You've rung that number once, ever, and the one time was me. I don't know what they do with a man who goes quiet."
"I am seventy-four and I sell books that nobody wants," he said. "Let them notice."

It was the first time I'd told anyone what their small job was for, and he'd simply stopped. He had also made himself visible on my account, an old man in a cardigan, and on the way up I hadn't given that one minute's thought. I wrote it down in the car, because it belonged in the same folder as the rest.
<hr />

He gave me something before I left. I didn't ask for it. He went into the back and came out with a file and took one sheet from it: his copy of the receipt from 2011, for the 1931 printing. The professor's name. The date. The price, which was nothing, about a tenth of what I'd paid. And in the corner, in the same neat hand, two words.
Second impression.

"He always wanted it written down, which one," the dealer said. "On everything I sold him, even where there was only the one printing. I thought it was an affectation." He almost smiled. "I'm a bookseller. I thought it was a nice affectation."
I put the receipt in the folder with page 118 and the three rows. I thanked him and meant it. Buddy needed two attempts to get up, and the dealer held the door for him, with the bell.
<hr />
Ana rang when I was on the ring road. I put her on the speaker.
"Did you buy anything?"
"You went to a bookshop two hours away and bought nothing."
"I didn't go to buy. The man who wrote to me, the careful one. I wanted to ask him something in person."
There was a pause on the line, and it wasn't a bad pause. It was the pause of someone who has just heard a straight answer where she'd expected the charming one, and is deciding what to do with it.
"And did you?"
"Is this the measuring thing?"
"It's the measuring thing."
"Okay, Mulder," she said. "Drive safe. Give Buddy a biscuit from me."
I gave Buddy a biscuit. He took it without fully waking up, which is a skill.

I drove south with the folder on the seat beside me, thicker by one sheet, and somewhere past Zwolle I passed a long straight stretch of canal road with the water flat beside it. I didn't know yet what had happened there, and I didn't slow down.

chapters.title: A pension visit, Zwolle
chapters.what: Two additions the chain needs: the visitor pours his own coffee from the flask, and he asks Henk, lightly, whether he recalls anything else. One correction: the police report no longer calls Henk widowed, since Marijke is alive. Now sits between "Groningen" and "The week it vanished". Source: v7/13.
blocks: The man from the pension fund arrived at two, which was when he had said he would arrive, and he had a folder, and he wiped his feet.

Henk Boersma had been expecting a letter and had got a person instead, which he took as a courtesy. He was seventy-three and had worked thirty-one years for the same engineering firm in Zwolle, and he had started, lately, to say things at the bowling club that made the other men look at their shoes. Things about his father. His father had been a draftsman, and had kept notebooks, and had once said something to Henk about a bridge that Henk had been turning over for sixty years and had recently started to turn over out loud.

The man from the pension fund did not know any of that, as far as Henk could tell. He knew about the indexation. He explained it twice, patiently, with a pen, and the second time Henk understood it, and the man did not make him feel stupid for needing the second time. He had a way of leaving a silence open that made you want to put something in it.

The man had brought his own coffee, in a steel flask, and apologized for it: an old habit from years of sitting in other people's kitchens, he said, he never liked to put anyone to trouble. He poured it himself, into the cap. Henk made coffee anyway, because Marijke would have, and Marijke was at her sister's in Meppel until Monday, which the man was sorry to hear, he'd have liked to meet her. He admired the house, which was a decent house and had not been admired in some years, and he asked about the photographs on the dresser, and Henk told him about the children, and about his father, more than he had meant to, and the man listened in the way that very few people listen, which is without waiting.
"And do you recall anything else?" the man said, lightly, turning the cap of the flask on the table. "Besides the bridge."
Henk thought it an odd word for a pension man. Then he thought about the question, and said that he did, a little, and told him.
At some point, and Henk could not afterward have said at what point, they were talking about cars.
<hr />

The car was a 1994 Volvo estate in a dark green that Volvo no longer made, and Henk had bought it new, and it had done three hundred and ten thousand kilometers, and he could tell you what each of them had cost. He drove it twice a week. On Tuesdays to the shops, and on Sundays, while Marijke was at church, out along the canal road toward Hasselt and back, for no reason except that the Volvo liked a straight run and so did he.

The man from the pension fund liked cars. Not in the tiresome way; in the way of someone who had grown up with a father who kept one running past its time. He asked the right questions. He knew what the overdrive did. He laughed in the right place at the story about the mechanic in Kampen. And when Henk said, as he had said to a dozen people who had not heard it, that the car would outlast him, the man said, "I believe you," in a voice that made it a compliment to the car and not a remark about Henk.

Then he looked at his watch and apologized and said he had a problem that was not Henk's problem, and Henk said what is it, and the man said that he had a box to move, that afternoon, across town, a box of files from a colleague who had retired, and that the fund's car was a small thing with no boot to speak of, and he had been going to make two trips.
Henk said take the Volvo.
The man said no, he couldn't possibly.
Henk said he was seventy-three and the car was sitting in the drive doing nothing and he would be glad of the excuse to have someone else put gas in it.

The man said, if you're sure. And he was back in forty minutes, which was less time than it would have taken, and he had put gas in it, and he had also, Henk saw when he went out to look, run it through the wash on the way back, so that it sat in the drive in the late light the color it had been in 1994.
"You didn't have to do that."
"It's a beautiful car," the man said. "It deserved it."

He left the flask. Henk noticed it on the table after the car had gone and thought, he'll be back for that, and put it by the door. The man had shaken his hand there. He said the indexation would come through in the new year and that Henk would get a letter, and that if he had any questions he should ring the number on the folder, and Henk said he would, and did not notice until a week later that the number on the folder was the general number, the one with the music.
He did not notice, because by then it did not matter.
<hr />

On the Sunday Henk Boersma drove out along the canal road toward Hasselt, as he did, with the window down, as he did, and somewhere on the long straight after the pumping station the Volvo went off the road and into the water, at no great speed, in daylight, with nobody else on the road.

The police report said the driver was elderly and had, according to acquaintances, seemed distracted of late. It noted that the car was old and well maintained. It noted the absence of skid marks, which in a man of seventy-three, on a familiar road, in good light, it did not find remarkable.
The car was recovered. There was nothing wrong with it.

The folder from the pension fund was on the passenger seat, and the water had got into it, and the woman from the fund who came to the house afterward to help Marijke with the paperwork looked at it, puzzled, and said that it wasn't theirs, and that nobody from the office had been out to Zwolle that month, and that it must have been one of those firms that go round the retired. Marijke said a man had come, a nice man, Henk had said so on the phone, he'd brought his own coffee. The flask was still by the door. Nobody came back for it, and she couldn't bring herself to throw it out, and it is there now, on the shelf above the coats, and she will tell you about it if you ask.

chapters.title: The week it vanished
chapters.what: Now the last chapter of Part One, after Groningen. The job is not erased: it is renamed, given an owner and a backdated ticket, and his own ticket is closed against it; only his screenshot shows the old name. Frank's blank, the four key-holders and the Urfa coordinates are cut; he asks Pieter one question. Source: v6/08.
blocks: Beard Man knew how the professor died, because Beard Man knows everything the way a river knows everything. It's all gone through him and none of it has stayed in order.
It was the Sunday after Groningen. I'd gone to the market with one question, which is one more than I usually bring.

"Chair," he said. He was pricing a box of Reader's Digest condensed novels that nobody on earth would buy, and he priced them anyway, lovingly, at fifty cents each. "Blue one. Daughter found him. Monday. Bin hadn't been put out, that's how she knew, he always put the bin out. Nice man. Didn't haggle."
"You met him?"

"Sold him things. Years. Particular." He held a condensed Hemingway up to the light, as if checking it for the parts they'd left out. "Wanted first printings. Not first editions, mind. Printings. Most people don't know the difference. I told him the difference once and he said he knew, thank you, and I liked him for it."
"And the daughter sold you the books."

"Curtains," said Beard Man. "She does curtains. Deventer, four streets from the station. Didn't want the books, wanted the shelves. Said he'd stopped sleeping at the end. Said he'd be up all night with them." He put the Hemingway down. "Said the last few months he kept asking her the same thing."
I waited. He let me wait. It's the only power he has and he enjoys it.
"What thing?"

"Whether she'd be all right." Fifty cents. Fifty cents. "Which is a normal thing for a dying man to ask, and I told her so, and she said no, not like that. She said he asked it like a man checking a list."
Then he was off again, mid-sentence as always, the comet, the prophet. I stood there with my hands in my pockets and didn't hear a word of it.
"Who bought the furniture?" I said, when there was a gap.
"Man in a van." Beard Man shrugged. "Good coat. Polite. Didn't haggle either. Everyone's very polite about that house."
<hr />
The week itself I have to give in order, because the order is all I've got.

Monday I looked at the job. I'd got into the habit, the way you touch your pocket for your keys. I didn't open it. I looked at its line in the list: rcl-agg, no owner, fourteen minutes past two, nine seconds. Still there, same as every morning for six weeks. My ticket was still in the queue where I'd left it, number 41790, dying quietly.
Tuesday, the same. Wednesday, the same.
Thursday morning it was gone.

Nothing in red, no failure. The line wasn't there. I searched for the name and the search came back empty, and for about a minute I was a man whose floor had been taken away. I'd watched that thing run for six weeks. I had three nights of what it sent in a folder in my bag.
Then I did the boring thing, which is the only thing I'm any good at. I stopped looking for the name and sorted the list by time.
Fourteen minutes past two. Nine seconds. Forty-one kilobytes. Same address, the one that's only there while you're sending to it.

It was called bc-recon-nightly now. It had an owner: Business Continuity Program. It had a description: Nightly continuity reconciliation. Diagnostic. Introduced during platform migration. See #41822. Every mandatory field was filled in. It looked like every other line on the list. If I'd been reading the ingredients for the first time that morning I'd have gone straight past it.
I opened my own ticket. It had been closed. Resolved: duplicate of #41822.

I looked up 41822. It existed. It was a perfectly good ticket, a dull one, registering an old diagnostic job and transferring it to continuity, and according to its date it had been raised years ago, in the last month of the migration. I worked that month. I worked most of its nights.

Tickets are numbered in the order they're born. Mine was 41790 and I'd opened it in June. So here was a ticket thirty-two numbers younger than mine and several years older. Whoever wrote it had done everything properly, and filled in every box, and typed a date into the one field that lets you, and had either not known about the number or not cared, because who checks a number.

Then the backups, because I had to. I know what I wanted to find: last month's snapshot still saying rcl-agg, a sealed room with the old name in it. It said bc-recon-nightly. They all did, as far back as they go. For a minute that frightened me more than anything else that week, until I remembered how the thing is built. The backups don't store a job's name. They store its number, and look the name up when you ask. Nobody had been into the backups. They hadn't needed to. You rename a thing once and every old copy agrees with you by itself.

I'd spent six weeks with a book where somebody reopened a plate and changed one line. This was tidier than that. Nothing had been removed. I'd asked, in writing, for an owner and a purpose for the inventory, and I'd been given an owner and a purpose, and the purpose was Pieter's sentence from the stand-up, almost word for word. Everybody agreed with me. My ticket had been answered.

The only place on earth where the old name still existed was a screenshot on my laptop from the first Thursday, which I'd taken because I screenshot things. I put the screenshot next to the list. They disagreed. And for the first time in my life I was in the one position I've never been allowed: the paper said one thing and I said the other, and I was right.
It felt like nothing. It didn't feel like winning. It felt like a cold coming on.
The last thing I checked was when. The scheduler keeps a line for the most recent change to anything, and you can't type a date into that one. Modified: Wednesday, 16:52.
<hr />
The card was on the mat when I got home. A plain postcard, in an envelope, in a hand I knew by now.

Dear Mr. Klippe. They telephoned on Tuesday, the same lady. She asked whether I had heard anything further from you since the sale. I said that I had not. I have kept a shop for forty years and I do not think I have ever lied worse. I tell you so that you are not surprised by anything. I think it best that we do not write again.
I read it standing in the hall with my coat on and Mora trying to get her nose into the envelope in case it was food.

Saturday I'd told a man what his phone call does. Tuesday they rang him, and he lied to them, badly. Wednesday at eight minutes to five the thing I'd asked about got a new name, an owner and a ticket older than itself.

I can't prove the one caused the other. I've been paid for eleven years to notice when two things move a day apart, and I've never once been allowed to call that proof. But nothing else happened that week. I hadn't asked anything at work since June. The only thing I'd done was drive to Groningen and be plain.

So that was two things I'd learned, and I didn't like how they fit. Telling works. A man had stopped doing his small job because I'd told him what it was for. And they'd noticed him stop within three days, and the bill for that was on my hall floor, in his handwriting.
I put the card in the folder. Ana asked from the kitchen who was writing to me now, and I said the bookshop, about the book, and that was nearly true.
<hr />
Friday I went to Pieter.

Not in stand-up. His office, door open, the way you'd ask about a day off. I'd decided on one question, the dullest one I had, and I'd decided not to mention the old name, because I wanted to hear which name he used.
"Quick one. The two-fourteen job, the nightly one. Who owns it now?"
There was no pause this time. That was the difference. In June he'd had to go and find his sentence. Now it was right there on top.
"Continuity," he said. And then, kindly, because he is kind, "Which is you, as of the first."

"Your new lot. It's all theirs now, that end of things. So if you've got questions about it, from the first you can ask yourself." He smiled at his own joke, and it was a decent joke. "It's a good move, James. They asked for you. People don't get asked for."
"No," I said. "I suppose they don't."
"Have a good weekend."
I had a not very good weekend.
<hr />

I told Ana I had a cold. I did have a cold, in the way that you can have one if you need one. I sat in the kitchen most of Saturday with Buddy under the table and the folder open and did the thing I'm paid to do, which is work out what a system is from what it does, without being allowed to see in.
Two options, I told the dog, because by then it was a liturgy.

One. It really was an old diagnostic job. Some conscientious soul in continuity saw my ticket, tidied the job up, gave it a proper name and an owner, filed the paperwork somebody should have filed years ago, and backdated it so the audit would look right. People do that. I've done something like that. And a bookseller in Groningen got a courtesy call about a sale, and the two things landed in the same week because weeks are short.

Two. Somebody reads the queue where tickets go to die. Somebody learned on Tuesday that a helper had been told something, and by Wednesday afternoon the thing I knew about had a boring name and a boring reason and a place on a list nobody reads. And the man who knew it by its old name was being moved, from the first, to the one team in the bank that would never need to ask about it, because they own it.

I'd been giving option one eighty-five percent since June, out of habit. That Saturday I wrote down sixty, and looked at it, and crossed it out, and didn't write anything in its place. An error doesn't fill in the mandatory fields. An error doesn't get the purpose right, in Pieter's words, six weeks after Pieter said them. I'd wanted it to be an error more than I'd admitted. That was what the week cost me, and I noticed it go.
Mora brought me the toy at some point, wet, and put it in my hand, and I threw it down the hall without thinking, and she brought it back.

Here is what I had on the table. A thin book in two dead men's handwriting, with forty-one entries and mine at eleven. A date on its last page, the second of December, four months off, with a reference I didn't know how to read and one word under it. Three rows with my number on them. A receipt, a card, and a screenshot of a name that had stopped existing on Wednesday at eight minutes to five. And a letter from HR, which had come on Friday while I was in Pieter's office, confirming my transfer to the Business Continuity Program with effect from the first of the month.
So as of the first, the job was mine. I'd be the owner. If anybody ever opened a ticket asking what it was, the ticket would come to me.
Ana came down in the evening, looked at the table, looked at me, and felt my forehead with the back of her hand like a mother.
"You don't have a cold."
"Is it the new job?"
"Partly."
"Does it come with more money?"
"I didn't ask."

"Mulder," she said. "That's the first thing you ask." She took a biscuit for Buddy from the tin and went back up, and I sat there with a pen in my hand, thinking that she was right, and that I still hadn't asked who they were.

chapters.title: Deventer, March
chapters.what: Small additions only: the professor's letter now argues, names the shelfmark and asks to consult it, and he is given the December sitting; the visitor photographs every page; the neighbor is given a card and the kind version; Beard Man sold the whole lot so that he would not have to telephone. Source: v6/09.
blocks: The old man had written to them on paper, with a stamp, to an address that was a foundation's registered office and nothing else. Two pages, in a hand that was not what it had been. Most of it was argument. The last four lines gave a shelfmark, asked to consult the item, and asked whether, before that, somebody might come and talk to him about his notebook.
So somebody came.

He parked two streets away, because he always did, and walked, because the walk told him things: the bin at the gate, not yet out; the curtains, good ones, chosen by a woman; the bicycle with a child's seat on it that belonged to a neighbor. He rang. He waited longer than a younger man would have waited. The door opened on a face that had been expecting him for a long time and had not expected him to look like this.
"You're not what I thought," the professor said.
"People say that." He wiped his feet. "May I?"

The chair was blue and the professor lowered himself into it the way you lower something you're afraid of dropping. The notebook was on the side table, closed, under the man's hand, and the man did not look at it and did not look away from it, and the professor noticed both, and smiled.
"Let me," the man said. "You sit."

He made tea in a kitchen that had a woman's handwriting on the calendar and a man's on the shopping list. He brought it through. He sat where he was told to sit, which was the chair opposite, the one with the better light on it, and he understood that he had been placed, and he let it happen, because there was no harm in it.
"I'll say what I've got," the professor said, "and you'll say nothing, and then you'll go. That's how it works, isn't it?"
"More or less."

"Forty-one," the professor said. "My grandfather found the first eleven. I found the rest. I've never published. I've never told anyone but my daughter that the book exists, and I told her it was a bibliography, which it is." His hand on the cover. "I'm not asking you to confirm anything. I'm old and I'm not sleeping and I'd like, before I stop, to have asked somebody. That's all."
The man drank his tea.

"They're all the same edit," the professor said. "Did you know that? I expect you know that. Forty-one books and it's always the same correction, in different clothes. A hand comes out. A giver goes. Early becomes first. Nobody ever adds anything. You only ever take one thing away." He was looking at the window now. "It's very disciplined. I've admired it, God help me. Thirty years I've admired it."
"You wrote us two pages of that," the man said. "Nobody answers that part. You also asked to consult an item, and you gave the shelfmark."
"A student of mine saw it on a crate. I've had it nine years."
"The answer to that part is yes. The room sits once a year. The second of December. You'd come in person and ask at the desk."
"December." The professor looked at his own hand for a while. "You people have a sense of humor."
"It's the date there is."

The professor opened the notebook at the last page, where the reference already was, and wrote the date under it, slowly, and one word under the date, and closed it and put his hand back on the cover.
"There," he said. "I wanted to have done it."
"You should rest," the man said, gently.
"Is that what you came to say?"
"I came because you asked." He put his cup down. "Nobody comes if you don't. That's the only rule I know for certain."

The professor laughed, which turned into something else, and he waited it out with his hand over his mouth, and then he said, "My daughter's going to be alright. Tell me that, at least. You can say that."
"Your daughter's going to be alright."
"You say it like you mean it."

"I do mean it." He stood. He took the two cups to the kitchen and rinsed them and left them on the rack, the way a guest does. When he came back the professor's eyes were closed and his hand was still on the notebook.

He lifted the hand, which weighed very little, and took the notebook to the window, and photographed every page, flat and square and without shadow, the way he had been taught. Then he put it back and put the hand back on it. The hand closed. He stood for a moment in the good light looking at an old man asleep in a blue chair, and then he let himself out, and pulled the door until it clicked, and walked the two streets to the car.

He made one call. "He's asked. Yes. In person. He's been given December; he won't be there. I have the pages, all of them. The original's on the side table. I'd say weeks." A pause. "I'd rather wait. A body's a fingerprint, you've said so yourself." Another pause, longer. "Understood."
Eleven days later the bin was not put out on a Monday and the daughter let herself in with her key.

He came back for the furniture in June, with a van and a man he paid in cash, because the daughter had put a card in the window and the card had been reported to him and it was cleaner to be the buyer than to be anything else. He bought the shelves and the blue chair and he did not haggle, and when he asked about the dresser she said no, that one was her mother's, she was keeping that, and he said of course, and the daughter, who had her father's hands, said she was glad the shelves were going to somebody who wanted them.
"And the books?" he said, lightly, as he had planned to say it.
"Oh, those went," she said. "Weeks ago. Man from the market. He takes anything, by the crate. I couldn't look at them."
He stood in the emptied room and let his face do nothing at all.
"Of course," he said. "That's the best thing for them."

Before he left the street he rang the bell of the neighbor with the bicycle and gave her a card with a foundation's name on it and a telephone number. The professor's papers were of some interest, he said, and the foundation was concerned for their conservation; if anybody came asking after them she would be doing the old man a kindness to ring. She asked how Hendrik had seemed to them, at the end. He said the professor had written some rather confused letters, and had not been sleeping, and that everybody had been very fond of him. She said that was just what she had thought herself.

He drove the chair and the shelves to a lock-up near Zwolle, and he went through the chair, the lining and the cushions and the frame, properly, and found nothing, and the following Sunday he went to the market in a good coat and stood in the cold at a stall where a man with a beard was talking about a comet, and he looked at the ground, where the crates were, and there were two, and they were full of Reader's Digest.
"Professor's books," he said. "Were there any left?"

"Sold the lot," Beard Man said, not unkindly, mid-sentence. "One chap. A fellow left me a number, said to ring if anyone asked after one title in particular. Nobody asked after one. He wanted all of them. I don't ring for a lot."

He thanked him. He bought a condensed Hemingway for fifty cents, because a man who buys nothing is remembered. And he went and sat in the car, and he did not call anybody for eleven minutes, and then he did.

He was not blamed. It had been a question of weeks, and he had been right to wait. His standing was confirmed at the review. He had the photographs. The only thing that changed was that the original was now in a stranger's kitchen, and he would have to find the chap who'd taken the lot, and he had always, in his way, enjoyed that part.

chapters.title: Croton, 530 BC
chapters.what: 🟡 v9 — Claude, 16 Nov 2026. [Interlude, real]. EDITED. Now told as what the source is: a contemporary rival's verse mocking Pythagoras, quoted centuries later, with no place or year in it. Three factual slips corrected (who wrote it down and when, Croton still exists, other lines of Xenophanes survive). Source: v7/16.
blocks: The date and the town are a guess. Pythagoras is thought to have moved to Croton, in the south of Italy, around 530 BC, and to have acquired a following there. The story itself gives no place and no year.

Xenophanes told it. He was a poet from Colophon, a contemporary of Pythagoras, and he was not a friend. He made fun of most things people believed, and he told this one the way you tell a story about a man you think is a showman: to make the room laugh.
Once, he says, Pythagoras was passing by when a puppy was being beaten. He took pity on it and said: Stop. Don't beat it. It is the soul of a friend of mine. I knew it when I heard it cry out.

That's the whole thing. Four lines of verse. The poem they came from is lost, and the four lines survive only because Diogenes Laertius copied them into his life of Pythagoras some seven hundred years later, as an example of what people said about the man.
Nobody knows if it happened. Nobody knows who the friend was. The puppy is not described. We aren't told whether the beating stopped.

What we know is that about two and a half thousand years ago somebody was already saying that a dog could carry a person he had loved, and that you could know it by the voice. And that the oldest mention of the idea we have was written by a man who thought it was ridiculous, and wrote it down so that everybody could see how ridiculous it was. The first time it appears, it is already a joke.

chapters.title: Frank's kitchen
chapters.what: James now arrives wanting his own evidence killed: Frank kills the screenshot, James copies Frank's two columns for his own material, and on the stairs Frank says the job is a honeypot, which Pieter told the team. Mora is under the table. The half-remembered orphan job and the closing lines about noise are cut. Source: v6/10.
blocks: Frank asked me round on a Saturday, which should have told me something, because Frank is twenty-nine and single and lives in a flat where the kitchen is also the living room and the bedroom is a mezzanine, and men like that don't ask colleagues round. They ask friends round. I'd apparently crossed a line without noticing, the way I cross most lines.
"Beer," he said, at the door. "And I need you to look at something. Properly. With the face."
"I don't have a face."
"You absolutely have a face. Pieter calls it the audit face." He looked down. "You brought the horse."

I'd brought Mora. Frank lives up three flights and Buddy doesn't do one. She went past him into the flat, found the table, got under it, and began a slow negotiation with something that had fallen there during an earlier period of Frank's life.

I'd also brought a sheet of paper, folded in my jacket, and that was the real reason I'd said yes. On Monday I was moving to continuity. The job I'd asked about in June had a new name, an owner and a ticket older than my question, and the only thing left on earth that said otherwise was a screenshot I'd taken on a Thursday without knowing why. I wanted somebody to try to kill it. Not Ana, who'd be kind. Somebody who'd enjoy it.

There was a television on with the sound down. A hearing, somewhere, men in suits behind a long table, a caption with the word phenomena in it. Frank had it on the way you have the weather on. Neither of us looked at it all evening.
<hr />
He went first. It was his kitchen.

The warm-up was flat earth, which a cousin of his had gone in for, and which took about as long as it deserves. Ships go down over the horizon hull first. The shadow on the moon in an eclipse is always round, and only one shape throws a round shadow from every side. "Also," I said, "it's four in the morning in Tokyo right now. Ring someone." He ticked something on his laptop.
The second thing was a video.

Somebody had sent it to him, somebody who sends him things, and he wanted it killed and he wanted to watch me do it, and I'll admit the persona enjoyed that. It was a montage. Dates of earthquakes against phases of the moon, with a voice over it that had learned to sound like a documentary and a graph that went up and to the right with the confidence of a man who has never had to show his working.
"Right," I said. "Pause it. Go back. The graph."
He went back.

"It's not a graph. There's no axis. It's a line somebody drew on a picture of a graph. Second thing: what's the baseline? How many earthquakes happen on days that aren't full moons? He's never going to tell you, because the answer is the same number, and if you've got no baseline you've got no correlation, you've got a list of nights that something happened, and every night something happens." I drank. "Third thing, and this is the one that matters. Look at the dates he picked. He's got fourteen. There were two hundred quakes above magnitude six in that period. He picked the fourteen that fit. That's a man with a drawer full of socks telling you every sock is blue, having thrown the red ones away first."
