Frank was grinning. "Go on."
"That's it. It's noise. It's beautiful noise, somebody spent a week on the voice, but you don't need me for it. You need a sock drawer."
"I needed to hear you say it." He killed the video. "Okay. Round three. This one's got a book."
<hr />
Round three was the one about the missing three hundred years.

You might know it. There's a theory, and it has a book, and the book has footnotes, and the footnotes are what get you, because they look like the real thing. The claim is that a stretch of the early Middle Ages never happened: that a few hundred years were inserted into the calendar by people with reasons, and that's why there's so little from that period, and that's why a certain emperor seems to have done too much in one lifetime.
"I don't believe it," Frank said. "Obviously. But I can't kill it. Every time I go to kill it the footnotes come up."
"Tree rings," I said.
"What?"

"You don't need the footnotes. Trees. There's a continuous record of tree rings going back twelve thousand years, overlapping, logs out of bogs matched to logs out of roofs matched to living oaks. Year by year. No gaps. If somebody had inserted three hundred years into the calendar, there'd be three hundred years of rings missing, and there aren't. The trees don't know what year the pope said it was." I drank. "Also the Chinese kept their own calendar and their own eclipses and never got the memo. Astronomers can run the sky backward; you can't fake where the moon was. It dies on tree rings in four minutes."
Frank looked at me for a while.
"Then why is there a documentary?"
And that's the thing about Frank. He doesn't want to be told a thing is stupid. He wants to be told why someone made a film about it.

"I don't know," I said. And then, because it was Frank's kitchen and the beer was good and I'd had a bad two weeks: "Here's what I notice, for what it's worth. A theory that dies on oak needs a footnote. Somebody gave it drone shots. When I see an explanation working harder than the mystery, I notice. When I see the ridicule working harder than the mystery, I notice that too."
"You think it's a plant."

"I think it's a sock drawer. People get shown the blue ones so that when a red one turns up they say oh, that's one of those." I shrugged. "Or a man with a book needed a second mortgage. It's usually that."
Under the table Mora sneezed, twice, at whatever she'd won.
<hr />
Then he showed me how he sleeps.

He has a list. I should have guessed; he's that kind of mind. On his laptop, a document, years old, headed Things people believe and under it two columns: Still standing and Dead. He's kept it since university. When he hears a claim he puts it in the left column, and when it dies he moves it to the right, with the date and the reason, and he's never once moved anything back.

"Everything goes in. Everything gets a trial. Crashed saucers, dead: the metal was pots and pans, there's a magazine article from 1952. The leaked government documents from the eighties, dead: wrong typewriter, the signature was traced off a letter from 1947. The man who said he'd worked on the alien craft, dead: he lied about his degrees. The water memory thing, dead: a magician was in the room when they ran it blind." He scrolled. It was a long document. "And here's what I've got for your lot. The believers. You know what the single most damaging thing is, in the whole history of it?"
"Tell me."
He turned the laptop round. A scanned page, declassified, 1953, a panel of scientists convened by people who had reasons.

"They recommended it," Frank said, with real pleasure. "The debunking. They sat in a room for four days and wrote, I'm quoting, that the subject should be stripped of its special status and its aura of mystery, through a program of, hang on, training and debunking, using mass media, psychologists, and, I love this, Disney. Walt Disney. It's not a conspiracy, James. It's a memo. Whether anyone ever ran the program is disputed, I'll give you that for free. But every time one of your forum people says they're being laughed at on purpose, somebody did once write that down as a plan, and it's the most bureaucratic thing I've ever read. That's my trump card. It's not sinister. It's a committee."
I read the page. I took my time, because I take my time, and because I'd seen something, and I wanted to make sure it was there before I said anything, and it was.
"Read the next bit," I said. "Under the part you read. Out loud."
He turned the laptop back round. He read it. He stopped halfway and read it again, and I watched his face do the thing mine does when I put a finger on the right line of page 118.
"'The burden of proof is on the sighter,'" Frank said, slowly, "'not the explainer.'"
"Yeah."
"That's the opposite of science."

"It's a rule. Written down, by scientists, in a government document. Whoever sees the thing has to prove it, and whoever explains it away doesn't. That's a committee writing a standard of proof, Frank. And you've been using it for ten years, in that list, and so have I. I'm not saying the saucers are real. I think the saucers are mostly pots and pans. I'm saying somebody wrote down the rule for how we'd be allowed to check, and then it got taught, and then everybody forgot it had been taught."
Frank didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "Huh," and moved his cursor to the left column, and I watched him not move the 1953 memo to the right.
"It's still dead," he said. "The saucers."
"I know."
"I'm not moving it."
"I'm not asking you to."
"But the memo's—" He looked at it. "The memo's not in either column, is it. The memo's the table."
I didn't say anything. He'd got there on his own, and I've learned to shut up when that happens.
<hr />
"My turn," I said, and took the sheet out of my jacket.

Two pictures of the same job list, printed one above the other. The top one from June: a job at 02:14 with a name, nine seconds, forty kilobytes, and nothing in the owner column. The bottom one from last week: same minute, same nine seconds, a different name, an owner, and a ticket dated in May.
"Kill it."
Frank looked at it for about as long as he'd looked at flat earth.
"It's a screenshot."

"I can make you a screenshot of Pieter approving my raise. Give me ten minutes and I'll make you one of Pieter in a dress." He held up a finger. "Second. Jobs get renamed. Tickets get backdated; I backdated two on Thursday, because the form won't let you close what you never opened. Third, and this is the one that matters." He was doing me, and doing it well. "Who else has the top picture?"
"Nobody."
"Then it's your picture against the system, and the system has an owner and a ticket, and you have a JPEG." He slid it back across the table. "Dead. Sorry. Is that what's been up with you?"
"It's the part I can carry in a jacket."
"Get a better part."

He was right, and I'd known he would be, which is why I'd brought it to him and not to someone who likes me more. It took him under a minute. Eleven weeks I'd been carrying that picture around like a relic, and a man with a beer had just put it in the Dead column without getting up.
"Can I borrow your method?" I said.

I turned the sheet over and drew a line down the middle. Frank's headings were no use to me; I wasn't trying to decide what was true. I wrote could show a stranger on the left and only I have seen on the right, and I filled it in with my arm round it like a boy in an exam.
Left: two printings of a 1926 book, page 118. Anyone with both copies and a ruler gets what I got. A third copy, with a dealer's receipt.
Right: the screenshot, as of four minutes ago. A capture file from work that I could show a stranger exactly once, on my last day of employment. And the thin book.

That one I looked at for a while. Forty-one entries in two hands, bought off the ground from a man who has never told me his name. Anybody could have written it. I could have written it. I'd been treating it for two months as the middle of everything, and on Frank's kitchen table, in Frank's columns, it was a notebook from a market with a story attached, and the story was mine.
"What's the thin book?" Frank said. He reads upside down too. Everyone does but me.
"A notebook. From the market."
"Whose?"
"That's the problem."
"Right column," Frank said. "Anything with from the market in it is right column. I don't make the rules." He considered. "I do make the rules."
<hr />
He walked us down. Mora took the stairs the way she takes everything.
"Was that the 02:14 thing?" he said, behind me. "On your sheet. The one from stand-up."
"You know that's a honeypot, right?"
I stopped on the stair. He was behind me and couldn't see my face, which is the only reason I let it do what it did.
"A what?"

"A trap. Security leaves a thing lying about with no owner and waits to see who pokes it. Pieter told us Thursday. You'd gone down for your new badge." He laughed. "Years it's been sitting there, apparently, and nobody ever asked. Then you poke it at stand-up in front of nine people. You're the only one who passed, mate. That's probably why continuity wanted you. I wasn't meant to say. I'm drunk."
"Pieter told you that."
"Pieter told all of us. He said not to make a thing of it."
I said goodnight. I said it normally. The persona does stairs.

It's a twenty-minute walk and I did the sum on the way, with Mora pulling toward every bin. Pieter had now described that job three ways. In June, to my face: left over from the migration. Two weeks ago: continuity's, which is you. On Thursday, to nine people, once I was out of the room: a security trap. They couldn't all be right, and the last one I could test from where I stood, because I'd read what the job sends. A security trap watches who touches the trap. It doesn't keep a row that says a man wrote to a book dealer eleven days before he touched anything. Security doesn't read my post.

So either Pieter had lied to the team, or somebody had told Pieter that and he'd passed it on. I gave the second one better odds. Pieter is a bad liar. He pauses. And honeypot is a good thing to be told: small, flattering to nobody, and it explains why you shouldn't ask.
I'd also shown a colleague that I kept a picture of the old name, and Frank repeats things on staircases. I'd known that when I took it out of my jacket.

That left the right-hand column. The thin book would stay there until somebody who wasn't me said whose it was, and I could think of one person alive who might. Beard Man had mentioned her once, in passing, between a comet and a prophet. The family kept the furniture. There was a daughter.
Mora ate something off the pavement outside the kebab place, and I let her, which tells you where my head was.

chapters.title: The math
chapters.what: James now goes to Deventer first, carries the neighbor's kind version to Els and is shown out; the bucket line to Buddy brings her back a week later with the folder. He does the arithmetic and, instead of withdrawing, posts the page-118 difference as a test with the expected reply written down first. The pretext letter, the withdrawal and the recruiter's email are cut; the folder pages, the arithmetic and breakfast are reused. PLACEHOLDER kept as recommended: "a better place" is on the preferred side. Source: v6/11.
blocks: Hendrik Maasen's address was on a letter. One of his books had a note in it from a librarian about a renewal, typed, dull, sent to his house, and he'd used it as a bookmark and left it at page sixty. So I had a street in Deventer, and on the Saturday after Frank's kitchen I put Buddy in the car and went to look at it.
I told Ana I was going to see a man about a book. That was true of most Saturdays and not of this one.

The house had a for-sale sign. Good curtains, still up. I stood at the gate for a while like the worst client a realtor ever had, and then the door of the next house opened and a woman came out to move a bicycle with a child's seat on it, and saw me, and saw the dog, and decided I was all right.
"He's not there, love. He died in March."
"I know. I'm sorry. I bought some of his books."
"Oh, the books." She said it the way you'd say the drinking. She was sixty-something and kind, properly kind, the sort who takes the bins in for the whole row. "Did Hendrik write to you as well?"
"Write to me?"

"He wrote to everybody, at the end. Libraries. Foundations. He wasn't well, you know. He wasn't sleeping, and he'd got it into his head about his books, that somebody had been changing them." She bent and let Buddy smell her hand. "The foundation were very good about it. The gentleman who came for the furniture said he'd sent them some very confused letters, and that everyone had been fond of him. They're concerned for the papers. For their conservation. He left a card, in case anyone came asking." She straightened up. "I suppose that's you. Shall I tell them you called?"

Conservation. It was the second time in a month I'd heard that word from a decent person holding a telephone number. The first one, in Groningen, had stopped ringing because I'd told him what the call was for, and I'd been pleased with myself all the way down the highway. I looked at this one. She wanted to have been a good neighbor, and she had been, and I had nothing to put in front of her but my say-so. A week earlier Frank had killed a screenshot in under a minute.
"Tell them a man with an old dog asked where the daughter's shop is," I said.

Four streets from the station. Curtains. I couldn't miss it. She said she'd ring that afternoon, and she was pleased to have something to tell them, and I thanked her. So that was my name on something again, or my dog's. I'd known it when I asked.
<hr />
Els Maasen had her father's hands. I'd never met her father and I knew it the second she put them on the counter.
Buddy went under the cutting table and lay down on an offcut of something expensive.

"I bought your father's books at the market," I said. "There was a letter in one. It's nothing, a library renewal, but it's his, so it's yours." I'd put it in an envelope and written my number on the envelope. "And I wanted to ask you about him."
"You're the one who took them." She looked at the envelope and didn't pick it up. "The man with the beard said somebody went through them spine by spine. Like Dad."
That was an opening. I had it right there. And what came out of me, warm and steady, in the voice I keep for these occasions, was:
"I'm sorry. I understand he wasn't well at the end. That he wasn't sleeping."
I watched her face shut.
"Who told you that?"
"His neighbor."

"Of course she did." She came round the counter. She wasn't angry. It would have been easier. "My father did the crossword in ink until the week he died. He was eighty-one and he could tell what you'd had for breakfast from your tie. He wasn't unwell. He was old, and he was right about something, and I don't know what. And since March every single person who has come through that door about him has been so polite. The man for the furniture. The foundation. Her next door, with a casserole. Now you." She held the door open. "Thank you for the letter."

I'd done it again. A stranger had handed me a sentence on a doorstep and I'd carried it four streets and delivered it, unchecked, in a kind voice, to the one person in Deventer who knew it was wrong. It's what I'd done at the grave. Apparently I'd learned nothing since the grave.
"Buddy. Come on."
He looked at me from under the table. He'd found the best floor in the province and he had no plans.
"Buddy."

Nothing. Els stood there holding the door. A bus went past. So I got down on one knee on a curtain-shop floor, with a woman waiting for me to leave, and said the first thing in my head, which was a piece of market nonsense I'd been told once over two crates of books.
"Listen. We all go back in the one bucket. The ones who held on come out together. That's the arrangement. So I'm not going without you, and you might as well get up."
He got up. Front legs, back legs, the grunt. We went out past her. She was looking at me oddly, and I took it for wanting me gone, and I said sorry again, which was polite, and she shut the door.
I told Ana the man hadn't had the book.
<hr />
She rang the following Sunday. Unknown number, eight in the evening, me at the sink.
"Why did you say that?"
"Who is this?"
"To the dog. In my shop. Why did you say that?"
It took me a second. "It's something a man at the market says. The one with the beard. He's got a theory about a bucket. I'm sorry, I wasn't—"

"My father said that." Her voice was very even. "Three dogs we buried in that garden. He'd stand there with the spade and say it, the same words, every time, and then he'd go in and not talk until supper. I've never heard anyone else say it in my life."
"I thought it was his. The market man's."
"Dad talked at that man every Sunday for twenty years. He must have kept some of it." A pause. "You weren't polite. You were on the floor talking to a dog. Come on Saturday. Bring him."

On Saturday she was gone ten minutes into the back, and when she returned she had a folder, cardboard, the kind with an elastic band, and she held it the way you hold something you've decided to be rid of.

"The furniture went to a man with a van. I kept the dresser. Mum's." She put the folder on the counter. "This was in the bottom drawer, under the lining paper. I found it in May. I've looked at it maybe four times. I don't know what it is and I don't want it in the house and I can't throw it away, because he hid it, and he never hid anything." She pushed it an inch toward me. "You seem like someone who checks things."
"Then check it. And don't tell me."
Buddy was under the cutting table again. She'd put the offcut down for him before we arrived.
<hr />

Three pages. Photocopies of photocopies; you could see the gray ghost of a staple in the corner, copied along with the text, three generations deep. The top of the first page said, in a typeface nobody had ever chosen:
PREFERRED FORMULATIONS. Fourth revision. For internal circulation to readers at level 2 and above.
Below that, two columns. Deprecated on the left. Preferred on the right.
I read it standing at my own kitchen table with my coat still on and the dogs waiting to be let out.

Deprecated: was given to. Preferred: arose among. Deprecated: taught by. Preferred: developed by. Deprecated: the earlier peoples. Preferred: the first peoples. Deprecated: brought. Preferred: discovered. Deprecated: shared. Preferred: coincident. Deprecated: remembered. Preferred: imagined.

Thirty-odd pairs, and every pair did what I'd found on the kitchen floor with a wet rope on my chest: it took the hand out. Nothing was ever added. Nothing was ever denied. If you read the right-hand column on its own it was perfectly respectable. It was how every careful scholar I'd ever read already wrote. Nobody had told a lie. They'd written a house style, for the house that decides what careful sounds like.
The last row on the page sat a little apart from the others, under the word Consolation. The right-hand side said: a better place.
The left-hand side had no words in it at all. It had a reference. Letters, a dash, numbers.

I sat down then, in my coat. I'd said that phrase at a grave in the spring, or one of its cousins, in a warm voice, along with sixty other people. And I knew the reference. I got the thin book out and opened it at the last page and put it beside the photocopy, and it was the same one, character for character. Whatever people used to say before they said a better place, somebody had thought it safer not to type it even on a page for level 2 and above. They'd filed it and given the shelf. And Hendrik Maasen had written that shelf on the last page of his notebook, with a date and the word Ask.

The second page was about dates. Where a date is contested, prefer the later. Where a sequence is contested, prefer the one in which the simpler precedes the more complex. Each with a line of justification that sounded like every methods section I'd ever skimmed.
The third page had a heading.
WHEN A READER NOTICES.

Four paragraphs. The first said that a reader who notices a change between printings is to be treated as a bibliographical inquiry and answered as such: courteously, fully, with reference to the ordinary practice of the trade. The second said that a reader who persists is to be offered the opportunity to publish, in an appropriate venue, with an appropriate framing. The third said that a reader who persists after publication is to be reviewed.
The fourth paragraph was two lines long.
In no case is a reader to be contradicted. Contradiction confirms. The preferred response to a correct reader is agreement, followed by reclassification.

I read that one four times. Then I let the dogs out, because they'd been very patient, and stood in the garden in my coat watching Mora try to eat a leaf, and thought about Pieter in June, in his nice voice. They asked for the person who reads things. I'd been agreed with at stand-up and reclassified by the first of the month.
<hr />
The math came the way everything comes to me, slowly, at a kitchen table, while I was trying to do something else.

Page one said level 2 and above. So there's a level one. So there are levels. And a document doesn't get a fourth revision unless it's been used, by enough people for enough years to wear out the first three. I've written fourth revisions. They're what happens when a thing is boring and necessary and has been for a decade.
So: how many people?

I'm not a statistician. I'm a man who counts breaths. I started with the ones I'd actually met. A dealer in Groningen with a telephone number. A neighbor in Deventer with a telephone number. A manager who told nine people a job was a trap, and nine people who believed him. Somebody who could rename a job. Somebody who could date a ticket in May.

None of them knew each other. That part I'd expected. What took me longer, and it's the only clever thing I worked out that month, was that they hadn't been told the same thing. The dealer and the neighbor got conservation, because you tell people who like old paper about old paper. Frank got honeypot, because you tell an engineer about security. Each reason was small, and true enough, and each one explained why you needn't ask anything further. Nobody in that list would need to know what the others were for. Nobody would even need to know there were others.

You couldn't do it with a cabal. A cabal can't keep a secret in a town. You'd do it with a handful of people who know and a great many who've each been given one task and one reason. In a company of five thousand you'd want somebody for the tickets, somebody for the job, somebody to tell a manager what to say. Call it ten, to be safe. One in five hundred.

In a town this size that's a hundred and sixty people, and most of them were asked to do one small thing once by somebody pleasant, and did it, and have never thought of it since. The woman with the bicycle is one. She took the bins in for him.

I could feel what the number wanted from me. It wanted me in a submarine. Stop ringing my mother, skip the beer after work, give Beard Man short answers, and treat everyone on the surface as possibly the man with the van. I got as far as not answering one text from Frank. But going quiet isn't a check. It's just being frightened with a reason, and page three had handed me something I could actually test.
<hr />
The thing with Ana happened over breakfast on the Monday, and it was my fault.
"You were up at four," she said. Not a question.
"The payments thing."
She buttered toast. She's a careful butterer, corner to corner, and she did the whole slice before she said anything else.
"The payments thing finished in June. You told me. You said good catch in a voice and did the thing with your hands."
I didn't say anything. There wasn't anything.

"I don't mind that you're up at four," Ana said. "I mind that you've started having a thing you tell me and a thing you don't. I can see the join. I've always been able to see the join, that's the entire reason you married me, you said so, on the third date, you said you're the only person who's ever caught me." She put the knife down. "So. Caught. What's the four o'clock thing?"

And I had enough by then. I could have put the three pages on the table and the thin book next to them and said: I think somebody keeps the wording of things, and I think they've noticed me. She'd have said okay, Mulder and asked a hundred questions, and whatever came after would have come with two of us in it.
"Reading," I said.

She looked at me for a long moment. Then she picked up her toast and ate it, corner to corner, and went to work, and didn't kiss the top of my head. She was quiet for a day. One day. She was perfectly nice the whole time, and by the evening I'd have paid anything to be shouted at.
One in five hundred. And the only person I was certain wasn't in, I'd just put on the outside.
<hr />

That night I set up the test the way I'd set one up at work. When you want to know what a system does with a certain kind of input, you send it that input, and you write down what you expect before you look.

So I wrote it in the Record first, with the date. If page three was real, the answer would be courteous and full. It would refer to the ordinary practice of the trade. It would agree with me, and it would not contradict a single word. If instead I got two people saying interesting and a third calling me an idiot, then Hendrik Maasen had hidden a joke under his wife's lining paper, and I could go back to golf.
Then I opened the forum, under the name they already had, and posted the plain version. This time it was a question about a sentence, with nobody dead in it.

Has anyone compared the two impressions of this 1926 survey, p. 118? First impression: "transmitted to the early." Second, 1931: "arisen among the first." Two typos and a plate flaw are uncorrected in both. Photographs attached.

Dry as toast. Buddy was asleep on my foot under the table. I knew it would be on a list by a quarter past two, with my number beside it and a two-word reason, and for once I'd picked the two words myself.
I pressed the button and went to bed.

chapters.title: The corporate day
chapters.what: Added: Pieter hands James a wellbeing referral in the car park with the reason already typed, James signs it on the hood and keeps the copy, Julian sees, James asks who decides who gets a seat, and that evening the polite reply to his post arrives matching page three. "From the spring" is now June. The passage where Ana already knows forty percent is cut, because she is not told until later. Source: v7/19.
blocks: The bank has a golf day, which it has never once had.

I need to explain that, because it's the kind of sentence that gets you a look. Every spring an email goes round about the golf day. Every spring there's a form, and a date, and a course an hour away with a name like a retirement home, and every spring, two weeks before, a second email goes round saying that in light of the current environment the golf day has been postponed, and nobody is surprised, because the current environment is always in light of something. I've worked there eleven years. I've filled in the form eleven times. I don't know why. I think it's the same reason people buy lottery tickets, which is that filling in the form is the enjoyable part and you'd rather not have it taken from you by realism.
This year they postponed it to September, and then nobody postponed it again.

I found out on a Thursday, when a calendar invitation arrived with a tee time on it, an actual tee time, 09:40, and a note from the organizer saying I was in a three-ball and to please confirm my handicap. I sat at my desk and read it twice. Then I got up and went to the window and looked out at the car park for a while, the way you do when something good has happened and you don't want anyone to see your face.

It had been eleven days since Els's folder and nine since I'd posted page 118. Three people had looked at it. Nobody had answered. I'd started checking the thread the way Mora checks an empty bowl, often and with the same result. I wanted one day in which the only document was a scorecard, which makes no claims about anything except how badly you played.
I confirmed my handicap. I rounded it down, which is a lie, but a traditional one.
<hr />

The course was an hour north, flat and windy, the kind of Dutch course that's a polder with ambitions. Buddy wasn't allowed, which I'd known and had still, on the morning, half thought about arguing. Ana walked me to the car with Mora at her heel and said, "Try to speak to a human," and I said I'd try, and she said, "A human, James, not a man who wants to tell you about his new wedges," and I said that was a very narrow definition of human, and she kissed me and said go.

Pieter was in the car park when I pulled in. He was wearing golf clothes he had clearly bought that week, all of them, in one shop. He waited for me to get out, and then he came over holding a plastic sleeve the way you'd hold a dish that belongs to someone else.
"I was going to do this Monday," he said. "Then I thought, not in the office."
It was a form. Wellbeing referral (line manager). My name, my employee number, and a box headed Reason for referral, which had been typed:
Recent bereavement (family). Disturbed sleep. Preoccupation with historical documents.
Under that, a line for the employee to sign.

"You don't have to see anyone," Pieter said. "Nobody rings you. It goes in the file, and then if you want a quieter quarter there's a reason for it on paper. That's how they explained it to me. It's a kindness, James. It's meant as one."
"Who wrote the reason?"
"It came like that. They usually do."
"I've never told anyone at work what I read."
Pieter looked at his new shoes. "You've seemed tired. Since the spring. People notice." Which wasn't an answer to what I'd said, and he knew it, and I let him have it.

Bereavement, fine. I'd taken a day for the funeral. Sleep, Ana could have told them, and nobody else. But at the bank I'm a man who plays golf badly and asks dull questions. The only places on earth that knew about the books were a dealer's telephone, a neighbor's telephone, a forum, and a list that went out at 02:14.

I'd read the sentence eleven days before, standing in my coat. The preferred response to a correct reader is agreement, followed by reclassification. Here was the second half, in a plastic sleeve, with a line for my signature.

At work, when a vendor sends you a diagnosis you think is wrong, you don't argue with the diagnosis. You sign for receipt and you keep your copy, because the diagnosis tells you what they can see. Also, a man who refuses a kind form in a car park is a man with something to protect, and they'd write that down too.
"Is there a copy for me?"
"The yellow one."

I signed it on the hood of the car, with Pieter's pen. The hood was still warm. He said, "Good man," with more relief than the occasion needed, and tore off the yellow sheet for me, and went to find his three-ball.
So that's in my file. A form that says I'm a grieving man with a hobby, signed by me. Anything I raised at work from then on would be read through it, and I knew that when I picked up the pen.

Across the car park a man was standing at the open trunk of something German, pulling on a glove, looking our way. I didn't know him at that distance. I folded the yellow sheet into my back pocket and went to play golf.
<hr />

I was in a three-ball with two men from Treasury. I'd never met them. I knew within forty seconds that I wasn't going to meet them now either, because the first thing one of them said, as the cart girl went past with the drinks, was something about her that I'm not going to write down, and the second one laughed, and they both looked at me to see if I'd laugh too, and I did the thing I do, which is smile in a way that could be read either way and look at my glove.

Fine. I've played with worse. You play your own ball. I teed off, badly, and walked after it, and the Treasury men talked to each other about a boat, and the wind came across the flat land with nothing to stop it, and for about six holes I had a form in my pocket and didn't think about it.
Then I saw him on the practice green.

It was Julian. The stranger the starter had paired me with on a Wednesday in June, the one with the swing I'd have paid for, who'd asked about Buddy before he asked my name. We'd played most Wednesdays since. I'd told Ana about him, which I never do; she'd said, "You've made a friend," in the voice she uses for the dogs when they've done something clever.

He was in a company polo, putting, with a vendor's lanyard round his neck, the blue ones they give the sponsors. He looked up as my three-ball came past on the way to the seventh. He saw me, and his face lit up.
"James!"
He came over. He shook my hand with both of his. He asked after the dogs, by name, both of them, and I felt the Treasury men behind me recalibrating something.
"What are you doing here?"

"Working, I'm afraid." He lifted the lanyard like it was a joke. "I told you I was in continuity. I didn't say whose. I sell you people your seats. If your building burns down on a Tuesday, where do you all sit on Wednesday. I talk to people like your head of risk about things that will never happen until they do. It's a living. The golf's the only good part."
I said he'd never mentioned it was us. He said I'd never asked, and that he'd found the less you said about continuity the more people trusted you to provide it. Everyone laughed. I laughed.

He knew the organizer, it turned out. When I came off the ninth the three-ball had been rearranged, the Treasury men paired off with each other and a sponsor, and I was walking to the tenth tee with Julian, whose surname I didn't catch that day because he said it the way people say surnames they expect you to forget.
<hr />
The back nine was the best golf I've ever played. I'd like to say that was the company and it probably was.

He was good, properly good, and generous with it the way good players sometimes are and usually aren't. He didn't give me tips. He watched me hit a seven iron thin into a bunker and said, "I'd have done exactly the same," which was a lie and a kindness in the same breath. He talked about nothing. The wind. A client in Antwerp who'd insisted on a recovery site with a view.
"You were doing paperwork on a hood," he said, on the eleventh. "On a golf day. I nearly came over and confiscated it."
"A wellbeing form."
"Ah. They gave me one of those once." He lined up a putt. "Sign everything, is my advice. It's the ones who won't sign that people worry about." He holed it.

On the twelfth I asked him my one question of the day. I was on the continuity program now, as of the first, and I'd been reading its lists for a month, and there was a thing I hadn't found in any of them.
"The seats. Who decides who gets one?"

"The client." He didn't look up from his ball. "You tell us how many, we make sure there's a desk and a phone and a sandwich. We count chairs, James. Who sits in them is your lot's business, thank God."
It was a dull answer, and I wrote it on the scorecard anyway, next to my six.
At the fourteenth he asked about Ana.

Not how's the wife. He asked how she was doing, since her grandmother. He remembered. I'd mentioned it once, in June, on a tee box, in the half-sentence you give a stranger, and he'd kept it, and here it was, three months later, offered back to me carefully like something I'd lent him.

I told him more than I'd told anyone. Not about the book; I had enough sense left for that. About Ana. About how the grief had changed shape, from a thing that lived with us to a thing that visited, and about the knitting she hadn't finished, and about how I'd been bad at it, at the funeral, at saying the thing people say. He listened. He didn't fill the silences. And when I was done he said, "You're hard on yourself, James. Most people never notice they're lying at a funeral. You noticed and it's still bothering you in September. I wouldn't call that a defect."
I three-putted the fourteenth. I didn't care.
<hr />

There was a dinner afterward, in the clubhouse, the kind with a raffle. I didn't stay for it and neither did he; he had another client, he said, the glamorous life. We stood in the car park in the last of the light with the wind dropping and he said we should play here again, properly, not at a corporate thing, and I said yes before he'd finished the sentence.
"Bring the old boy," he said. "Buddy. He can ride in the cart."
I said he'd like that.

"And James." He had his car keys in his hand and he turned them over once. "If work's ever not fine. You've got my other number now." He nodded at my phone, where he'd put it, on the thirteenth, while I was looking for a ball.
He drove off in something German and quiet. I stood there a while longer than I needed to.
Ana rang while I was still in the car park.
"Did you speak to a human?"
"I did."
"A real one?"
"Julian. He was there. It turns out it's us he sells to. Disaster planning. He asked after you. He remembered about your grandmother."
There was a pause.
"That's nice," Ana said, and it was, and it was also the voice she uses when she's filing something. "Was he nice?"
"He was great. I played the best back nine of my life."
"Then I'm glad." Mora barked in the background at something only Mora could see. "Come home. Buddy's been at the window since four."
I didn't tell her about the form. I had it in my back pocket the whole call.
<hr />

The answer came that evening. I was at the kitchen table with the laptop, Buddy on my feet, and I checked the thread the way I'd checked it for nine days, and there it was. A username I didn't know. The account was a week old.

It was a lovely reply. It was long and polite and it knew a great deal. Variants of this kind were common, it said. The author had very likely revised the sentence himself before his departure. The Leiden houses of the period had been notoriously casual about recording such things, as was the ordinary practice of the trade. It thanked me for the care I'd taken over the photographs. It agreed with every word I'd written, and nothing in it contradicted me.

I got the folder out and put page three beside the screen, and went through the first paragraph with a finger. Courteously. Yes. Fully. Four hundred words. With reference to the ordinary practice of the trade. He'd used the actual phrase. Then I opened the Record and looked at what I'd written before I posted. Three out of three.

I took the yellow sheet out of my pocket and laid it next to the photocopy. Paragraph one had arrived at nine in the evening from a stranger. Paragraph four had arrived at nine in the morning from my manager, in a plastic sleeve. Whoever they were, they'd answered me twice in one day, kindly, and one of the answers had my signature on it.

So I decided something, at that table, and it seemed sensible at the time. The form said I was tired. Fine. From Monday I'd be tired. No tickets, no questions at stand-up, nothing in a queue with my name on it. I'd be quiet at work and read what they sent me.
I wrote the stranger a short thank-you, because that's what a bibliographical inquiry does.

chapters.title: A car park
chapters.what: The handler now reports that the subject signed the form and stopped asking; the review moves once, from the spring to the end of the year (the first of only two moves in the book). The handler's name, "the second time", the style guide in the voice's list and the newly bought flask are removed so the chapter agrees with the rest. Source: v6/13.
blocks: He took the call in the car, in the long-stay car park behind the station, because the car park had no cameras on the third level and because he had always preferred to be told things while looking at concrete.
"He's signed," the voice said.
"Yes. On the hood of his car. I watched him do it. He asked for his copy."
"And since?"

"Eighteen holes. One question, who decides who gets a seat. I said the client." He watched a woman two rows over fail to reverse into a space, and then succeed. "He's easy. He wants a friend and doesn't know it, which is the best kind. He's left the job alone. No tickets, nothing at his stand-up. He's stopped asking."
"He's stopped asking at work."
"He's stopped asking."

A silence with paper in it. He knew the silence. It was the sound of a sentence being weighed, and he had chosen the sentence carefully, and he had chosen it to be light, and he waited to see whether the lightness would hold.

"You said stopped asking," the voice said. "I've got a ticket we had to close for him, a screenshot we can't account for, a letter to a dealer, and a dealer who no longer telephones. I've got a neighbor who rang in a visit to the daughter. I've got a question on a public board that had its answer last night, and he said thank you. I've got a reading on the index that moved the week he found the notebook and hasn't come back down. That's not a man who's stopped asking. That's a man who's stopped asking out loud."
"He signed a form that says he's tired."
"He kept the copy. You told me so yourself. That's worse. You know that's worse." A pen, somewhere, on a desk he'd never seen. "I'm going to put the review at the end of the year."
"It was the spring."

"It was. And now I've got a reader who signs what he's given and goes quiet, and a handler who tells me that's good news. I didn't bring it forward. You did. Every time you make him smaller than he is, I have to make the date nearer than it was. That's the arithmetic. You've always known the arithmetic."
He didn't say anything. The woman two rows over got out of her car and looked at how she'd parked it and got back in.
"How near are you?" the voice said.
"Near enough to know what he loves."
"Which is?"
"The old dog. The wife. Being right about a thing nobody else checked." He considered. "In that order, I think. He'd say the wife. It's the dog."
"Good. Then stay there. And don't tell me he's stopped. Tell me what he's doing. I'd rather hear it from you than read it off the index."
"Understood."

The line went. He sat for a while with the phone in his lap and the concrete in front of him and did the arithmetic the voice had said he'd always known, which was that a date had just moved three months because of a verb, and that the verb had been his.

He had, in his coat pocket, a flask. He'd bought it in June, the day after he'd said he was a flask man, because until then he had never owned one, and he'd found that he wanted the sentence to have been true when he said it.

He put the phone in the glovebox. He drove to the lock-up near Zwolle and sat in the blue chair for twenty minutes without turning the light on. Then he drove home, and fed a cat that was not his, that belonged to the flat, that came with the flat, the way the flat came with the name on the bell.
The review was moved to the end of the year. The index was read on Monday. It was up.

chapters.title: Leiden
chapters.what: New opening: James posts the reply beside page three, Noor writes to make him take it down, and he deletes his own evidence before she gives an address. In her kitchen she now says why the plain version is the one removed, gives the professor's rule, hides a cold hand, and tells him to find the money and that the reference is a depot shelfmark. The French report is cut to a paraphrase; Verhoef's grandson is no longer a named person; the closing lines are cut. Source: v6/14.
blocks: I thanked the stranger on Wednesday night. On Friday I did the next thing, which is what I'd do at work with any message I'd seen twice: I put the two copies side by side and asked who else had received it.

Under his reply, in the same thread, I posted two photographs. On the left, his first paragraph. On the right, the first paragraph of page three, cropped, with the heading left on: WHEN A READER NOTICES. And one line from me. Has anyone else had an answer in these words? The right-hand image is from a photocopy, date unknown.

I should say what that name was. For twelve years, under a handle that was a joke only I understood, I'd posted did-you-knows. The light kind. The steam engine. The calendar. A door ten meters up a wall. Never a theory. A man standing at the edge of the strange and dark corner with his hands in his pockets, saying huh, look at that, and leaving. A few hundred people followed it. Ana knew about it and thought it was sweet.

By Saturday morning forty people had looked at the two photographs and nobody had said a word. At noon there was a private message, from an account that had been registered nine years and had never posted. I checked that before I read it twice.

Take that down. Today, before tonight. You have put their own page on a public board under a name they can match to a house, and people who do that get visited. I was Hendrik Maasen's last student. He showed me that page on a photocopy in 2009. Take it down and I will tell you where I am.

I looked at the post for a long time. It was the only thing I'd ever made that sat in Frank's left-hand column: two documents that shouldn't match, matching, in public, with a date on it. Without it I had a polite reply to a dull question and a folder from a curtain shop.
Also, Els had said don't tell me, and I'd had her father's hidden page on the internet for a day. I hadn't told her. I'm not sure that's better.
I deleted it. I took a screenshot first, and then remembered what Frank thinks of screenshots. Then I wrote back: Done.
Four minutes later, an address in Leiden. Next Saturday, two o'clock. Drive. If you have a dog, bring it. People with dogs look like nothing.
<hr />
Her name was Noor Haverkamp, and she lived in Leiden, which is where the plates were.

She had been Hendrik Maasen's last doctoral student. She'd left the university in 2017, when the library's special collections were "restructured" under a digitization grant, which is a sentence that sounds like nothing and that she said in a tone I recognized, the tone I use for the word migration. Now she repaired paper for a living. Freelance.
Her kitchen was small and the table was covered in a sheet of glass, and under the glass, I understood after a while, was a page from something four hundred years old that she was keeping flat.
"Don't put your coffee on it."
"Wouldn't dream of it."
"Everyone dreams of it. It's a table." She looked at Buddy, who had come up her stairs one at a time with me behind him like a man moving a piano. "Is he clean?"

"Then he goes under." He went under, and lay down with his chin on her foot, and she let him. She was fifty, maybe, gray at the front, with the hands of a person who does one thing extremely carefully all day. "You want to know if you're mad."
"I want to know who else has seen that page."

"Better. Me. Hendrik. Whoever typed it. And as of yesterday week, forty people on a forum, thanks to you." She pulled a folder across the glass and didn't open it. "He showed it to me once, in his office, with the door shut. He said, Noor, if you ever see this phrasing in the wild, assume the person is not a scholar. Then he never mentioned it again, and I thought he'd gone a bit strange. Then they restructured the collections, and I understood what strange was for." She looked at me. "The man who answered you used the first paragraph nearly word for word. It's a template. They don't even change it."
"Why would they?"
"Exactly. Nobody has ever noticed it twice."
<hr />

I'd brought the thin book. She put on gloves to touch it, which told me more about her than anything she'd said, and she went through it the way I'd have gone through it if I'd been a better man, slowly. She stopped where I'd stopped, at eleven. Then she stopped at twenty-six.
"You've looked this one up."
"It's not a book."

"No." Entry twenty-six was a paper. Verhoef, A. Utrecht, 1993. Withdrawn before publication. Reclassified: instrumentation. And then, in the professor's hand, the only entry in the list with a note on it: two rooms, 40 m, correlated. Copy from the family, 2015. Same edit: "shared" → "coincident."

"Somebody in the family kept the original," Noor said, "with the word shared in it. The version in the department's archive says coincident. They couldn't see why anyone would have bothered. Hendrik could." She turned the page with one gloved finger. "It's the only entry that isn't about the past. Everything else is a hand being taken out of a story about the beginning. This one's a hand being taken out of last Tuesday. Two people in two rooms, and something went between them."
"That pair's in the folder. Shared, coincident. Page one."
"Then the page is newer than 1993, or the paper was the reason for the pair. I've wondered." She almost smiled. "He'd have liked you. You read the list."

I asked her the thing I'd been stuck on since the kitchen floor. "Why bother? Go into any bookshop. There's a whole wall of it. Gods who came down and taught farming. Lost civilizations. The hand's on every cover, in gold. Why spend ninety years taking it out of a book about flood legends that nobody reads?"

"Because of the wall." She had a paperback on the glass, French, tabbed near the back, and she pushed it toward me without opening it. "That's a report by a private committee, 1999. Retired officers, engineers. It was sold in a magazine. One chapter is a thought experiment: if you were the ones visiting, how would you manage a population like us? Texts, they suggest. Films. Sects. It's been on sale for a quarter of a century and nobody has touched a word of it, because look where it's shelved. With the crystals." She took her hand off it. "It's in every bookshop, James. That's where it's allowed to be. Loud, and silly, and next to a book about angels. What they remove is the plain version. The dull book by the careful man. The one you'd believe."
"They don't stop you talking."
"They stop you being heard. And if they can't, there's a word for what happens next, and it's from a budget meeting."
"Reviewed."

"So you've read page three properly." She closed the thin book. "Hendrik had a rule. He gave it to me the week I left, in these words, and I've kept it nine years. I'm fairly sure I'm already being watched. Until we're a hundred percent, never publish, never ask, always hide. If anything happens to me, know I was right." She took the gloves off. "I have never published a word of this. Not a footnote. I repair paper, and my mother's in a home I can pay for, and nobody has ever come to my door. I broke the rule last Saturday to write to you, because yours was the kind of post that gets a door knocked on, and it had his page in it."

I knew what my visit might be worth to somebody. A neighbor in Deventer had rung me in a month before. If anyone was keeping track of where the man with the old dog went, I'd just parked outside her house. I'd known that when I rang the bell.
<hr />
Before I left she opened the thin book again, at the back.

She read the last page. The reference, the date, and the word Ask in her supervisor's hand. She didn't say anything. She sat back, and she put her right hand under her left arm, flat, tucked in, the way you'd carry a newspaper. It was a warm kitchen.
So I asked the dull question. "Is your hand cold?"
She looked down at it as if it were somebody else's.
"Hendrik asked me that," she said.
That was all I got. She took the hand out and pointed at the page with it.

"That's a depot shelfmark. When they took the collections apart, everything went to the foundation's depot. I packed crates for three weeks. I wrote that one on a lid myself, and I told Hendrik, which I shouldn't have." She tapped the date. "It's a shed in a business park, out east. There's a reading room, and it sits once a year. I've never been let in. The ground floor is rented to a bank, for emergencies. Desks, in case their own building burns down."

I didn't say anything. I'd been a month on a program whose whole purpose was desks in case the building burned down, and there was a welcome pack in my drawer with an address in it that I'd had no reason to read twice.

"And find the money," Noor said. "Hendrik never looked. He thought money was vulgar. But paper doesn't pay for itself. Somebody pays for that shed, and the grant that emptied my library, and whoever answers forum posts for a living. You work in a bank."
<hr />
I asked her the math on the way out, standing in her hall with Buddy sitting on my foot. She was the only person I'd met who could take it.
"One in five hundred," I said. "That's what I get. One in five hundred people has been asked to do one small thing, once, and been given a reason."
"That sounds low."

"You're counting the wrong column." She had her hand on the door. "You've worked out how many it takes to run it. Fine. Now do the other number. How many have noticed? In a hundred years? Hendrik. His grandfather. Whoever kept that paper in Utrecht. Me. You. That's five I can name without trying, and I'm a woman who repairs paper in Leiden." She opened the door. The street was wet and ordinary. "And then ask yourself why there's a list of forty-one books and not a list of the people. Whether nobody made one, or somebody did."
"Somebody did," I said. "It goes out at a quarter past two every night."
She looked at me for a moment.
"Then you know something Hendrik didn't," she said. "Don't write to me again." And she shut the door, kindly.

I did the other column in the car, on the back of a parking ticket, with Buddy breathing on my neck. It wasn't low. It came out about the same as the first: for every person who'd been asked to do one small thing, there was roughly one who'd noticed something small and kept quiet. The list at work only had the ones who'd said so.

On Monday I took the welcome pack out of my drawer. Recovery site. An address in a business park, east of the ring road. Landlord, a foundation. And a line I'd skimmed in my first week because it had my name in it and nothing else of interest: the annual test was on Thursday the fifteenth, by bus, and I was on the list.

chapters.title: Mexico City, 1994
chapters.what: 🟡 v9 — Claude, 16 Nov 2026. [Interlude, real]. NEW. Facts only about Jacobo Grinberg, his two-rooms experiment and his disappearance, with the note that the result was never solidly replicated and one sentence in which the narrator declines to connect his disappearance to anything else in the book. Source: NEW (entry 5.8; THE BOOK v8.2; REVIEW 01, 4.3).
blocks: Jacobo Grinberg-Zylberbaum was born in Mexico City on the twelfth of December, 1946. When he was twelve his mother died of a brain tumor, and people who knew him have said that this is where his interest in the brain began.

He read psychology at the National Autonomous University of Mexico. He went to New York for his doctorate and spent it measuring the electrical activity of brains, which is done by fixing electrodes to a scalp and recording what comes off it. Then he went home. He set up a laboratory, and later ran one at the university's faculty of psychology, and in 1987 he founded an institute for the study of consciousness.

He was not a marginal man. He taught, he supervised students, he published in journals of neuroscience. He also wrote more than fifty books, and many of them were about things his colleagues would not have put in a grant application. He spent years with Mexican shamans and healers and wrote down what he saw. The best known was a woman called Pachita, who worked in Mexico City and performed what her patients described as operations, with a hunting knife. Grinberg sat in on them. He did not claim to understand what he had seen. He said he had seen it.

Out of all this he built a theory. He called it syntergic theory. In outline it says that what we experience is produced where the activity of a brain meets a structure in space itself, which he called the lattice, and that one brain's activity can therefore affect another's without anything passing between them in the ordinary way. It is not an accepted theory. He knew that, and he thought the way to change it was to measure something.
So he designed an experiment.

Two people sat together in a room and meditated for twenty minutes, with the instruction to feel each other's presence. Then they were separated. Each went into a chamber shielded against electromagnetic signals, and the chambers were fourteen and a half meters apart. Both were wired to record brain activity. One of them was shown a series of a hundred flashes of light. The other was shown nothing and was not told when the flashes came.

A flash of light produces a recognizable response in the brain of the person who sees it. Grinberg reported that in about one case in four a response of similar shape appeared, at the same moments, in the brain of the person who had seen nothing. He called it a transferred potential. He reported that it did not appear in pairs who had not sat together first.
The paper was published in 1994, in a journal called Physics Essays, with three co-authors. One of them was a physicist at the University of Oregon. The title mentions Einstein.

It should be said plainly what happened to the result. Other laboratories have tried versions of the experiment since. A few have reported something like it. None has produced a replication that the field accepts, and most scientists who know of the work consider it unconfirmed. That is where it stands.
Grinberg was last seen on the eighth of December, 1994, four days before his forty-eighth birthday. A party had been planned. He did not come to it.

He was a man who traveled, sometimes without telling anyone, and it was a long time before his family treated his absence as a disappearance. When the police did investigate, they found no body and no trace of where he had gone. Nobody has ever been charged with anything. Several explanations have been offered over the years, some ordinary and some not, and none of them has been established.
His books are still read in Mexico. In 2020 a documentary was made about him. It does not say where he is.

I am not going to connect him to anything else in these pages: I don't know what happened to Jacobo Grinberg, nobody who has written about him knows either, and he is a real man with a real family who are still waiting to be told.
He has not been found. He would be eighty this December.

chapters.title: The drill
chapters.what: James now goes to the drill wanting to see the building, and does one thing there: he counts, finds nine named desks with no person, and writes the names down. He matches the shelfmark format through the shut glass door, asks the site manager who is upstairs ("Heritage"), and Julian waves at the right window. The Saturday scene where he only later connects the format is cut, since Noor has already told him. Source: v7/23.
blocks: The continuity program tests itself once a year, on a bus.

I'd been on the program six weeks by then. Pieter had announced it in his nice voice, the way you'd tell someone they'd been upgraded: they asked for the person who reads things. A woman called Saskia had walked me through a lobby telling me to notice everything, and I'd noticed that she said it like a line she'd been given, and I'd noticed that my badge, when I touched it to the reader on the new floor, made a different sound. Higher. One note up. I don't know who tunes those things, but somebody does, and somebody had decided I was a semitone more important than I'd been on the Friday.

Continuity is the department that plans for the building not being there. Floods, fire, the thing nobody says out loud. If the bank can't open its doors on a Tuesday, continuity knows where everyone sits on Wednesday. It's a department made entirely of lists.

The test works like this. Forty named staff, chosen in advance, get on a bus at seven in the morning and are driven to the recovery site, and they sit at desks that have their names on them, and they log in, and they pretend the building has burned down, and at four o'clock they get back on the bus. It's called a drill. I was on the sheet. Number forty, the last name on it. Pieter was twelve.

I'd have gone without being told. Since Leiden I'd wanted to see that building, and here was the bank offering to drive me there and give me lunch. I had a card in my shirt pocket with the reference from the last page of the thin book copied onto it, letters, dash, numbers, in case I got near anything to hold it up to.
<hr />

The bus went east, out past the ring road and into the flat country where the business parks are, the kind of landscape that's nothing but sheds with company names on them, each one the size of a village and containing, as far as anyone can tell, three cars. The recovery site was one of these. Low, long, gray, behind a car park with a sign at the entrance that said the name of a foundation and, underneath, smaller, the name of a company I knew from a blue lanyard at a golf day.

That part was no surprise. He sells the bank its recovery seats; this was where the seats were. I'd have been more surprised if his company's name hadn't been on the sign. I got off the bus with the other thirty-nine and collected a lanyard of my own, a temporary one, white, with my name printed on it and a number.
Forty.
They gave us a sandwich. At eight in the morning. I've never understood the sandwich at eight; I think it's less about hunger than about giving people something to hold.
<hr />
Inside, it was an office. Nobody tells you that about the end of the world: it has carpet tiles.

A big open floor, a hundred and fifty desks maybe, in rows, each with a screen and a phone and a laminated card with a name on it. Some of the cards had our logo in the corner. The rest were other banks, other companies, other people's Tuesdays. Everyone shares the site; that's how the economics work. You don't buy a building for a fire that might never come. You buy a seat in a building somebody else owns, and you hope that when your fire comes, theirs hasn't.

My desk was at the back by the window. Desk forty. My name was on the card, spelled right, which almost nobody manages. The card was whiter than its neighbors. I sat down and logged in and the screen came up exactly as it would at work, same wallpaper, same six things I'd left open, and for a second I was at work, and then I looked up and saw people I half knew sitting in rows under strip lights eating sandwiches. I looked under the desk, out of habit. No dog. Nobody had thought to allocate one.
Pieter came past. He was in the second row, and he'd walked the length of the floor to find me, which he didn't need to do.
"Settling in?"
"It's a desk."

"It is a desk." He looked at the window. "Good spot, actually. You can see the car park." He said it as if the car park were a view, and then he said, in exactly the same voice, "How's the program treating you?"
"Lots of lists."
"You like lists."
He nodded, and stood there a moment longer than the conversation needed, like a man who wants to say something and can't find the sentence in the building. Then someone called him, and he went.

I did the drill. You log in, you open the things you'd open, you ring a number and tell a voice that you're operational, and the voice says thank you and you hear it typing. By eleven I'd done everything the laminated card asked of me and I had five hours left.
So I did what I do at any recovery test, on anybody's system. I counted.

It's the whole discipline, really. You count what was supposed to come over, you count what arrived, and if the two numbers differ you've got a job for the afternoon. Forty of us had got off the bus; I'd counted lanyards at the door because I can't not. I took my sandwich for a walk along the rows and counted cards with our logo on them.
Forty-nine.
I did it again from the other end, in case I'd counted a pillar. Forty-nine. Forty of them had a person behind them, eating. Nine had a card, a screen, a phone, and a chair pushed in.

It's a bank of five thousand people and I don't know most of them, so an unfamiliar name means nothing. But a drill has a sheet, and the sheet had forty names, and I'd read it, twice, because I was on it. None of these nine were. I went round again and wrote them on the back of my own laminated card with the pen they'd given us. Nine names. Eight I'd never seen. The ninth I knew from the label of a beer.
Nobody asked what I was doing. A man reading desk cards at a continuity test looks like the test.
<hr />
Then I read the rest of the building, since it was there.

The fire plan by the door. The evacuation routes. A floor map, laminated, with our floor in blue and a second floor above us in gray, labeled, in a smaller font, ARCHIVE (FOUNDATION), NO ACCESS. A list of extensions, and at the bottom one that said Reading Room.

There was a staircase at the far end, behind the kitchenette, with a tall window on the landing and a glass door at the top. I went up. I touched my badge to the reader, and it made no sound at all, which is a sound in itself. I didn't try the handle. I stood there like a man who's wandered into the wrong part of a hospital, and looked through.

A corridor. Carpet, better than ours. A door at the end with a window in it, and through that a room with a long table and a lamp and shelves, and a desk at the near end with a woman at it, her back to me, doing something with a card index. An actual card index, wooden, with drawers. I hadn't seen one since I was a child.
And in the corridor, against the wall, a trolley of gray boxes, spines out. Each one had a label.
I took the card out of my shirt pocket and held it up against the glass, next to the nearest box, like a man checking a lottery ticket.

Same letters at the front. The dash in the same place. The same number of digits after it. The box on the trolley and the line on the professor's last page were about a shelf and a half apart, by my arithmetic, and the same people had numbered both.
So Noor was right, and I'd now seen it myself, through a door, which put it in the left-hand column. The appointment the professor hadn't lived to keep was up one flight of stairs from desk forty.
"You're not badged for up there."
A man in a high-visibility jacket, on the stairs below me, friendly. The site manager; it said so on him.
"I know. I was being nosy. Who is it, upstairs?"
"Heritage." He said it the way you'd say accounts. "Old papers. Different tenant, same generator."
"Who pays for the generator?"
"Not me, mate." He laughed. "There's more sandwiches if you want one."
I went back down and sat at desk forty and looked at the car park, which Pieter had called a view.

Julian was in it. A good coat, one hand in his pocket, standing by something German and quiet. He wasn't talking to anyone. He was looking up at the tall window on the stair landing, where a minute earlier a man had stood holding a card against a glass door. Then he looked along the building to my window, which from out there should have been a sheet of gray, and he found the right pane, and he waved.
I waved back. It's what you do.

So that was seen. I'd come to look at their building and been watched doing it by the one person there who knew what I read, and I couldn't even be annoyed, because he sells the seats and it was his shed. He got in the car and drove away.
<hr />
The bus went back at four. Pieter sat near the front. I sat at the back with the laminated card in my pocket, nine names on one side and my own on the other, and watched the sheds go by.
At home, Buddy was at the window. Ana said he'd been there since three.
"How was the end of the world?"
"It had a sandwich."
"Of course it did."

I had two questions when I got on the bus home and I still had them at midnight. Who were nine desks for, in our colors, if not for anyone on our sheet? And who pays for a generator that a bank's emergency floor shares with an archive? Both of them were questions about a contract, and contracts I could get. I was on the program. Reading them was my job.

chapters.title: The money
chapters.what: James no longer finds the annex and the invoices by reading a folder: his first program task is to reconcile Annex C against HR and sign it. Saskia tells him his role was ticked in June; he finds nine names with no HR record and takes them to Pieter, who says leave it, sign; he reads the no-animals line with Buddy in the car, and signs. That evening he pulls the invoices himself and learns what his initials support. The kitchen-floor scene with Ana is cut, because she is not told until later. The receipts opening and the invoice passages are reused. Source: v7/24.
blocks: I'll give you the rule first. It isn't mine.
When the files are gone, look for the receipts.

Everybody knows the famous version. In 1973 the head of an intelligence agency ordered a program's records destroyed, and they were, and four years later some twenty thousand pages turned up anyway, because they'd been filed with the financial records. The men who burned the files were thinking about what the files said. The men who kept the receipts were thinking about whether the money added up. The second kind is boring, and boring is what survives.
I didn't know I was following the rule. I thought I was doing my job.
<hr />
On the Monday after the drill Saskia gave me my first real task on the program, with the face of a woman handing over a chore she'd been dreading.

"Annex C. Seat allocation. Once a year somebody checks that everyone with a seat is a real employee with the right number of dependents, and signs that they've checked. Then your line manager countersigns and it goes to the vendor. It's due Wednesday. It's very boring."
"I'll need a role to open it."
She looked at her screen. Then she looked at it longer.
"You've got it."
"I asked ten seconds ago."

"No, you've had it. It came through already ticked." She scrolled. Saskia owns the access reviews; a grant she didn't make is, to her, a stain on a tablecloth. "The third week of June. That's not right. Nobody had asked for you in June."
"Who ticked it?"

"It doesn't say who. It says approved." She frowned at it a little longer, and then I watched her decide it was somebody else's problem. "It'll be a batch. They pre-provision things. Wednesday, James."

The third week of June was the week I'd opened a ticket about a job with no owner, three weeks before anybody said the words the person who reads things. Somebody had laid me a place at this table before I'd been invited to sit down. I wrote the date on the back of the laminated card, under the nine names.
<hr />
It was a list. Everything in this story is a list. I've come to think that if you want to do something large and have nobody look at it, you do it as a list, because nobody reads lists.

Forty-nine rows. Desk number, name, employee number, role, and a column headed dependents per allocation with a two or a three or a four in it. Desk one was Anneke de Wit, our head of risk. Desk twelve was Pieter. Dependents per allocation: 3. He has two children. It took me a moment to get to three, and when I did I decided not to mention at home that a wife is a dependent.

Frank wasn't on it. I wasn't on it. Desk forty, where I'd eaten a sandwich on Thursday, belonged to a man in Legal who'd been off sick since March. I'd been sitting in for him. That was why my card had been so white.

Reconciling is what I do. You take their list and your list and you match on the one field nobody can misspell. I pulled the staff export from HR and joined it to the annex on employee number, and forty rows lit up.
Nine didn't.

The nine had no employee number. Where the number should be, each had a reference in a different format, beginning with a V. I took the laminated card out of my drawer and turned it over. The same nine names I'd copied off the empty desks. Eight strangers and a man who makes beer, who had a four in his dependents column.
Nine people with a desk in our block, in our colors, on our contract, and no record of ever having worked a day for the bank.
<hr />

I took it to Pieter on Wednesday at ten. It was meant to be a five-minute countersignature. I'd played at seven, and Buddy was down in the car in the basement garage, windows open, on his blanket, which is allowed for exactly as long as nobody asks.
I put the annex on Pieter's desk with the nine rows marked in pencil.
"These aren't staff."
He didn't need to look. "Vendor allocations. They sit under our block. It's a contract thing; it's been like that since before I got here."
"One of them's a brewery."
There was the pause. I've known Pieter's pause since June. He looks slightly to the left of you, and he seems to be listening for something.
"Leave it, James," he said. "Sign."
He'd said two of those words to me once before, at stand-up, in front of nine people, in his manager's voice. This time it sounded like he was asking a favor.
I read the rest while he waited, because I read the rest. Under the table of names there were two pages of terms in small type. Access. Badging. The hours of the canteen. And among them, one line.
Companion animals are not accommodated.

I thought about Buddy, four floors below me, asleep in a car. I thought about what kind of emergency has a canteen and a number of children per desk and has had to write that sentence down. Somebody had asked, once. Somebody had wanted to bring a dog, and they'd needed a clause.
"That line," I said.
Pieter leaned over. "It'll be insurance. It's in all of them."
It isn't in all of them. I've read all of them.

I'd like to say I weighed it. What I thought was: this is a lifeboat with a guest list. Some people have paid to sit down if the worst happens, some of them aren't ours, and Pieter's children are on it, so Pieter isn't going to ask. That seemed like the whole of it, and quite enough. And a man who won't sign is off the program by Friday and reading none of it. And the dog was in the car.

So I did what I do with a reconciliation that doesn't reconcile. I signed it with the exception written in. Reconciled against HR. Forty matched. Nine vendor allocations, no HR record, noted per line manager. My initials at the foot of each page, four of them, and my name at the end. Pieter countersigned without reading my note, or having read it and decided it was fine.
"Thank you," he said, and meant it.
I kept the signer's copy. I went down to the garage and let Buddy out and walked him round the visitors' spaces until he'd forgiven me.
<hr />
That evening I looked for the money, because Noor had told me to and because I still had a generator I couldn't account for.
Kitchen table, laptop, Buddy underneath with his chin on my foot. The program gave me the contract ledger, read-only, and nobody had ever asked me not to read it at home.
The generator took four minutes. The foundation owned the building and billed the bank a share of the running costs every quarter, sixty percent, fuel and servicing. Dull. Correct.
But the foundation also invoiced the bank for something else. One line, separately, every quarter.
Continuity reconciliation (recall index). Per flagged person. A number of persons, a rate, a total. Approved, for the last thirty quarters, by the same initials. A. de W.

I read it the way I'd read the sentence on page 118. First time, nothing: a service line, the kind that gets approved because it was approved before. Second time: per flagged person. Third time, out loud, to a dog: recall index.

I knew that verb. It was in the file I'd captured in June, in the reason column, next to numbers that weren't mine. Recalled. I'd taken it for a product term. And I knew what flagged meant, because I'd been flagged. Three times that I'd seen, with a two-word reason each.
The ledger went back thirty-one years, so I went back thirty-one years. I put the number of persons in a sheet, quarter by quarter, and looked at it the way I look at anything that should breathe.

It didn't breathe. Costs wobble. This sat flat for years, the same count every quarter, and then it stepped up, once, by a clean amount, like a dial being turned one click. Then flat again. Six steps since 1994.
The last step was dated the Monday after I'd asked my question at stand-up.
I sat with that. Eleven words, said aloud in June in front of nine people, and the next Monday a foundation had put its price up by one click and somebody in risk had initialed it.
They hadn't only counted me. They'd billed for me.

Then I did the thing I should have done at ten that morning, which is read what a document rests on. Every invoice in the ledger had a line at the bottom in small type. Basis: client reconciliation, Annex C, as signed.
Continuity reconciliation. I'd spent three days doing something called a reconciliation, for something called continuity, and I hadn't once set the two words side by side.

I don't know how a seat list supports a bill for people who ask questions. I've thought about it since and I still couldn't draw it for you. What I know is what the paper says: the bill cites the annex, and this year's annex has my initials on every page. Next quarter's invoice would go to Anneke de Wit for approval, and if she ever turned it over to see what it stood on, she'd find me.
That's what I'd signed. I learned it about eleven hours after signing, which for me is quick.
I took the signer's copy out of my bag and put it in the folder with the yellow sheet. Two forms in three weeks, both with my name at the bottom in my own hand.

And one more thing followed, the kind I can't leave alone. If somebody is billed every quarter for a number of persons, somebody is counting persons. Every night, presumably, at a quarter past two. The job I'd asked about in June had been renamed and given an owner and a ticket, and I'd been told, in effect, that this was the end of it, and I'd been quiet at work for three weeks like a tired man.
It was still running. It had to be. The invoice said so.
In the morning I'd go and look.

chapters.title: Enjoy it while it lasts
chapters.what: Meerwijk is gone; James never changes employer. He goes to look at the renamed job and the new tools hide it under a default on page 212. He tells Saskia what the rule hides, guesses wrong about what she was told, and she logs it with a kind note about sleep. He writes his rule. Days later he takes Julian's tip, Julian K. fixes it in eleven minutes, and James sees that the narrowing and the fix come from one address. The defaults passage and the eleven-minute email are reused. Source: v6/15.
blocks: In the morning I went to look, and I couldn't.

The old job list was gone. Not the job; the list. That week the bank had switched on the new monitoring tools, the ones Frank had sent the link about in the spring. AI-driven. Finds the anomalies for you, no humans needed. He'd put it in the team channel again on the Monday, same words, same little skull. It's here. Enjoy it while it lasts, boys.

Everything I used to read now came through the new thing. It was faster, and it had graphs. I searched it for anything running at 02:14 and got nothing. I searched for the job's new name. Nothing. I listed every job owned by continuity, which is a short list, and it wasn't there.
My first thought was that they'd finally deleted it. My second was the invoice. You don't bill per person for a count nobody's making.
So I read the defaults.
