When you buy a thing that watches, it comes with opinions. Out of the box, before anyone's touched it, it already knows what's normal and what isn't, what to wake you for and what to let through. Those opinions are called defaults, and nobody reads them, because they're long and they're boring and they've been chosen by experts, and the whole promise of the thing is that you don't have to. You install it. It watches. You sleep.
Four hundred pages. I read them at my desk over two days, like a man eating a phone book.

On page two hundred and twelve, in a section about scheduled jobs, there was a class of thing the tool had been told not to report. Not to log, not to display, not to alert on. A pattern, in the dry language of patterns: jobs held by a continuity function, on a nightly schedule, emitting small payloads to unresolved addresses. Classified, out of the box, as noise. Visible only to a role called vendor support.
My job. My forty kilobytes. Described in one sentence, in a default, in a product sold to ten thousand companies, as the one shape the watcher need never look at.
At the foot of the page: Rev. 4. Next review: 31 December.

It was the second document I'd held that autumn that was on its fourth revision. I'd have given a lot to see the third. In June the job had no owner. Now it had one, and here was a rule that said held by a continuity function. Somebody had kept the rule up to date.

Nobody had hidden anything from me in particular. I want to say that plainly. There was no locked room. Somebody had been boring in the right place. They'd written one sentence into the defaults of a tool that would be installed everywhere by people who'd never read it, and from then on every company that bought it had a watcher that had been told, before it opened its eyes, what it would never have to see. My access hadn't been taken away. It had been narrowed by exactly one shape, by a setting, and no person had needed to decide it.
<hr />
I took page 212 to Saskia. Printed, with the sentence underlined.
I've gone back over the next four minutes more than I've gone over most things.

I told her. Standing at her desk, in the voice I use for incident reviews, I told her what the rule hides. There's a job at 02:14. It sends out a list of staff numbers with a reason beside each. The people on it are people who asked something, or wrote to someone, or posted. I'm on it. A foundation bills the bank for it, per person, and has done since 1994. And this page is why nobody sees it run.
She listened to all of it. She's a good listener; it's her job to hear why people want things.
Then I made it worse. I thought I knew what she'd been told, and I wanted her to know I knew.
"They'll have told you it's a security trap," I said. "A honeypot. It isn't one."
"A what?"
"That's what Pieter told the team."

"Nobody's told me anything about a trap." She wasn't defending herself. She was puzzled, and it was real. "James, it's a default. It came in the box. Every client has that rule. I've got the ticket for the ruleset right here, it says accepted as shipped, I didn't write a line of it and neither did anyone in this building." She turned her screen a little, as proof. "I was told it cuts down the noise. Which it does."
So that was my one guess, and it was wrong, and the first thing she'd learned about my theory was that it was wrong about her.
She looked at her screen again, at something that wasn't the ticket. She does the access reviews. She sees what's on a person's file. She didn't say the word referral and she didn't have to.
"Are you sleeping?"
"That's not—"

"I'm asking because I have to log this. Somebody queries a ruleset, I log it. I'm going to put that you asked about rule 212 and I explained it's a vendor default." She was already typing. "And I'm going to put that you seemed tired. Because you do. And because if anyone reads this later I'd sooner they read that than something worse."
"Could you leave that part out?"

"I log everything. That's why they trust the log." She looked up, and she was kind about it, and I'd have preferred almost anything else. "Go home. It's four hundred pages of settings. Nobody should read that."

I went back to my desk. I'd told a colleague the truth with nothing in my hands but a printout of a default and my own say-so. Frank would have had it in the right-hand column before I'd finished the first sentence. And now it was in her log, under my name, with a note about sleep. Three papers in a month, and this one I hadn't even been asked to sign.
<hr />

That night I wrote a rule. Kitchen table, Buddy underneath, the Record open at a clean page. I don't make vows. But I write rules for systems all day, and it had become obvious that I needed one for me.
I tell nobody until I know what they were told and can put their own paper in front of them.

It looked sensible written down. Rules do. What they were told, because I'd just seen what happens when you guess. Their own paper, because mine was a market notebook and a dead screenshot, and Saskia had a ticket.
I didn't ask myself what it would cost to keep, or who'd be paying while I kept it. I should have. I underlined it instead.
<hr />
I stayed narrowed for five days. I did my lists. I was tired, as agreed.
On the Wednesday, at seven, on the sixth green, Julian said, "You look like a man whose bank's being difficult."
"It's got new tools."

"There it is." He crouched for Buddy, who was in the cart and stayed in the cart. "Hello, old boy. Is he being a misery? He's being a misery." And then, standing, easily, the way he said everything: "If it's an access thing, and it's always an access thing, whoever sold you the tools will have someone. They always have someone. That's what you're paying them for. Ask."
"Ask who?"
"Whoever's name is on the invoice. That's who you always ask. The person who'd be embarrassed."

I knew whose name was on the invoice. I'd looked it up the week before: the tools had come through the same company whose name was on the sign outside the shed and on a blue lanyard at a golf day. So a man was standing on a green telling me to write to him, in the third person. He must have known I could see that. I think it was meant as a kindness I could see through, the way you let a child watch you hide the egg.
Fine. It was also a test I could run. If the man who sells the seats could open what page 212 shuts, that told me something about who'd shut it.

I wrote that afternoon. Two dull lines. Could someone help me with a view that seems to be restricted by ruleset default 212. The reply took eleven minutes. It was from a man who signed himself Julian K., who was sorry to hear it, who'd had a word, and who thought it'd be sorted by close of play.
It was sorted by four. Saskia came past my desk and said, "Oh, that got through, did it, good," in a voice that meant it hadn't gone through her.

I wrote back to thank him. He wrote back that it was nothing, that these things were always a setting somebody had forgotten, and that if I needed anything else he was the person who'd be embarrassed.

Then I did the dull thing and put the two invoices side by side. The one for the tools that had narrowed me. The one for the support hours that had just fixed it. Same supplier. Same post box. The problem and the rescue had been billed from one address, eleven minutes apart. At work we have a word for a vendor who breaks something and then mends it while you watch. We call it a demo.

And there was the job, on my screen, under the vendor-support view. New name, owner continuity, a ticket. It had run that morning at 02:14 for nine seconds. Forty-one kilobytes. One more than in June.
I didn't capture it. I looked at the number for a while and closed the view.

So Julian could see my access. He'd known it was narrowed before I'd told him what the trouble was; I'd said new tools and he'd said access. If he could see that, what else could he see? My tickets? What I'd posted? What I read?
I'd never tested a person. I test systems, and paper. But I knew how I'd go about it with a system, and I decided to find out.

chapters.file: 26 — A room with a long table.md
chapters.title: A room with a long table
chapters.what: Added: this is one region with one handler to a bank; the plan for James is to buy him; the schedule will reach him through the annex he signed, and what he does with it is the test. Corrected to the new chain: invoice and annex in place of the ledger, June in place of July, no listening inside the house, and no date moves here (the review stays at the end of the year). Source: v6/16.
blocks: The table was long because the room had been built for twelve and was only ever used by two, and Bram Lievens sat at the end of it with his back to the window because he liked people to have the light, and because he'd been told once that it was kind, and he had taken it to heart.
"Sit anywhere," he said. "No, not there. That's where the chairman sits when there's a chairman. Sit here. How's the dog?"
"Which?"
"His. The old one."
"Slow. Happy. He puts his hand on its head when he's thinking and doesn't know he's doing it." He sat. "I've told you that."

"You have. I like hearing it." Bram had a folder and didn't open it. He never opened the folder in the first ten minutes; he'd explained once that the folder was for after, that the first ten minutes were for the man, and that he'd learned this from someone who'd learned it from someone, and that it was the only part of the job he'd have missed. "The access went through."
"Yes. Eleven minutes. He thanked me."
"He thanked Julian."

"He thanked the name on the invoice. He knew whose it was. He's that sort." He put his hands on the table, flat. "He's found the foundation's line. He's seen the steps. He'll have the dates by now. The last one's June."
"June," Bram agreed, mildly. "That was you, I think. Your bank."
"That was the index."

"The index is a number, Julian. Somebody has to read it to somebody, and somebody has to write the sum down, and in this region that's me, and I write what I'm told." He smiled. He had a good smile, apologetic, as though the world had been arranged slightly to his advantage and he'd noticed and was sorry. "One region. One handler to a bank. You've got yours and I've got eleven of you, and the people I answer to have never asked me the name of a single dog. So tell me what he's doing. Not what he's stopped. You've been asked that before."

"He's reading. He's quiet at work. He signed the form and he signed the annex, with a note on it, in his own hand, about nine names. He plays on Wednesdays and he's happy on Wednesdays. He's been to Leiden."
"We know about Leiden. Leiden's been quiet for nine years. Leiden's a model." Bram turned the folder a quarter turn on the table without opening it. "And the other thing?"
"Not yet, or no?"

"Not yet." He said it carefully. "He's close to it. He talks to the dog on the course when he thinks he's alone. I've heard some of it. He's got all the parts and he's never put them together, because he's a man who checks paper, and it isn't on paper."
Bram was quiet for a moment, and then he did open the folder, and took out one sheet, and turned it round so that the light fell on it, and slid it halfway down the table, where it stopped.
"I'd like you to look at this and tell me what you see. Honestly. I'd like to know whether I'm reading it right."
Two columns. The left one was a code and a number and a date. The right one was the same code, and a different number, and the same date.
"It's the weekly."

"It's the weekly for one subject. His. Since the spring." Bram sat back. "Left is reporting. Posts, inquiries, letters to dealers, visits to curtain shops. That's what the nightly job gives us; anyone can fill that column, a machine fills it. You can see him go loud in June and go quiet the day he signed. Lovely. Textbook. The right column is the index." He let it sit. "Which has gone up every week since the spring and has not come down once. Not when he went quiet. Not when his access was narrowed. Not when you gave it back."
"I fill in the right column. I don't understand it."

"You fill it in because you can. I can't. Nobody who hasn't had it can see it in somebody else, which is why we keep people like you." He said it without envy, as far as could be told. "I'll tell you what I was told, which is more than I should, because I like you, and because I think it'll make you better at this." Bram folded his hands. "It was never belief. We don't count belief. Belief's weather; belief goes up every time somebody puts a light in the sky on television and down every time a magician's in the room. The index counts the ones who've stopped being afraid. That's all. A reading, every week, of how many people in a given population have stopped needing what we sell."
The man at the table didn't move.

"A frightened reader is a reader," Bram said. "He publishes, or he doesn't; he's loud or he's quiet; either way he wants something, and if a man wants something you can seat him. A man who's stopped being frightened doesn't want a seat. He doesn't want to be believed, even. He just looks. And you can't house that, Julian, and you can't laugh it off a stage, because he's not on the stage. He's in a kitchen with a dog."
"He's not stopped being afraid. He's not sleeping."

"He's afraid of us," said Bram. "That's different. That's useful. Fear of us is a man who'll take a seat. I'm talking about the other thing. The one that was in him at his wife's grandmother's funeral and has been going out of him, a little, every week since, like a bath." He looked at the sheet. "He hasn't crossed. You're right. But his slope is the steepest I've seen since Leiden, and Leiden went quiet nine years ago and we've never had a reading on her since, because she stopped reporting, and a machine can only fill the one column."
"So what do you want from me?"

"What I've always wanted. Be near. Know what he loves. And when he gets there, which he will, I'd like to know the week." Bram slid the sheet back to himself. "In the meantime we do the decent thing, which is buy him. That's the plan. It's a good plan; it's the one we had for you. A man who signs what he's given can be given something better to sign. He put his initials on the annex. So next quarter's schedule goes to whoever reconciled the annex, which is how these things have always been routed, and nobody has to hand him anything."
"He'll read it."

"Of course he'll read it. He reads the canteen hours. There'll be eleven addresses on it and he'll know one of them." Bram closed the folder. "What he does then is the test. If he comes to us about it, he can be seated. If he goes anywhere else with it, I'll want to know where."
"And the wife?"
"She'll find it. They always do. Let her. A frightened wife is a seat we don't have to pay for."
He stood, which meant it was over.
"You still take him coffee?"
"Wednesdays."
"Good. I like that."

The index was read on Monday. It was up. The review stayed at the end of the year, and the man with the flask drove to Zwolle and sat in a blue chair and did not turn the light on for longer than usual.

chapters.title: Leiden, nine years ago
chapters.what: Added Kalder's line: when it went through him there was nobody there, so he asked for the seat. The review date no longer moves in this chapter (the two moves are in "A car park" and "The leak"); the crossing is filed and he asks for names. American spelling. Source: v7/27.
blocks: The library was being restructured, which is the word people use when a library is being taken apart, and Julian Kalder had a clipboard.

He was thirty-four and good at this. The foundation sent him wherever a collection was being moved, because collections being moved are where things go missing, and because he had a gift, noted early and used often, for learning the names of everyone in a building in the first two days and using them, correctly, in the third. Porters, cataloguers, the woman who did the tea. He didn't do it as a technique. That was the thing his handlers had understood about him before he had: it wasn't an act. He liked people, briefly and completely, the way some men like weather.

The transfer took three weeks. Forty thousand volumes from a university annex that was closing to a depot that wasn't, in numbered crates, by van, with a manifest. Kalder's job was the manifest. He stood at the loading door with the clipboard and ticked, and talked, and by the end of the first week the porters were telling him about their divorces.

The conservators worked upstairs. There were two of them. One was a man in his sixties who treated Kalder with the polite contempt of someone who knows what a clipboard means. The other was a woman of about thirty called Noor, who did not treat him with anything, because she did not, as far as he could tell in three weeks, treat people. She worked. She had a bench by the window with a lamp on an arm, and she sat at it with a scalpel and a bone folder and a sheet of something three hundred years old, and she did not look up when he came in, and she did not look up when he left, and on the second day he had learned her name and used it and she had said, "Yes," without turning round, and gone on with what she was doing.
He thought about her more than he thought about the manifest. He noted this, and filed it, as he'd been taught to file things about himself, under attention, and went on.
<hr />
On the last day there was nothing left to tick.

The vans had gone. The porters had gone. The old conservator had shaken his hand with two fingers and gone. The building was empty in the way buildings are when the thing they were for has been taken out of them, and Kalder walked through it once, as he always did, checking, and found her still at her bench by the window, with the lamp on, doing nothing.
Not working. Sitting. Her hands were flat on the bench and the bench was clear.

He stood in the door. He said her name. She turned round, and looked at him, and he had the sensation, which he had not had before and has had exactly once since, of being looked at by someone who was not, at that moment, afraid of anything at all.
"Would you like some tea," she said. "There's a kettle. It's the last thing."
He said yes. He said it the way he said yes to porters.

She made the tea at a sink in the corner, in two mugs that had been left because nobody wanted them, and brought it over, and put his on the bench, and sat back down on her stool, and he sat on the one the old man had used, and she said nothing.

For twenty minutes. He timed it afterwards, from the clock on the wall, because he needed a number to put in the report. Twenty minutes, in an empty building, with a lamp on, with a woman who was not performing silence at him, not sulking, not waiting for him to speak, not doing any of the things that silence usually is. She was just there. She drank her tea. Once she looked out of the window at a tree. Once she looked at him, briefly, with something that might have been curiosity and might have been kindness and was, he decided later, both, and then she looked away again, and the clock went on.
And somewhere in the twenty minutes the thing went through him.

He has tried to describe it since, to people whose job it is to hear it described, and he has never done it well. It was not a light. It was not a voice. It was more like the moment on a long flight when you realize the engine noise has stopped and you cannot tell whether it stopped a second ago or an hour. Something that had been running in him for thirty-four years, so constantly that it had become the sound of being him, was not running. And in the quiet where it had been, he understood three things at once, completely, without words, the way you understand that you're falling.
That he was going to die.
That this was not a problem.
That it had never been a problem, and that everything he had ever done had been built on top of its being a problem, like a city on a fault.

He put the mug down. His hand was steady. She looked at him then, properly, and he saw that she knew, and that she had known it would happen, and that this was why she had asked him to stay, and that she would never say so.
"Thank you for the tea," he said.
"You're welcome," said Noor.
<hr />
He drove to Zwolle that night because Zwolle was where you went.

The office above the courtyard was lit. He sat in the chair across from the man he reported to and made his report, which was mostly the manifest, forty thousand volumes, no discrepancies, and then he said that there was one other thing, and he said it in the voice you'd use for a discrepancy.

He told them. He gave the time. He gave the name. He described the twenty minutes as accurately as he could and watched the man across the desk write it down, and he watched the man's face, and he saw in it something he had not expected, which was recognition, and something else he had, which was arithmetic.
"And you're sure," the man said.
"I'm sure."
"And it's gone. The fear."

The man was quiet. Then he turned to the screen on his desk, which Kalder had never been shown and was now, without ceremony, being shown, and he added two rows to a column. Kalder watched him do it. A code, a date, a place. One for a conservator in Leiden and one for a man with a clipboard, two people who were, as of that afternoon, no longer afraid, and had therefore been counted. The man said the date for the region would be looked at in the spring, with the rest, and that two rows did not move it. He said it as a kindness.
"That's what we do," the man said. "You've seen it now."

Kalder said he understood. He did understand. That was the strange part, the part he has never managed to explain to the people whose job it is to hear it: he understood what the column meant, and what it meant for the woman at the bench, and he felt, about it, nothing he would have called fear and nothing he would have called guilt. He felt interested. He felt, for the first time in his life, that he could see the whole machine, and that it was beautiful, and that he was good at it.
He asked two things. He has thought since that they were the only decisions he ever made.
"When it went through me," he said, "there was nobody there."
The man waited.

"In the library. She was across the bench. But in the thing itself, nobody. No hand. I've read the accounts you keep; most of them have somebody in them." He heard his own voice and it was easy, it was the voice he used with porters. "I'd like a seat. The lower floor. I understand there are allocations."
The man wrote that down too.
"And who else? On the list, for this region. Who else has it gone through. I could go and see. I'm good at going and seeing. I'd know it now."
<hr />

They gave him more names. He was right; he did know it now. That is the thing nobody tells you about the right column, the one that matters, the one that only the crossed can fill: it isn't a mystery. Once it has happened to you, you can see it in someone else's face across a room, the way a man who has broken his leg can tell, in a crowd, who has broken theirs. He saw it in a retired engineer in Zwolle. He saw it in a dealer's customer in Groningen who turned out not to have it yet. He saw it, nine years later, in a man on a golf course who asked about the dog before he asked anyone's name, and who didn't have it, not yet, but was going to, and Kalder could see the date on him like a watermark.

The seat came with the names. He had asked for it, in the office in Zwolle, in the same breath as the names, and nobody in the room had thought that strange. A seat on the lower floor of a shed in a business park, with dependents per allocation, and he had no dependents, and he took it, and he has never once regretted it, and he will tell you so. When he is asked why, by the people whose job it is to ask, he gives the same answer every time: because when it went through him there was nobody there, and a chair is a place where somebody will be.

He went back to Leiden only once. Nine years later, on a Friday, with a clipboard, and a kind voice, and a list of her clients and her mother's care-home place. She made him tea again. She said nothing again. He timed it. It was shorter.

He had crossed, in an empty library, in twenty minutes, over a mug of tea that nobody wanted, and he had come back from the other side with the one thing the crossing is supposed to take from you still in his hand. Not fear. Fear had gone, and never come back. The other thing. The wanting.

He is the exception the book has to carry, and he knows it, and if you asked him he would say that he is not the exception. He would say he is the proof. That a man can see the whole of it and choose the seat. That seeing is not the same as leaving. That the organization has always known this, and has built on it, and that it is the one true thing they have.
He would say it kindly. He would ask about your dog.

chapters.title: On land
chapters.what: Kept the pub terrace, the toaster story and Ana's part; "Dave" is now Julian throughout. The Deventer slip, the threat about houses and dogs and the end of the friendship are removed (Deventer is said at the barbecue, per Structure 01). Added: Julian uses the professor's word "decanting", James sets a trap by naming a book that does not exist and Julian knows it, the hearings run on the bar television, and Ana proposes the barbecue, which James accepts without telling her why. Source: v6/18.
blocks: The pub by the course has a back terrace with heaters, and on a Saturday in November you can sit out till nine if you keep your coat on and lie to yourself about the temperature. Ana had come to meet us. Her idea. She'd said on the phone, I'll come for the last hour, I want to see you two being idiots, and here we were, and we'd been idiots for eighteen holes and she'd arrived in time for the beer.
Buddy was under the table on a folded towel the barman keeps for him. Julian had found that out before I did, which is the kind of thing he finds out.

Inside, over the bar, a television with the sound down was showing a hearing. Men in suits behind a long table, a caption with the word phenomena in it. It had been going for weeks. A pilot would describe something he'd seen with his own eyes, and then a man from an agency would say that a review had found nothing, and then another pilot, and then another review. Each one paired. Nobody in the pub was watching. I'd stopped watching it too, which I noticed, and which I'd have called progress if I hadn't just read what a style guide says about readers who go quiet.
Ana was on her second glass and telling him about the toaster.
"Three weekends," she said. "Three. Every wire in the house. I'm standing in my own kitchen holding a toaster like a woman in a hostage video."
"Did he find it?" Julian said.
"He found a label. Somebody had labeled a fuse wrong in nineteen ninety-something." She squeezed my arm. "He was so happy. I've never seen him happier. Not on our wedding day."
"Fair," I said.

"That's a good day," Julian said, and meant it, and smiled at me over his glass. "It's the same with old wiring as with old wine. You don't fix it in place, you decant it. Pour the whole house into new copper and leave the sediment in the walls."
Ana laughed. I laughed a beat late, and I'll tell you why.

Decanting. The professor had written it in a margin, in pencil, in the thin book, next to entry nineteen, and I'd had to look it up on the Tuesday, because he hadn't meant wine. He'd used it the way you'd use it for a library: taking a collection out of one building and pouring it into another, so that it keeps its order and loses its address. It's a word people in his trade use. I had never heard it said aloud in my life, and I'd now heard it twice in one week, once from a dead man and once from a man who sells desks.
That can happen. Words do that. You learn one on Tuesday and the world is suddenly full of it. I know that effect; it has a name, and I've used it on other people for years.

But I've also spent eleven years at a bank being paid to notice when two systems that shouldn't know each other start using the same word, and my job has one rule about it. You don't argue with the coincidence. You send it something and see what comes back.
<hr />

So I set a trap, the way I'd set one at work. If you want to know whether a system is really reading a feed or just saying it does, you put something in the feed that isn't true and wait to see if it gets repeated.
I let the toaster story finish. I let him tell one about a client in Antwerp. Then, when Ana had gone in to find the bathroom, I said, as a man says things on a terrace:
"You read, don't you. Old stuff. You said once."
"When I can. Why?"
"I picked something up this week I think you'd like. Dutch, 1950s, a little book about the Leiden printing houses between the wars. The Quiet Presses. Van der Berg, I think. Hard to find."
There is no such book. I'd made it on the spot out of three words I liked, and I'd never say it twice, which is the point of a test input: you have to be able to recognize your own.
He didn't pause. That's what I keep coming back to. There wasn't the half-second a man takes to search his memory and come up empty and decide whether to admit it.
"Oh, that one," Julian said. "Yes. Dry as a biscuit. The chapter on the type foundries is the good bit." He drank. "You're going to need a lamp for that typeface."
I said I expected so.

Ana came back out and sat down and put her cold hands on my neck, and I made the noise you make, and Julian laughed, and we talked about a dog at the club that had eaten a scorecard. Nothing happened to his face. Nothing happened to mine either; I've had years of practice at a table. The heaters ticked. On the television behind the bar another man in uniform described a light and another man in a suit described a review.

Here's where I'd got to by the second heater cycle. Either a man had just been polite about a book, the way you nod at a title at a party, and I'd caught a friend in a kindness. Or he had a reason to be seen to have read what I read, and the reason was not that he liked old print. The first one I'd have believed of most people. He'd given me the chapter on type foundries, though. You don't invent a chapter to be polite. You invent a chapter when the question is a test and you know it is, and you'd rather pass loudly than fail quietly.

I didn't know which. I still didn't know in the car. What I knew was that I'd lied to a friend on a terrace, and made up a book, and that if I was wrong about him I'd just done something small and ugly to the one person in eleven years who'd asked about my dog before my name. And if I was right, then he knew I'd tested him, because a man who nods at a title that doesn't exist has either heard of it or hasn't, and he'd made his choice with his eyes open. That title was out of my hands now. I couldn't take it back and I couldn't use it twice.
"Same time Wednesday?" he said, standing, putting a note under his glass.
"Wednesday."
"Bring the biscuit book."

He kissed Ana on the cheek. She let him. He crouched by the table and said something to Buddy, who did not take his chin off his paws, and he laughed at that, the way you laugh at an old dog's dignity, and went.
<hr />
"I like him," Ana said, in the car. "He listens. Men don't listen like that."
"You were quiet."
"Eighteen holes."

"You were quiet in the way where you've found a label." She looked at me. "Don't do the face. I'm just saying. You two have been playing for five months and I've met him once, on a terrace, in the dark, in a coat. I want to see him in daylight with other people. See if he's real."
"He's real."

"Then it'll be easy." She watched the ring road go past. "A barbecue. Next Saturday, before it's too cold. Frank. That man from your forum you keep saying you'll have round. Henk from two doors down, so it isn't weird. And golf man."

I'd been trying, since the second heater cycle, to think how I could get Julian in a room with other people and a control. Somebody who hadn't read the thin book. Somebody who'd hear a made-up title and say never heard of it, which is what honest people say. Frank, for instance, who'd put it in the right-hand column before the sausages were done.
"Yes," I said. "Good idea."
"That was fast."
"It's a good idea."

She looked at me a while longer, and then let it go, and turned the radio on. I drove. Buddy slept in the back. I didn't tell her why I'd said yes so quickly, and she knew I hadn't, and that was one more thing I hadn't told her, which by then was a list of its own.

chapters.title: The gorilla mask
chapters.what: He now says yes to the barbecue as a test with a control (the invented title dropped on Frank), the restored post is the one he deleted for Noor, "Deventer" is said here, and he builds the watcher that night; the lab-coat line and the decision to go quiet are cut. The cost is said once: the lane, the fourth gate, the bowl. Source: v6/17.
blocks: Ana wanted a barbecue, and I said yes in about two seconds, which should have warned her.

She'd been asking since September. You've been nicer since Wednesday golf man, bring him round. Then October happened and I went back into the submarine and she said it again, less nicely: bring him round, Mulder, I want to see the person who makes you normal.

I had a reason and I didn't give it to her. At the pub I'd named a book that doesn't exist and Julian had said he knew it. That's one reading. At work you don't wake anyone up for one reading. You want the same value again, from somewhere else, next to something you know is healthy. So I wanted Julian in a garden with other people in it, and I wanted Frank there, because Frank is the healthiest control I know. He has never once pretended to have read anything.

So: the last Saturday of October, a heater on the patio, coats on. Frank. Gert from two doors down, who is fine, and who turned out to have opinions about my grip. A man from the forum, a lonely one, who'd worked out where I lived from a photograph and turned up with a bottle of wine and theories, and whom Ana, to her enormous credit, fed.
And Julian, with a six-pack of something craft and his flask, because he's a flask man.

Everybody came round the back. That was my doing. Buddy sleeps across the front hall and I didn't want twelve people stepping over him, so I'd sent a message that morning: back lane, fourth gate, mind the bowl. Julian came early to help with the ice and I met him at the gate. He looked at the latch, which is the kind that lifts, and at the steel bowl just inside, and asked whose it was.
"Buddy's. He won't drink from the one in the kitchen if he's been out. Don't ask me why."
"I wouldn't dream of asking him," Julian said, and stepped over it carefully, the way you step over something that belongs to somebody.
<hr />
Frank told the gorilla story with tongs. Ana had given him tongs to stop him talking with his hands and it hadn't worked.

"Forty-three," he said. "California. Desert. They're testing the first American jet, properly secret, nobody's supposed to know jets exist. And the test pilots, who are bored, because test pilots are always bored, get fed up with the other pilots at the base radioing in going what the hell was that, no propeller, going like hell, right, and the brass going you saw nothing. So one of them puts on a gorilla mask. And a bowler hat. And a cigar. And he flies the jet right up alongside some poor bastard in a propeller plane, and waves."
"That's not true," said Ana.

"Every aviation book I've ever read says it's true, which is almost the same thing." Frank turned a sausage. "Point is, the poor bastard lands and goes I saw a plane with no propeller flown by a gorilla in a hat, and what happens?"
"They laugh at him."

"They laugh at him forever. He's gorilla guy. He was right, James. He saw a jet. He was the first man in his squadron to see the future, and he spent the rest of his life being the man who saw a gorilla. And nobody had to deny anything. They just stuck something stupid to the truth and let him carry it." He pointed the tongs at me. "That's your lot. That's the whole technique. You don't hide the plane. You put a gorilla in it."
"Handle with humor," I said.
"What?"
"Nothing. Something I read."
Julian had been by the heater with a beer, quiet, very good at being quiet. "That's a good story, Frank," he said, in the tone of a man who collects them, and Frank beamed, and the sausages burned.
That was when I did it. Frank was still glowing. Julian had come over to top up Ana's glass and was a step and a half behind him.

"There's a book you'd like," I said to Frank. "The Quiet Presses. Van der Berg, I think. Dutch, fifties." The same words, in the same order, that I'd used at the pub. "It's all in there. The gorilla, the lot."
"Never heard of it."
"Out of print."
"Sounds made up." He said it happily, to the sausage. "Sounds like a book you'd invent to win an argument."
That's what a healthy system returns. No pause, no nod. Never heard of it, sounds made up, next.
I didn't look at Julian. I looked at Ana's glass. The wine stopped going into it for about as long as it takes to read a line, and then it went on.
So I had my second reading. I also understood, a little late, that a test with a witness is a test the witness gets to watch. He'd heard me run it.
<hr />
I went in for more plates, and somebody had sent me a link. is this you?? Two question marks. The link was to my own thread.

I should say which thread. In the summer I'd posted the reply I got about page 118 next to the wording in Els's father's folder, paragraph against paragraph, and a woman in Leiden had told me to take it down before it got me visited, and I had. I'd watched it go.

It was back. Under my name, with my photographs, dated the day I'd first posted it. And it was longer. After my last dull sentence there were two more, in my voice. Almost. The same dryness, and then a turn at the end, about who had really ordered the second impression, and which old families stood behind the Leiden printing houses. Bloodlines. A word I have never typed in my life.

Nobody had removed anything. They'd added. Two sentences. Enough that anyone who went looking for the man who'd asked about page 118 would find a man who also had views on bloodlines, and would file him, courteously and fully, under the usual thing.

I deleted it again, right there, plates on the counter. Then I posted a short dull note: A post under this name about page 118 was deleted by me in the summer. Someone else restored it and added two sentences I did not write.
Eleven people saw it. The forum shows a little number. Eleven. The version with the bloodlines had been seen by six thousand.

That's the arithmetic. I'd spent my life believing that the truth, said plainly, in the right place, would do its own work. Here was the right place and here was the truth and here was the number eleven.

I didn't think it was him. I need to say that. I thought it was a them, some pleasant man at a desk with a template. I put the phone away. I took the plates out. Julian looked up from the heater and said, "You alright, Jim? You look like a man whose bank's being difficult," and I laughed, because it was our bit by then, and said, "It's not the bank."
<hr />
He was, I'm going to say it plainly, wonderful.

He was good with Gert. He let the forum man talk at him for twenty minutes about the Sphinx and said "huh" in all the right places and never once let his face do what mine was doing. And he was good with Ana. Better than good. He asked her about her grandmother. Not sorry for your loss. He asked what she'd been like, and Ana told him about the knitting, the undoing and redoing, and he listened the way almost nobody listens, with his whole body turned to her and his beer forgotten, and when she'd finished he said, "She sounds like somebody who knew the doing was the point," and Ana's eyes went bright and she went inside for a minute.
She found me in the kitchen later. "I like him."
"I know."
"You never bring anyone home. Eleven years. You've never once brought a person home that you liked." She put her hand on my chest, flat, the way she does. "He's kind. He's actually kind. Keep him."
<hr />
It was nearly dark when he said it. We were by the fence, the three of us, Frank on his third telling of the gorilla, and the forum man asked where I found my books.
"The market," I said. "A man with a beard."
"Estate sales, mostly, isn't it," Julian said. "That's where the good ones come from. There was that professor's place near Deventer, last spring. A whole house of books."
He said it lightly. He'd said everything lightly all afternoon.

I have never said Deventer to him. Not on the course, not at the pub, not once. I have a face for tables and it held. "Before my time," I said. "I just buy what the man with the beard puts on the ground."
"Lucky man," said Julian, and I didn't know which of us he meant.

I filed it, and I want to be exact about where. Under he sells to half the east of the country. Under estate sales are in the paper. Under I ran a test on him an hour ago, and this is what a clever man does when he's been tested: he runs one back. The third one was the right folder. I put it in all three anyway.
Buddy never went near him.

All afternoon. Buddy goes near everyone, eventually, slowly, paying for every step. It's his whole policy. He went to Gert. He went to the forum man, which was a kindness. Then he lay down in the kitchen doorway and watched Julian for four hours and did not come out, and Julian, who'd asked about him before he asked my name, who'd crouched on a green to say hello, never once tried.
Mora went over once. Sniffed his shoe. Came back. Didn't go again.
"Does it bother you?" I asked him, when I brought him a beer. "He usually does the rounds."
Julian looked at the doorway for a moment. "Nobody's ever asked me that," he said. "People ask why the dog doesn't like them." He took the beer. "No. He's allowed."
Old dog, I thought. Tired. Too many people.
<hr />
That night, after the forum man had been put in a taxi with his theories and his empty bottle, Ana fell asleep on my chest at ten and I lay there with one arm dead, looking at the ceiling.

I'd got what I wanted. Two readings and a control. And I knew what it had cost, in one sentence: Julian had now walked my back lane, counted to the fourth gate, and stepped over the bowl my dog drinks from, and I'd sent him the directions myself.
Ana shifted. "You're thinking," she said, asleep.
"You're always thinking. It's like sleeping on a fridge." She settled. "He's nice, though. Golf man."
"Yeah," I said. "He's nice."
I couldn't sleep, so I thought about the number eleven instead, because eleven was at least a number.

Here's what the gorilla does, and it took me a barbecue to see it. It doesn't only make you laughable. It makes correcting it laughable. The man who says I never wrote that about bloodlines is a man talking about bloodlines. I could delete the post every morning and they could put it back every night with one more sentence, and each round I'd look a little more like the forum man in the taxi.
I couldn't win that. But I do know what to do when somebody changes a thing and says nothing changed. It's the only thing I know. You keep a copy from before.

So at one in the morning I went down to the kitchen and built what I build at work. It isn't clever. Once a night it copies my own threads and every public page of the forum, keeps each night's copy, and in the morning shows me what's different: what was added, what was taken out, and under whose name. A watcher. I've built forty of them for other people's systems. This was the first one I'd built for me, on my own laptop, with a dog asleep on my feet.
It needed a time to run. I gave it 02:14. I'd like to call that strategy. It was spite.
I ran it once by hand to see that it worked. It reported no changes, because it had nothing to compare with yet. One copy is no use to anybody.
Tomorrow there'd be two.

chapters.title: The promise
chapters.what: Small corrections only: his fear now has its specific reason (they can write as him, so the promise must be said to her face), the finished-sentence tell is cut, Deventer is corrected to a town he never named to Julian, and the narration says Julian, not Kalder. Source: v7/30.
blocks: It was four in the morning and I was on the kitchen floor, which by now you'll have gathered is not news.

What was news was that I was frightened. Not the interesting kind. Not the kind I get at work when a system starts telling me what it is, which has a pleasure in it I've never admitted to anyone. The other kind. The kind from a corridor when I was sixteen, which I'd spent twenty-five years making sure I never felt again by the simple method of never being responsible for anyone.
Four hours earlier a man had stood in my garden with a beer and said Deventer.

He'd said it lightly. He'd been saying everything lightly all evening, to everyone, and everyone had loved him, Ana most of all; he'd sat with her for twenty minutes by the back door while the sausages burned and listened to her talk about her grandmother and the knitting, and I'd watched her face do the thing it does when someone is actually listening, and I'd been grateful to him. I'd stood at my own barbecue being grateful to him. And then later, by the fence, with Frank telling the gorilla story for the third time, an hour after I'd asked Frank about a book that doesn't exist, Julian had mentioned a town. A small one. In the east. Where a man I never met had died in a blue chair.
I have never said the word Deventer to him. I've been there. A woman who sells curtains knows that, and her father's neighbor, and nobody on a golf course.

That wasn't what had me on the floor, though. I'd had since the pub to get used to the idea of Julian. What I hadn't got used to was two sentences about bloodlines. I'd read them forty times that night, on the laptop, between building the thing and testing it, and they were good. They sounded like me on a bad day. Somebody could write as me. And if they could add two sentences to a post about a book, they could add anything, anywhere, under my name: a threat, a confession, a goodbye. The day I needed Ana to believe me, there might be a page of me saying the opposite, dated the week before.

Buddy wouldn't go near him. All evening. Buddy, who goes near everyone, who has pressed his old head against the leg of every plumber and courier and Jehovah's Witness that has ever crossed our threshold, had lain in the kitchen doorway and watched Julian for four hours and had not once come out.

Ana found me at four. She came down for water and she didn't turn the light on, because she knows, and she sat down on the floor across from me with her back against the oven, and the dogs rearranged themselves around her the way they do, and she waited.

I didn't tell her about Deventer, or the post. I couldn't. I didn't have the sentence yet; I had a town and a paragraph and a dog in a doorway, and if I'd said it out loud at four in the morning it would have sounded like exactly what she'd been afraid, for months, I was becoming.
So I said the only thing I had.
"One day," I said, "I'm going to need you to believe me."
She didn't say anything.

"I'm going to say something, and it's going to sound mad, and I'm not going to be able to prove it. And I'm going to say it to your face. Not in a message, not in an email, nothing with my name at the top. You'll know it's me because I'll say it the way I'm saying this. And that day I need you to run."
"Take the dogs and go. To your mother's. Wherever. Don't ask me, don't wait, don't pack. Go."
She looked at me for a long time in the dark. Then she said, in her ordinary voice, the one she uses for the shopping and the toaster and whether we're out of coffee:
"Run where? I've got a Doberman."

And I laughed. I didn't mean to. It came out of me like something breaking, and Mora lifted her head at the sound and put it down again, and I sat on my own kitchen floor and laughed with my hand over my mouth so I wouldn't wake the street, and Ana watched me do it with her arms round her knees.

When I stopped she was still looking at me. And then her face changed, the whole of it, the way a room changes when someone turns the big light off and leaves the lamp, and she said, in the other voice, the one I've heard maybe four times in fifteen years:
"Okay."
Just that. Not okay, what's going on. Not okay, but. Okay.

I've thought since about what it cost her. To be asked that, by me, at four in the morning, with no reason given, and to say yes. I think it cost her more than anything I did afterwards cost me. I think it was the bravest thing anyone did in the whole of this, and nobody will ever count it, because it happened on a kitchen floor between two people and a Doberman and an old dog who had spent the evening in a doorway, watching a man who asked about him before he asked my name.
She got up and got her water. At the door she stopped.
"He was nice to me," she said. "Julian. Tonight. He was really nice."
"I know."
"I liked him."
"I know. So did I."
She nodded. "That's the bit I don't like," she said, and went up.

chapters.title: The schedule
chapters.what: The schedule now routes to him at the bank because he initialed Annex C (no second employer, no ledger room), he asks Ana to go before she reads it, "companion" is the annex's word, and after she leaves he takes his precautions: the eleven addresses into the watcher, the kennel, working from home, a camera on the front door. Source: v6/19.
blocks: It came to me because I'd signed for it. That's the only reason.

Earlier that autumn I'd reconciled Annex C and put my initials at the bottom, and in a bank your initials are a forwarding address. Whoever signs off the seat annex gets the program's quarterly paperwork to acknowledge. So on a Tuesday, between a capacity report and somebody's leaving card, there was an item in my queue called Continuity transfer schedule, Q4, thirty pages, with a button that said Acknowledge.

I'd expected a list of bunkers. I'd been reading too much. It was a list of transfers. Dates in the right-hand column, through the end of the quarter. In the left column, what was being transferred: records, mostly, by category, from the bank's own collections to the foundation's depot, each with a reference number, the way a careful institution moves things. Deaccessioned. For conservation. For review. Four hundred years of never throwing anything away, and here was the bank quietly sending things out of the building on a timetable.
And in the middle column, under a heading that just said Visit, addresses.

Not many. Eleven in the quarter. People who'd be visited in connection with the transfers, I assumed: readers of the records being moved, academics, dealers, the kind of people who'd notice a shelfmark had gone. One in Zwolle. One in Apeldoorn. One on a farm road I had to look up.
And one that was ours.
Our street. Our number. In a column headed Visit, with a date eleven days off, a Saturday, and in the notes field, where the other lines said things like pension and estate, one word:
Companion.
I knew the word. I'd initialed it. Companion animals are not accommodated, Annex C, a third of the way down, and I'd thought of Buddy in the car and signed anyway.
I printed the page. I acknowledged the item, because not acknowledging it would have been the louder thing to do. Then I went home.
<hr />
I didn't show her. I asked her to go to her mother's for a couple of weeks and I didn't say why, which is the stupidest way I know to ask Ana anything.
"Just until the—"
"No. You don't get to send me to Mum's like a parcel. Is this the thing from the kitchen floor? The run thing?"
"Not yet."
"Then no."

That was dinner. Afterward I went to let the dogs out, and I left my coat on the kitchen table, over the page, because I am apparently a man who hides things under coats. When I came back in Ana was standing at the table with the coat in one hand and the page in the other, reading. She'd read it upside down first, through the gap. She reads better upside down than most people the right way up.
She didn't say anything for a long time. Then she put her finger on a line.
"Why is our address on this?"
"It's a work thing. It's got the bank's name on it. Why is our house on a work thing, in a column that says visit." Her finger moved. "What's companion."
I could have said I didn't know. I'd been saying it for months, each time lying by exactly the width of a word I was too frightened to say.
"It's the dog," I said.
Ana looked at me.

"It's a word from a contract at work. A list of people who get a desk if the building burns down, and their families. There's a line in it that says companion animals aren't included. I signed it." I heard my own voice and it was very flat. "Somebody has put that word next to our house, next to a date. I don't know who. I don't know what a visit is. I think it's Julian. I don't know that either."
"Julian sells fire drills."
"Julian asked about Buddy before he asked my name."

She sat down. Not in a chair. On the floor, by the radiator, where Buddy was, and she put her hand on his head the way I do when I'm thinking. I'd never seen her do it before. She'd got it from me, the way I'd got the chin-on-the-head from her. We'd been trading gestures for eleven years without noticing, and this was the first one I'd given her that she didn't want.
"James," she said.
That's the first time. Eleven years. Mulder, Scully, you, hey, dickhead, with love. Never James. It landed in the kitchen like a plate.

"I'm not leaving you. I want to be really clear about that, because you're going to do the thing where you decide what I meant. I'm not leaving you." She stroked the dog. "I'm leaving the address. The address is on a list. I'm not stupid, I can read a list. And I'm taking Mora, because Mora barks at the postman and if somebody's coming to visit a dog I'd rather it was the one that bites." She looked at Buddy. "I can't take him. Mum's flat is up two flights. You know he can't."
"I know."

"So you keep him. And you keep that" — the page — "and whatever's in the folder called Reading, and you sort it out, or you don't, and either way you ring me every night at nine, and if you don't ring I'm coming back with my brother and a bat." She wiped her face with the back of her hand. "I don't believe any of it. I want to say that too. I don't believe there's a they. I think you've found a thing that doesn't fit, like you always do, and you've pulled it, like you always do, and this time something on the other end pulled back, and it's a person, not a they, and he was in our garden drinking our beer, and I liked him, and I'm so angry about that I can't see."

"Don't. Don't do the voice. Don't tell me a did-you-know. You haven't told me one since the pub and I noticed. It's the first thing you've ever stopped doing without telling me, and I've been waiting for you to see that I'd noticed." She stood up. "Help me pack the dog."
<hr />

We packed the dog. Mora's bowl, Mora's lead, Mora's toy, which she carried to the car herself, wet, in a state of joy, because the car means the course or the vet and both are the best thing that has ever happened. Ana's bag took four minutes. She's always been able to leave a house in four minutes. Her grandmother taught her, she said once. It's what a woman learns when the situation at home isn't ideal: where the bag is.
At the door she stopped. The hat was on its hook. She looked at it for a second and didn't touch it, and that was somehow the worst part.
"Nine o'clock," she said.
"Nine o'clock."
"Every night."
"Every night."

She put her hand on my face. Not squeezing. Then she took it away and went down the path with the Doberman pulling her toward the best thing that had ever happened, and I stood in the door with an old dog leaning on my leg and watched my wife leave the address.
The car went. The street was quiet. Somewhere, a bin.
<hr />
So I did what I do when I'm given a date. I got ready for it.

I gave the watcher the eleven addresses. It's the same build, with one more thing to read: the public notices, which in this country means the family announcements in the regional papers, the houses going up for sale, the businesses being wound up. Everything a street says about itself in print. If anything was published about any of the eleven, it would tell me at 02:14 with the forum.

I rang the vet and booked Buddy into the kennel, Thursday to Monday, around the Saturday. The girl asked if we were going away. I said sort of. If somebody was coming to visit a dog that Saturday, the dog would be in a building with a night nurse and a locked door.
I told Pieter I'd be working from home for two weeks. He said fine a little too quickly, the way he says most things to me now.

And I put a camera over the front door. Forty euros, the size of an egg. It sends a picture to my phone when anything moves on the path, which so far has meant the postman, a cat, and me, looking up at it.
That was the plan. The house would never be empty by day, the car would be in the drive, the door would be watched, and on the one day that mattered the dog wouldn't be there.
I sat down on the floor by the radiator, where she'd sat, and put my hand on Buddy's head.
"Eleven days," I told him. "We can do eleven days."
He didn't have a theory. I had a date.

chapters.title: Washington, 1953
chapters.what: 🟡 v9 — Claude, 16 Nov 2026. [Interlude, real]. KEPT. "Long weekend" is now four days in January; the long quoted sentence is left with Frank and the room is given here; claims I could not stand behind are cut or softened (page count, the classification dates, "never mentioned it again", the "lamb among wolves" quote, the burden-of-proof policy). Source: v7/32.
blocks: They met on a Wednesday in January, in a room in Washington arranged by the Central Intelligence Agency, and they were done by Saturday. Four days.

Five men. H. P. Robertson, who chaired it, a physicist from Caltech who had worked for the government through the war and after it. Luis Alvarez, who would win the Nobel Prize fifteen years later for something else entirely. Lloyd Berkner, Samuel Goudsmit, Thornton Page. Physicists, an astronomer, the kind of men who are asked to sit on panels because their names end arguments. Air Force officers came in to brief them, and an astronomer from Ohio State called Allen Hynek sat in, who was the Air Force's consultant on the subject and who would spend the rest of his life changing his mind about it.

The subject was flying saucers. The Agency called them unidentified flying objects, which was newer and sounded less like a joke, and the reason the Agency was interested at all was not that it believed in them. It was that the previous summer, in July, so many people had reported them over Washington that the reports had jammed the channels the Air Force used for real things. Radar operators at National Airport had tracked them. Jets had been scrambled. The newspapers had the story for a week. And somebody at the Agency had looked at the volume of traffic and thought, not what are they, but what would happen if the Russians did this on purpose, the night before they did something else.
So: five scientists, four days, and a question that was really about the telephone.
<hr />

They watched films. That is documented, and it matters, because the films were the best evidence the Air Force had. One had been taken by a Navy warrant officer in Utah, over Tremonton, the summer before: a cluster of bright dots moving against a blue sky, which Navy photo analysts had spent about a thousand hours on and concluded were not birds, not balloons, not aircraft. The panel watched it, and watched it again, and decided they were birds. Seagulls, probably. In the sunlight.

They heard the cases. They heard about radar returns and weather inversions. They heard Hynek, who was not yet the man he would become, say what the Air Force had hired him to say. They were, by every account including their own, unimpressed, and they were unimpressed quickly, in the way of clever men who have been asked to look at something beneath them and intend to be fair about it for exactly as long as it takes.

By Saturday they had a report. It was short, and it was secret. A cut version was let out a few years later. The full text was not public until the 1970s, and when it was, people who had spent twenty years being laughed at read it and understood, for the first time, that the laughing had been a recommendation.
<hr />
The panel found no evidence that the objects were a direct threat to national security. That was the headline, and it was true, and if the report had stopped there nobody would remember it.

It did not stop there. It found that the reports themselves were the threat. That the continued emphasis on them was resulting in a threat to the orderly functioning of the protective organs of the body politic. That the channels could be clogged. That the public could be made to panic, or could be trained to ignore real things.
And so it recommended a program. Of training and debunking.
That is the word. It is in the document. Debunking. The aim, the report said, was to reduce public interest in flying saucers, and the means were television, motion pictures and popular articles.

It suggested who might help. Psychologists familiar with mass psychology. Advertising experts. It suggested, by name, that the Walt Disney company might be approached, because of its experience with the public. It noted that the amateur groups which had formed around the subject, the civilian clubs with their newsletters, should be watched because of their potentially great influence on mass thinking.
Then the five men signed it and went home. Robertson to Caltech. Alvarez to Berkeley and, in time, to Stockholm. It was four days' work.
<hr />
Here is what is not in the report, and should be said.

Whether anyone ever ran the program as written is disputed. What is not disputed is that the Air Force officers who spent the next decade explaining lights in the sky as Venus or a balloon, to farmers and pilots and policemen who knew what Venus looked like, could not have been working from the report. It was secret. Most of them never saw it. If they were given a reason, the reason was clogged channels and the public good, and it was believable, because it was partly true.

Hynek was in the room. He went on explaining for another thirteen years, and then in Michigan in 1966 he offered swamp gas to a room full of reporters as a possible explanation for some lights, and the country laughed at him, and something in him finished turning. He spent the rest of his life on the other side. The point is that he did the work for thirteen years, and that the work got done.
Five of the cleverest men in the country, four days, and a recommendation that whatever people were seeing, the thing to do about it was to make the subject ridiculous.

The subject did become ridiculous. For a generation, in the richest country on earth, a pilot who reported something he could not identify knew he would be laughed at, and mostly didn't. The clubs with the newsletters became a joke, and the joke became the word, and the word is still the word.
If you want to read it, it is online. Look for the Robertson Panel, January 1953. It has been public for decades, and it has never once been news.

chapters.title: A street, night
chapters.what: The visit is no longer deniable: he is there to recover the original notebook, the car in the drive and the camera on the front door are why he cannot go in by day, and four days before the printed date he uses the back lane and the bowl, which is his own choice. His report leaves the dog out. Source: v6/20.
blocks: He walked the street twice, once in each direction, because a man who walks a street once is going somewhere and a man who walks it twice has lost something, and people forgive the second.

The Doberman didn't start up. He'd expected it to and had planned for the wait, and the silence told him what he'd been told the week before, which was that the wife had gone and taken the loud one. He stood for a moment at the corner with his hands in his coat and let the information settle, the way you let a drink settle, before you decide what it's for.

The gray car was in the drive. It had been in the drive on Monday at ten and at three, and on Tuesday at eleven, and a man who is at home on a weekday with his car outside is a man who has decided to be at home. There was something new over the front door, white, the size of an egg, with a small red light in it. He admired that. It was pointed at the path.

What he had been asked for was simple. The pages had been photographed in March, all of them, flat and square. What was wanted now was the original, because a notebook in two hands is a different thing from a photograph of one, and because it should never have gone to a market in a crate. He had been asked to recover it. He had been given a date for the visit, four days off, and a method, which was the usual one: ring the bell, wipe your feet, be kind. Nobody had told him what to do about a man who would not leave his own kitchen.

The lights were on. Kitchen, and one upstairs. Through the kitchen window, the end of a table, a coat over something on it, a shelf by the far wall with a sleeve of pale green on it, needles still in.
The old dog was at the window.

Not barking. Standing, with its front feet on the low sill where the radiator was, looking out, at him, steadily, the way it had looked at him from a doorway all one afternoon in October. He looked back. He'd always liked dogs, and the liking was not a tool, whatever the people above him assumed, and the old dog knew it wasn't, and had decided that it didn't matter, and he respected that more than he respected most of what he'd been told in rooms.
"Hello, foreman," he said, quietly, to the glass.
The dog didn't move.

He walked to the end of the street and along the back lane, where the gates were, counting, and stopped at the fourth, and looked at the latch, which was the kind that lifts, and at the gap under the gate, which was the width of a hand, and at the bowl just inside it. He had stepped over that bowl with a bag of ice. The old dog was let out last thing at night and drank from it, and from no other. The man had told him so himself, at this gate, in October.
He stood there for a time that he did not measure.

Then he crouched, and did what he had come to the lane to do, which took less time than tying a shoe, and walked back along the lane, and round, to the car. He'd parked it at the far end, under the one streetlight that was out, which he'd arranged in September with a catapult and a ball bearing, because it was a long job and a man thinks ahead. He sat. He didn't start the engine. He took the flask out of the glovebox and found it empty and put it back.

He didn't look at his phone. He didn't look at the house. He looked at the windshield, at the drops on it, and he thought about a sentence, the way he sometimes did, turning it to see if it had a side he hadn't seen. A frightened wife is a seat we don't have to pay for. It had a side. The side was that the wife had gone, and had taken the loud dog, and the man had stayed with the one that couldn't do stairs. A man like that does not leave the house for a date on a schedule. He leaves it for one thing.
At eleven the kitchen light went off. At twenty past, the one upstairs.

At ten past two the kitchen light came on. At a quarter past, the front door, and the man in his socks with something large in a blanket, and the gray car going out of the drive faster than it had ever gone in. The egg over the door watched it leave.

He gave it five minutes. Then he went in by the lane and the gate and the kitchen door, which was not locked, because a man carrying a dog does not go back to lock a door. He did not turn on a light. He lifted the coat. There was a page with a bank's name on it, and under it two green books that he left, and a folder that he left, and a thin one with no title on the spine. He took the thin one. He put the coat back as it had been. He was in the house for under two minutes, and he did not go near the front.
He drove to a flat with a name on the bell that wasn't his, and fed a cat.

In the morning he wrote three lines. Item recovered. Wife absent. Subject not approached. He read them twice before he sent them. He did not write a line about the dog. Nobody had asked for that part, and he had learned that the lines nobody asked for were the ones that got read.

chapters.title: The vet
chapters.what: It now happens four days before the date he was guarding: the vet has Buddy booked for Thursday, the camera shows a quiet front door, the thin book is gone, and he says it plainly. In Leiden he shows Noor the watcher's record of his post; she refuses to be a witness and writes the shelfmark from memory. Ends on the van; her silence and the turn to the floor are moved to the next chapters. Source: v6/21.
blocks: It started at two. Of course it did.

The sound woke me. Not a bark. Buddy hadn't barked since the summer; he'd stopped bothering, the way he'd stopped the stairs. It was the other sound, the one every dog owner knows from the inside of their own sleep, and I was on the landing before I was awake and in the kitchen before I'd turned a light on, and he was on the floor by the radiator, on his side, with his legs going.

I got the blanket under him. I got the car keys. I rang the number on the fridge, the one Ana had put there in June in her careful hand, EMERGENCY VET, with a little heart, because she puts hearts on things, and a woman answered on the second ring and said bring him, and I carried a twelve-year-old dog to a gray car in the rain in my socks.
The girl on the night desk typed his name while I stood there holding him.
"Buddy Klippe," she said. "We've got him booked in for Thursday."
"The kennel. Thursday to Monday."
"Yes," I said. "He's early."

The vet was young and kind and unhurried, and unhurried was the thing. She didn't rush. She looked at him and listened to him and put a hand flat on his chest the way Ana puts a hand on mine, and she said, "Okay. Okay. Not tonight, I think." And then, because I must have had the face: "I mean it. I don't say that. He's old and something's upset him badly and he's dehydrated, and I'm going to keep him for a few hours and give him fluids, and you're going to go and sit in that chair, and it's not tonight."
"What upset him?"

She looked at me the way vets look at you when the real answer is I don't know and they've been trained not to say it. "Something he ate or drank, maybe. Old dogs get into things. Did he get into anything?"
"He can't get into anything. He can't do the stairs. He drinks from a bowl by the back gate and eats what I give him."
"Then I don't know," she said, which I liked her for. "Sit down. I'll come and get you."
I sat down. There's a chair in every vet's waiting room at three in the morning and I've now sat in it. I had my phone in my hand and I did nothing with it for a long time.
Then I looked at the date. It was Wednesday. The schedule said Saturday.
<hr />

They let me take him home at six, on the condition that I brought him back on Thursday as planned, which the vet said with a straight face. I carried him in through the front, under the camera, and the first thing I did, before the blankets, was look at what the camera had seen. One clip. Me, at a quarter past two, in socks, with a dog. Then four hours of a path.

The kitchen was the kitchen. The light was on, because I'd left it on. The back door was shut and not locked, because I'd gone out the front with my arms full. My coat was on the table where it had been for a week.
I don't know why I lifted it. I'd like to say instinct. I think I just wanted my coat.

The page from the schedule was there. The two green books were there, and Els's father's folder, and the laptop, which is worth more than everything else on that table put together. The thin book wasn't.
I looked for it the way you look for keys: properly, twice, in places it had never been. Then I stopped and stood in my own kitchen and said it out loud, to the dog, because it needed saying plainly.
"I watched the date and the door."

A date somebody had printed for me, and the one door with a camera on it. I'd booked a kennel for the Saturday. I'd sat in this kitchen for a week so the house would never be empty by day. And someone had put a hand under the back gate on a Tuesday night, and waited for me to carry my dog out the front, and walked in the other way. I'd shown him the lane. I'd told him which bowl.

I thought about the police for as long as it takes to hear the sentence. Someone took a notebook with no title and left the laptop. I had photographs of every page; I'd taken them the night I first opened it, for the Record. A photograph of a notebook is a thing anyone could have made. I could have made it. Frank had already told me which column that goes in.

I made a bed on the kitchen floor out of every blanket in the house and lay down next to Buddy, in my coat, and slept badly. I woke twice, and both times he was awake, watching me, his head on his paws, the way he watches me go up the stairs from the bottom step.
Neither of us could help the other. Neither of us left.
At nine in the morning I rang Ana. I didn't wait for nine at night.
"He's okay," I said, first, before hello, because she'd hear it in my voice otherwise. "He had a bad night. He's okay. The vet said not tonight. She meant it."
Silence. Then: "What happened?"

"Something in his water. I think. The bowl by the gate." I had my hand on his head. "The date's Saturday. I had everything ready for Saturday. It was last night, round the back, and while I was at the vet somebody came in and took the professor's notebook off the kitchen table. Nothing else."
A long breath. "Are you saying Julian—"
"I'm saying what happened. I don't know who. I know who's walked that lane."
She didn't say anything for a while. When she did, her voice was different. "Send me a photo of him."
I did. Asleep, on the blankets, gray to the eyebrows.
"Okay," she said. "Okay. Nine tonight."
"Nine tonight."
<hr />
It was a photo that finally got me to check a person.

I had the barbecue pictures on my phone, the ones Ana had sent me afterward, look at your face, look at Gert's hat. In two of them, in the background, by the heater, there was Julian. And that afternoon I sent one of those pictures to Noor, in Leiden, because I was asking her about the forum man. That was all. The lonely one with the theories, who'd found our house from a picture; I wanted to know if he was a known thing, if he was harmless. I cropped it badly. I left in the heater.

She rang me that night. She'd never rung me. We'd messaged and I'd sat in her kitchen, and she had never once used a telephone, and it rang, and I knew before I answered that it wasn't about the forum man.
"The man by the heater."
"Julian. He's a golf friend. He sells the bank its—"
"His name's Kalder."
I was standing in the kitchen. I sat down on the floor, next to the dog.

"Julian Kalder. He was in the department the month after Hendrik retired, overseeing the transfer of the collection. He was in and out for three weeks, with a clipboard, and he was very kind about it. He learned everyone's names. He asked about my mother. He brought his own coffee, in a flask." Her voice was perfectly steady and I could hear what it cost. "I haven't seen him for nine years and I'd know him in the dark. Why is he in your garden?"

I'd like to say it took me a minute. It took no time at all. I'd known since the pub, the way you know a disk is going: every reading fine, and a noise. Julian K. on the invoice, who fixed my access in eleven minutes. The lanyard. The word from the professor's margin. Deventer. I'd had all of it, and all of it was mine, things I'd noticed, alone. What Noor had just given me was the one thing I'd never had on him, which was somebody else. A second person who'd seen that face nine years before it asked about my dog.
"He asked about Buddy first," I said. "On the course. Before he asked my name."
"Yes," said Noor. "That's what he does."
<hr />
I went to Leiden on Thursday. I took Buddy to the kennel first, since he had a reservation, and the girl on the desk said there he is as if he'd been away on business.

On the train I built the thing I was going to say to her. It went: you know him. You can place him. You were there, in the department, and you're a scholar, and you've got a name, and if you say it, publicly, with mine, then there are two of us, and two is a pattern, and a pattern is something a style guide can't reclassify.
I'd built her into a witness. On a train. Without asking.
She let me say it, the whole thing, standing in her hall with my coat on, and when I'd finished she said, "Your post is back up."
"I know."
"You told me you'd deleted it. I gave you my address because you'd deleted it."

I got the laptop out of my bag, in her hall, and showed her. It isn't much to look at. A list of nights. The first four: no post, only my dull note saying I'd deleted it. The fifth night: the post, back, dated the summer like always, with a third sentence that hadn't been there at the barbecue. My deletion the next morning. Two nights of nothing. Then the post again, and a fourth sentence.
"I take it down. They put it back, a little longer each time. This shows which is which." I turned the screen toward her. "It's the only proof I've got that I did what you asked."
She read it the way she reads paper, all of it, including the dull columns. "That's well made," she said. Then: "No."
"Noor—"

"No to the other thing. And you knew I'd say no, you've known since my kitchen, and you built it anyway, on a train, because you needed somebody to believe you. I'm not going to be that, James. The reason I'm alive is that I never once needed it." She wasn't angry. That was the thing. "A reader who persists is to be offered the opportunity to publish. You've just offered me one. In my own hall. You've done their job for them, and you've done it because you're frightened, and I understand, and no."
I stood there.
"Ask me something else," she said. "You're good at it when you're not frightened. Ask."

So I asked the thing I'd actually come with. "The notebook's gone. They took it on Tuesday night. I've got photographs of the last page, but a photograph is mine, I could have written anything and photographed it. The reference. Is there anyone else alive who's seen it?"

She looked at me for a moment. Then she went into the kitchen and came back with a slip of paper and a pencil, and wrote, against the wall, in a conservator's hand, without looking anything up. A letter, four digits, a slash, two more.
It matched. I didn't need to check. I checked anyway, against the photograph on my phone, one character at a time.

"It was on a crate," she said. "Nine years ago, in the transfer. I saw it for about four seconds and I told Hendrik that evening, and he wrote it at the back of his book and sat on it for nine years. And then last winter he wrote to them. Two pages about his rights and four lines asking to see it. That's not asking, that's arguing with a request attached.
