They gave him the second of December, and he was dead in March." She put the slip in my hand. "Nobody has ever simply asked. Go on the day. In person. Write it on their slip like any reader and put it on the table. And don't argue. You'll want to. You'll have a bag full of things. Ask first."
"Why are you giving me this?"
"Because you asked instead of argued," Noor said. "For once. Go home to your dog."
<hr />
I sent her one message on Friday morning. Thank you.
An hour later she answered. She'd never been quick before. One line.
There's a van on my street.
I rang. It rang out. I sent are you all right? ring me, and watched the screen for a while, like a man waiting for a kettle.

chapters.title: Leiden, Friday
chapters.what: Unchanged apart from American spelling; it now sits where the reader sees the bill for James's visit before he hears of it in "The other ten". Source: v7/35.
blocks: He came at two, because two is when people have eaten and not yet started wanting to go home, and he had a clipboard, and he wiped his feet.

Noor's studio was the ground floor of a house on a street of houses, with a bench by the window and a lamp on an arm, and she was at the bench when he knocked, and she saw him through the glass, and she did not pretend not to know him.
"Julian."
"Noor." He smiled. It was a real smile; that was always the problem with him. "It's been a while. May I?"

She let him in. She has asked herself since why she let him in, and the honest answer is that it did not occur to her not to. He was a man she had made tea for once in an empty building, and he had been, that afternoon, the only person in nine years who had sat with her in silence and come out the other side changed, and some part of her had been glad of him ever since, the way you are glad of a stranger who once held a door.

He admired the studio. He meant it. He asked about the sheet on the bench, which was a seventeenth-century letter with a tear across the signature, and he asked the right question, which was not what is it but what will you do, and she told him, because it was interesting and because he was interested, and he listened without waiting.
Then he opened the clipboard.
<hr />

He did not threaten her. She has told this to one person, and she told it to him carefully, and the care was in that sentence: he did not threaten me. He did something that she still, a year on, cannot find the right word for, and the nearest she has come is itemized.

He had a list of her clients. Not a long list; she is a conservator in a small city and there are perhaps forty people and institutions who send her work, and he had them, with dates, with what she had done for each and what she had charged. He read a few aloud, not all, in the tone of a man confirming a delivery address. The university library. Two auction houses. A museum in Haarlem. The archive of a foundation whose name she knew, because it was the foundation that had closed the library nine years ago, and because, she understood now, watching him turn the page, it had been her best client ever since.
He had her accounts. Not the figures; the shape. He knew which quarter had been thin and which client had paid late, and he mentioned the thin quarter, lightly, as one mentions weather.
He had her mother.

Not a photograph. A name, and the name of the care home in Oegstgeest, and the name of the ward, and the fact, which Noor had not told anyone, that the place had come up after a nine-month wait and that there were, she had been told, four people behind her on the list. He did not say anything about the four people. He said he was glad her mother was settled. He said it in exactly the voice he had used, nine years ago, to say thank you for the tea.
And then he closed the clipboard, and put it on the bench beside the seventeenth-century letter, and he said the only thing that could, if you were being very generous, be called the point.

"There's a man called James," he said. "I think you've met. I like him. I'd like him to be all right." He turned his tea mug a quarter turn on the bench, which was a thing he did. "The best way for him to be all right is for everyone who's spoken to him to have spoken to him about paper. Which is what you do. Which is all you've done." He looked at her. "Isn't it."
She did not answer. She had learned, from a professor, a long time ago, what a silence is for.

He waited. He was good at waiting; she had taught him, in a way, which was a thought she put down and has not picked up. And when it was clear that she was not going to speak, he nodded, as if she had, and said, "Good. That's good, Noor," and stood up, and thanked her for the tea.

She had made him tea. She noticed that only after he had gone. At some point in the afternoon, without deciding to, she had got up and filled the kettle and made him tea in the mug she keeps for clients, and he had drunk it, and she had not been afraid of him for one second of it, and that was the thing she could not forgive herself for.
<hr />
He left at twenty to three. He had timed it; she saw him glance at the clock on the wall as he picked up the clipboard, the way you check a parking meter.

She sat at the bench until it got dark. She did not work. The letter with the torn signature lay where it was, and she looked at it, and thought about a man who had once sat in an empty library and been made new over a mug of tea, and had gone out into the world with the new thing in him, and had used it, every day since, for this.

The professor had been right. He had been right about everything, which was his tragedy and hers. Never publish, never ask, always hide. She had kept the first two for nine years. She had broken the third twice, once in her kitchen and once on a Wednesday night on the phone, for a man with a dog who had asked her a question on a forum, and this was the invoice.

Her phone was on the bench. There were two messages on it from James, from that morning, after the call: thank you, and then, an hour later, are you all right? ring me. She had rung him on Wednesday night and said the name, Kalder, the man by the heater, he oversaw the library, and she had been, for the length of that call, the professor's student and not his warning. She looked at the second message for a long time. Then she turned the phone off, and did not turn it on again.

Quiet is a thing you can be made. She knows that now. She knew it before; the professor told her. But there is a difference between being told a thing by a dead man and having it done to you, on a Friday, by someone kind, with a clipboard, who wipes his feet.

chapters.title: The other ten
chapters.what: Moved up, before the floor. His own alert goes off, he checks the ten addresses against public records himself, learns from a colleague that Noor has stopped taking private work, and drives to Zwolle with Buddy, where he writes down Henk's words from Marijke and is given the flask. He tells her nothing, because of his rule. The phone calls with Ana and the plan to tell the helpers are cut. Source: v7/41.
blocks: Saturday came, the date I'd been guarding, and nothing happened on it. I sat in the kitchen from seven in the morning with the camera open on my phone and my dog in a kennel across town, and the postman came, and a cat. On Monday I collected Buddy, who walked out slower than he'd gone in but under his own power, and the girl on the desk said he'd been no trouble, which I already knew.
Noor's phone rang out on Friday. On Saturday it went to a message. On Sunday it did nothing at all.
Then on Wednesday, at 02:14, my own phone buzzed on the kitchen floor, where I'd more or less moved since the vet.

The watcher isn't supposed to wake me. It leaves a report for the morning. But I'd given the addresses a louder setting than the forum, the way you do at work with the one system that matters, and this was the first time it had used it.
1 new notice. Family announcements. Match: Boersma, Zwolle.
It was a thank-you.
For the many cards, the flowers and the kind words after the death of my dear husband Henk Boersma, my warmest thanks. They have been a great comfort. M. Boersma, Zwolle.

People put those in the regional paper here, a few weeks after a funeral, when the cards have stopped coming and they've run out of ways to answer them one at a time. I lay on the floor and read it three times. Then I went looking for the notice it was thanking people for, which took four minutes. Henk Boersma, seventy-three. Suddenly. October. The date on the schedule against that address was three days before he died.

The watcher hadn't missed it. It had done exactly what I built it to do, which was look forward. I'd given it eleven addresses and told it to tell me about anything new, because I was guarding a date, and it had not occurred to me, the professional, to ask the first thing I ask about any system I'm handed. What happened before I got here?
I'd had the page for two weeks. I'd looked at it the way you look at a bill you can't pay, which is quickly, and only at the line with your own name on.
Eleven addresses, and one of them was mine. That left ten.
<hr />
I did it the dull way, because the dull way is the only way I trust.

Public records. Death notices, which in this country are published in the regional papers and online, and are searchable if you know the format and have the patience. The land registry, which tells you who owns a house and when it changed hands, and charges you for each answer. The chamber of commerce, for anyone with a business. Houses for sale. Church newsletters, which are all online now and which nobody thinks of as a record. The dullest layer of a country, the layer that never makes the news, where a life leaves marks the way a glass leaves rings.
The schedule gave addresses, and addresses in this country are enough.
It took three evenings.

Zwolle I had. The regional paper gave it four paragraphs in October: the canal road toward Hasselt, a Sunday morning, an old green Volvo, no other vehicle. The police were quoted as saying the driver may have been distracted.

The second was in Apeldoorn. A woman in her fifties. Not dead. The chamber of commerce showed her translation agency dissolved in October. The land registry showed the house sold three weeks after the date on the schedule, quickly, for less than the neighbors had got. Then nothing. No new address in any record I could reach.

The third was a village outside Raalte. A retired teacher, a widower, seventy-eight. Not dead either. His church's newsletter wished him well in his new room at a care home forty kilometers away and said he would be glad of cards. The house was listed nine days after the date on the schedule. The photographs still had his books in them.

Three. Each one plausible. I said that to myself at the time and it's true. A man of seventy-three on a road he knew too well. A woman selling up. An old man who couldn't manage his stairs. If you handed those three to anyone, a policeman, a journalist, Frank, they'd shrug. Three things happened in three towns in the east of the country in one autumn. That's not a pattern. That's a region.
The fourth, fifth, sixth and seventh had gone quiet.

That's the only word I've got for it. No death notice. No sale. No dissolved company. But nothing new either, in any record, since the date on the schedule. In two of the four there was a last trace that bothered me: an account that had posted every few days for years and stopped; a sports club's newsletter that had listed a man as treasurer for a decade and in its November issue listed someone else, with no thanks and no farewell.
Four people I couldn't find and couldn't not find.
The eighth, ninth and tenth had dates still to come. The nearest was the twenty-eighth: a street in Hengelo, a woman's name alone on the land registry since 1987. I wrote the three dates down.

So: three resolved, four quiet, three to come. I count things for a living and I know what random looks like. It's clumpier than people think. You get runs that mean nothing. This wasn't clumpy. This was every past date on a list followed within three weeks by a plausible ending or by silence. That's not a run. That's a schedule being kept.

And it was the first thing in all of this that nobody had handed me. The thin book came in a crate. The folder came from Els. The job, the annex, the schedule itself: everything I had, somebody had put where I'd look. This I had pulled myself, out of records anyone can read. I'd have liked to think nobody knew I'd done it. The land registry sends a receipt for every lookup, with your name on.
<hr />
On Thursday I rang the workshop. Noor rents a press at a bindery in Leiden and the number is on her invoices. A man answered.
"She's not taking private work anymore."
"Since when?"
"Friday. Institutions only. If it's a family Bible I can give you another name."
"Is she all right?"
"She's working." A pause. "She said somebody might ring and ask that, and that I was to say she's working. So I've said it."

I thanked him. I'd been to her house twice, with my face, and rung her from my own phone, and somebody had spent a Friday making sure she would stop answering it. That was the bill for the shelfmark, and it had gone to her.
At nine I rang Ana and told her Buddy was eating. She asked what I was doing tomorrow.
"Driving to Zwolle. To ask a woman a question."
"What question?"
"I'll tell you when I know if it was the right one."
She let that go, which she wouldn't have a month ago. "Take Buddy."
"He's barely out of the kennel."
"He's old and he sits in the car and he makes you look like a man with a dog instead of a man with a question. Take Buddy."
I took Buddy.
<hr />

Zwolle is a nice town and the house was in the nice part of it, a decent house on a street of decent houses, and there was a green Volvo in the drive, old, immaculate, the kind of car that gets washed on Sundays. I hadn't expected the car. I don't know why. They'd pulled it out of a canal and somebody had brought it home.

I'd thought about what to say for the whole drive and thrown all of it away by the time I rang the bell. I'd decided to say I was from the pension fund. I'd decided to say I was a journalist. Standing on the step with an old dog sitting at my heel I found I was going to say the forty percent of the truth that fits in a doorway.

She was small and neat and seventy, and her name, she told me later, was Marijke, and she looked at me, and then at Buddy, and her face did the thing people's faces do when they see an old dog, which is soften before they've decided to.

"I'm sorry to bother you," I said. "My name's James. I saw your notice in the paper. I'd like to ask about something your husband used to say. I don't work for anyone. I've got a dog, in case that helps."
She looked at me for a long moment. Then she looked at the Volvo.
"You'd better come in," she said. "He likes a kitchen, does he? Henk's did."
Buddy went under her table and lay down against her feet, the way he does with people he's decided about. She put her hand down and found his head without looking.
<hr />
She told me a good deal that I'm keeping, because she told it to me, and some of it was just a woman talking about her husband to a stranger with a dog.

Henk's father had been a draftsman, and he'd had a thing he said. Henk had heard it as a boy and taken it for a story about the war, and had thought about it, on and off, for sixty years. Then in the spring his brother died, and Henk came home from the funeral and sat in the car in the drive for an hour, and when he came in he said: it isn't Father's. It's mine.
"And after that he said it to everybody. The bowling club. The man who does the gutters. They'd started looking at him. I told him, Henk, leave it. Nobody wants to hear it."
"What did he say? The words. Can you remember how he put it?"
"I can say it in my sleep. He said it the same way every time. That's what frightened me."
"Would you mind if I wrote it down?"
She looked at the notebook, and at me, and I think that was the moment she decided. Nobody had written anything of Henk's down except a policeman.
She said it. I wrote it. I read it back to her and she stopped me on one word. I'd written afraid.
"Frightened," she said. "He said frightened."
I crossed it out and wrote it again and read her the whole thing.
It was a bridge, in the rain. Somebody had hold of my hand and said not to be frightened, only to hold on.

"That's it," Marijke said. "That's all of it. He never had anymore than that. A bridge, he didn't know where. Rain. And a hand." She turned her cup. "And then he'd sit on his own. His right hand. He'd put it under his leg like a boy who's been told not to touch something. He said it went cold. I bought him gloves, in May."
I kept my face still.
"Did anybody ask him about it? Apart from the bowling club."

"The man from the pension." She said it without any weight. "In October, while I was at my sister's. He rang ahead and he came when he said and he wiped his feet. Henk told me on the phone that night. A nice man, he listened, he liked the car. He'd brought his own coffee in a flask and apologized for it. He borrowed the Volvo for an hour to move a box, and brought it back washed. And Henk said, he was so pleased, he said: Marijke, he asked me if I recalled anything else. Nobody asks me that."
She got up and took something down from the shelf above the coats and put it on the table between us. Steel. Unmarked. The kind you can buy in any shop.

"He left that. Nobody came back for it. The pension people said they'd never sent anyone. I thought, well, somebody did." She looked at it. "Three days after, Henk went out along the canal road while I was at church. They said distracted. I had the car checked, afterward, by the man in Kampen that Henk trusted. He had it a whole day. He told me it was the best-kept Volvo he'd seen in twenty years, and he was sorry, he'd hoped to find something."
Buddy sighed under the table.
"He wasn't distracted," she said. "He was happy. That week. He'd stopped saying it for a while, because I'd asked him, and that week he started again, and I thought, oh, let him."
<hr />

I had the page in my bag. Her address, a date, and in the notes field the word pension. I had two other addresses that had been tidied the way hers had, and four that had gone quiet, and a woman in Hengelo with two weeks. I could have put all of it on her kitchen table next to a flask.

I didn't, and for once I can say why. I have a rule. I tell nobody until I know what they were told and can put their own paper in front of them. I knew what she'd been told: distracted. But the page in my bag wasn't her paper. It was the bank's, with my acknowledgment on it. The last time I told somebody a true thing with nothing of their own to rest it on, she wrote a kind note about my sleep. So I told Marijke nothing, and it wasn't only cowardice this time.
At the door she said, "You wrote it down like it was worth something."
"It is."
"Then tell me one thing. Is he somewhere? Henk." She had her hand on the frame. "You came about what he said. Is he somewhere?"
She'd let me into her kitchen and given me her husband's sentence, and that was the question it cost her to ask, and I didn't have it.
"I don't know," I said.

"No," she said. "The minister didn't either, he just took longer." She went back in, and came out again with the flask, and pushed it at me. "Take it. I don't want it in the house now. You'll know what to do with it."
I didn't. I took it.

She looked at the Volvo, and at the dog, and at me. "You're not from anyone. I believe that. You've got the face of a man who's not from anyone." And she closed the door gently, the way you do when there's an old dog on the step.
<hr />
I sat in the car for a while before I started it. Buddy was asleep on the back seat. The flask was on the passenger seat and the notebook was open on my knee.
A bridge, in the rain. A hand. Somebody saying not to be frightened.

I'd had cold mud, and a low gray sky, and a hand, at a funeral in the spring, for the length of a camera flash. I'd filed it under no sleep. I'd filed it more than once. And here was a retired engineer in Zwolle I'd never met, who'd had a place, and weather, and a hand, after a funeral, and had been asked very politely whether he recalled anything else.
One of those is a tired man at a grave. I didn't have a folder for two.
I closed the notebook and put it in the glovebox. Then I took it out again and put it in my coat.

chapters.title: A corridor, sixteen
chapters.what: Unchanged apart from the title, one number (twenty-five years, to match his age) and American spelling; it now sits after "The other ten", directly before the floor. Source: v6/22.
blocks: The corridor has a machine at the end of it that sells chocolate and crisps and one kind of sandwich, and the boy has been looking at the machine for forty minutes, because it is the only thing in the corridor that isn't a door.

He has a coin. His mother gave it to him, from her purse, without looking, the way she has given him everything for the last three days, and said get something, and he has not got something, because getting something would mean walking to the end of the corridor and the end of the corridor is further from the room, and he has decided, without deciding, that the distance matters.

He doesn't know what the machines in the room are for. There are four of them and they each make a different sound and nobody has told him which sound is which, and he is sixteen, and he reads everything, and he has read the little cards on the front of two of the machines and they are in a language that is almost English and isn't, and he is ashamed, in the corridor, that he wants to know what they do more than he wants to be in the room.

A nurse comes out. She's nice. They've all been nice. She crouches, which is wrong, because he's taller than her standing, and she says, "He's comfortable," and the boy nods, because he has learned in three days that comfortable is the word they use when the other words have run out, and that you nod.
"Is there anything you want to ask?"

He has eleven things. He has written them in his head in order. What the sounds are. What the number on the second machine means and why it went from 94 to 88. Whether the thing in the bag is the same thing it was yesterday, because the bag is a different color. Whether comfortable is a measurement. Whether anybody here knows, actually knows, not guesses, what happens in the room on the last night, because he has a feeling, from the way the nurses have started to look at his mother, that it is going to be tonight, and that nobody is going to say so, and that the not-saying is a kindness that he is expected to accept the way he is expected to accept the coin.
"No," he says. "Thank you."
She squeezes his arm and goes.

Later, in the room, his father's hand is on the sheet, and the boy looks at it, and he knows the hand better than he knows his own, the knuckles, the one nail that never grew right after the door, and he does not take it, because taking it would mean something and he does not know what, and he is afraid of doing the wrong thing in a room where everything is being done right.

A doctor speaks to his mother in the doorway. He is a kind doctor, and tired, and he has a clipboard, and he says a sentence that the boy will not remember and then another that he will. "There's some paperwork. Not now. Leave it for now."

Leave it for now. His mother nods. The boy watches her nod and watches the paperwork go away under a kind man's arm and understands, at sixteen, in a corridor, that there is a category of thing that is not his, that is handled, that goes away under an arm, and that the correct response is to nod.

It's tonight. Nobody says so. At four in the morning the sounds change and then there are no sounds and a nurse he hasn't seen before puts a hand on his mother's shoulder and says, very gently, "He's at peace now. He's in a better place."

The boy hears it. He hears it as a sentence. He turns it over, once, in the corridor, standing by the chocolate machine with a coin in his fist, and he thinks, clearly, in the voice he will have for the rest of his life: based on what? And then he thinks: don't. And he doesn't. He puts it away. He has nowhere to put it, so he puts it where there's nowhere, and he will find out, twenty-five years later, on a kitchen floor, that it's still there, exactly as he left it, with the coin.
His mother is crying. He holds her coat. He stands half a step behind and to the left. He is good at it. He has no idea what he's doing.

At six they let him go back in for a minute, alone, and the hand is on the sheet, and he does take it now, when it can't mean anything, and it's cool, and the knuckles are the knuckles, and he stands there holding his father's hand for the first time since he was small and thinks nothing at all, which is the only time in his life he will manage it, until the floor.
Afterwards, on the way out, he puts the coin in the machine. It takes the coin and gives him nothing. He looks at it. He doesn't press anything. He doesn't ask anyone. He leaves it.

The paperwork was done in the spring. He never saw it. He went back to school on the Monday and was fine, and was told he was fine by a series of professionals over the next twenty years, and was graduated by every one of them, and never once mentioned the machine.

chapters.file: 38 — The night he stops being afraid.md
chapters.title: The night he stops being afraid
chapters.what: The floor now has a cause: Henk's words are a second copy of what he filed at the funeral, so he sits down to read his own again. He gets the hand and no words, and the cold hand afterward. The many lives, the flashes "all his life", the observer entry and the job counting him are cut; the forty-one are one edit because each removes a report of something received. Source: v6/23.
blocks: I got home from Zwolle with a flask I didn't want and one sentence in a notebook, and I put them both on the kitchen table and looked at them until it got dark.

I know what to do with one copy of a thing. You file it. One odd reading from a tired system gets logged and ignored, and that's not laziness, that's procedure. I'd had a place, some weather and a hand, at a grave, on four days of bad sleep, and I'd put it under no sleep, and I'd have told anyone on my team to do the same.

But now there were two. A retired engineer in Zwolle whom I'd never met, after a funeral, with a bridge where I had mud. In my work, when two systems that have never spoken to each other report the same odd thing, you stop saying noise. You go back to the first one and read it again, properly.

The trouble was that the first one was the length of a camera flash, eight months old, and inside my own head, and I'd read it the way I read page 118 the first three times: fast, by its shape, looking for permission to stop. I wanted to read it slowly. There's no shelf to fetch it from.
So that night I sat down on the kitchen floor and tried to get it back.

That's all it was. Every door in the house shut. Phone in the drawer. Lights off except the one over the cooker, which Buddy likes, because it means food is possible. I sat with my back against the cupboard where his biscuits are, legs out, hands on my knees, and tried to remember a cemetery.

What I got was a memory of a memory. Gold light, crows, and a patch of cold mud I'd described to myself so many times it had gone flat, like a postcard of mud. I sat there for an hour remembering so hard that I got a headache, and Buddy watched me from the blankets with an expression I'd have described, in a review, as concern for a colleague.
The second night, the same. I tried a breathing thing from the forum and fell asleep and woke at three with my neck in the shape of the cupboard handle.

The third night I nearly didn't. I sat down, and Noor was working and not answering, and my wife was at her mother's with a Doberman, and there was a woman in Hengelo with a date against her name, and I thought: this is the stupidest thing you have ever done. You're a man on a floor. This happens to other people, the ones on the forums, the ones with the glow. You check paper. Go and check some paper.
And I'd checked all the paper there was. That was the thing. So I sat.
On the fourth night I stopped trying.

I don't mean I gave up. I mean something smaller and I can't make it bigger. I'd been trying to get it back for three nights the way you try to fall asleep, which is the one thing trying prevents, and on the fourth night, around two, with the cooker light on and the dog breathing, I thought: fine. It's not coming. Sit here anyway, because the floor's warm and the dog's here and there's nothing on upstairs. And I stopped waiting.
<hr />
It came back.
Not the memory. The thing itself, the same as at the grave, except that it didn't stop after a flash, because this time I didn't stop it.

My cheek was against cold mud. I could tell you there were small stones in it. The sky was gray and low and wrong, and I was lying down in a way you don't choose, and I wasn't frightened of that, which I noticed. And the hand was there. Cracked at the knuckles. Reaching for mine.
At the grave that's where I'd cut it off. This time it arrived. It took hold.

And I knew it. At the funeral I'd said almost knew, like a word in a language you've forgotten. There was no almost. I couldn't have given you a name, or a face; there wasn't a face. I knew it the way I know my own front door in the dark, the weight of it, where it sticks. I had known that hand all my life and I had never once seen it in this one.
Whoever it belonged to said something. I'm sure of that the way you're sure someone's talking in the next room. I didn't get the words. Henk got words. I got a hand, and it held on.
Then it was the kitchen.
<hr />
I checked. Of course I checked.

I sat on the floor and looked at the kitchen on purpose, the way you look at a room after you've been told a system's fine, to see if it is. The cooker light was on. The clock on the oven said 02:14, which I'd like to say I made up, and didn't. The dog's bowl was where the dog's bowl is. The fridge was humming the hum it has. Buddy was on the blankets with his head on his paws, watching me, awake, and had been, I think, the whole time. I was not glowing. I was a forty-one-year-old man in socks on a kitchen floor, and if Ana had walked in at that moment she'd have seen a tired man and a dog and said come to bed, and she'd have been right.
One thing was different. My left hand was on my knee. My right one I was sitting on.

I hadn't put it there. It was cold to the wrist, the cold you get from carrying shopping home in January, and I'd tucked it under my leg like a boy who's been told not to touch something. I looked at that for a while. A woman in Leiden at her kitchen table, with one hand under her arm. A pair of gloves, bought in May. It lasted about a minute. Then it was just my hand.
Nothing else in the room had changed.
What had changed was that I wasn't afraid.

Not brave. I don't mean brave. I mean that a thing that had been running in me since a corridor when I was sixteen, a thing I'd never once heard because it had always been there, the way you don't hear the fridge, had stopped. And in the quiet I could hear what it had been. Not the men in vans. The other thing. The one under the other ones. The one I'd asked a nurse about with my mouth shut at sixteen, and a grave about with my mouth shut at forty, and had built a hobby and a job and a persona and a folder called Reading in order never to hear myself ask out loud.

I hadn't been told what happens. I want to be clear about how little I'd been given: mud, a sky, a hand. No words. But the thing I'd been afraid of for twenty-five years turned out not to be the mud. It was a room where everything is done right and nobody takes hold of anybody. And somebody had.
It was gone. Like a bath. I sat there and listened to it not be there.
<hr />
"Buddy," I said.
He lifted his head.
"I think I've got a soul."

And I was embarrassed. On the floor, alone, to a dog. My face went hot. I heard the sentence in the kitchen and it sounded like the forums, like the glow, like a man in a tinfoil hat, and I nearly took it back, and then I thought: he's a dog. He's a professional. He's not going to tell anyone.
"Sorry," I said. "I know. Bit much."
Two thumps of the tail. He put his head back down. He's heard worse.
<hr />

Then the list read itself back to me. I didn't get up and fetch it. I couldn't have; it was gone off my table two weeks ago. But I'd read it thirty times, and I had it, and sitting there I understood I'd been reading it wrong, the way I'd read page 118 wrong: by its shape.

Forty-one entries. I'd had them in two piles. Forty about the beginning, a hand taken out of a story about where things came from. And one, twenty-six, about two rooms in Utrecht and something that passed between them. I'd asked Noor why the same people would care about both, and she'd said it was the only question.

They weren't two kinds. Transmitted became arisen. Shared became coincident. In another, about what small children say, remembered became imagined. In every one of the forty-one, somebody had received something, or handed it on, and a dull, trustworthy book had said so in a plain sentence. And in every one, after the second impression, nobody had. The thing just stood up by itself.

They never touched the wild versions. Noor had told me that in her kitchen and I hadn't known what to do with it: it's in every bookshop, with a crystal on the cover. What they took out was the sober one. The page a sensible person could check himself against.

Because that's what I'd been missing for eight months. I'd had a hand in the mud and nothing plain to put beside it, so I filed it, four seconds at a time. One person with that is a man who needs sleep. He needs a second copy before he's anything else: a page, or another person. Somebody had spent a century removing the pages. The people, I was starting to understand, they handled by appointment.
<hr />

I stayed on the floor till it was light. Not doing anything. Just sitting with it, and with the dog, the way you sit with a system that's finally reporting properly and you don't want to touch it in case it stops.

Somewhere in there I went back to a corridor. I knew I would. Sixteen, a coin, four machines with four sounds. A man saying leave it for now. A nurse saying he's in a better place, and a boy turning the sentence over once and putting it where there was nowhere. And a hand on a sheet that I didn't take until it couldn't mean anything.
I couldn't go back and take it. I'm not telling you I did. I sat on a kitchen floor twenty-five years later and knew what it would have been for.

At seven I got up, slowly, with the noise men my age make, and let the dog out, and made coffee, and stood at the back door watching him drink from the bowl by the gate. I'd scrubbed that bowl four times. He hadn't held it against the bowl.
At nine I rang Ana.
"I'm okay," I said.
Silence on the line. Then, in a voice I'd never heard from her, careful, the voice you use near something that might be real: "You sound okay."
"What happened?"
"I sat on the floor."
"James."

"I sat on the floor for four nights, and on the fourth one I stopped being afraid of the thing. The big thing. The one from the funeral. I can't tell you how and I'm not going to pretend I can. But I'm not afraid of it anymore, and I wanted you to hear it from me before you heard it in my voice." I had my hand on the dog's head. "And I've been keeping things from you in folders. I'd like to come to your mum's. Not to bring you back. To tell you. All of it, once, on a table. Twenty minutes. You can decide after."
A very long quiet.
"Bring the hat," Ana said.

chapters.title: Urfa, 1994
chapters.what: 🟡 v9 — Claude, 16 Nov 2026. [Interlude, real]. KEPT. One addition, saying plainly what moved (monumental building before farming) and that the burial and the "temple" are still argued; details I could not stand behind are cut or softened (the laboratory re-run, the distance to his earlier site, how much was dug, the cities comparison). It still never says Tresidder found it. Source: v7/38.
blocks: The hill had been looked at before. That is the first thing to say, because it is the thing that matters.

In 1963 a joint survey from Istanbul and Chicago had walked the plateau north-east of Urfa, in the far south-east of Turkey, near the Syrian border, cataloging anything that looked old. They noted a low mound with broken limestone slabs on top, and flint on the surface, and a mulberry tree that the local people treated as holy, and they took the slabs for the markers of a medieval cemetery, and they moved on. The hill was given a few lines in a report. The report was filed.

The farmers called it Göbekli Tepe. Potbelly Hill. They had been plowing around the stones for generations and moving the ones that got in the way, and nobody had asked them, and they had not thought to say.

Thirty-one years later a German archaeologist called Klaus Schmidt, who was forty and had been working at a site farther north that had since gone under the water of a dam, and was looking for somewhere of his own, read the survey's report. He read the line about the hill. He read about a cemetery and limestone slabs and worked flint, and it did not fit: flint like that, by the survey's own description, was wrong for the Middle Ages by about ten thousand years.
So in October 1994 he drove out and climbed it.
<hr />

What he saw from the top he described many times afterwards, and the description did not change, which in an archaeologist is a kind of honesty. The slabs were not gravestones. They were the tops of pillars, T-shaped, limestone, set in rings, mostly still buried, and the whole hill, as far as he could tell from standing on it, was not a hill at all. It was a mound of what people had put there. Fifteen meters of it. Deliberately.

He said he knew within a minute. He said, in the version he gave most often, that he had a choice on that hilltop, which was to walk away and tell nobody, or to spend the rest of his life there, and that there was no third option, and that he chose the second, and that he was right about the rest of his life, because he died in 2014, at sixty, with most of the hill still undug.

The first excavation season was 1995. When the dates came, the oldest pillars had been raised around nine and a half thousand years before Christ. Before pottery. Before farming. Before the wheel, before writing, before any of the things that the textbooks said had to come first, because you cannot build on this scale without a surplus and you cannot have a surplus without agriculture and you cannot have agriculture without settling down. That was the order. Everyone knew the order. Schmidt's pillars were some six thousand years older than Stonehenge, and they had been carved, with reliefs of foxes and boars and vultures and scorpions and a headless man, by people who hunted and gathered and were not supposed to have built anything.

He put it in a sentence that got him into trouble and is now in the guidebooks. First came the temple, then the city. Not the other way round. People had gathered to build this, and the gathering had required feeding, and the feeding had, perhaps, taught them to farm. The thing that the whole story of civilization said was the effect might have been the cause.

That is what moved, and it is one line: monumental building came before farming, not after it. The rest is still argued over. Schmidt believed nobody had lived on the hill, and that the builders had in the end buried their own enclosures on purpose; the people who dug after him have found reasons to doubt both. Nobody has moved the date back. The enclosures filled with rubble and bone and flint and earth, and the hill grew a mulberry tree, and farmers plowed around the stones, and a survey saw a cemetery, and the file was closed for thirty-one years.
<hr />
That is the record, and it is enough. But there is one more thing on the record and it belongs here.

Nobody hid Göbekli Tepe. There was no conspiracy. A survey team in 1963 looked at a hill and saw what they expected to see, because the thing they were looking at was not possible, and when you are standing in front of something that is not possible the human eye is very good at finding the possible thing nearby and settling on that. Gravestones. Medieval. Move on. The report was honest. The people who wrote it were competent. They were simply looking at a thing from the wrong side of a sentence that everyone knew was true, and the sentence did the rest.
It took one man, reading an old report slowly, to notice that the flint was wrong.
<hr />

About fifteen kilometers from that hill, in the autumn of 1929, an Englishman with one book to his name walked out of Urfa on foot, heading east, with a notebook, and did not come back. He was last seen on the road. He had spent a year in the region. He had, in his one book, said that the traditions of the first settled peoples appeared to have been transmitted to them, and two years after he disappeared somebody changed that to arisen among.

There is nothing in any archive that puts H. M. Tresidder on Potbelly Hill. The farmers who might have remembered an Englishman asking about the stones were dead by 1994. The 1963 survey did not record any earlier visitor. This book will not tell you he found it, because it does not know, and neither did the professor, and neither does James, and he has looked.
What is known is where he walked out of. And what is known is what was a morning's walk from the road, under a mulberry tree, in 1929, where it had been for eleven thousand years.

chapters.title: The long table, again
chapters.what: Kalder now sees the crossing on the Wednesday round, from the terrace, and no longer watches from the lane; no date moves; Bram authorizes the offer of five seats and says he will go himself when the time comes; the dog is admitted ("it was efficient") and the room does not like it. The depot transfer and the closing note about the review are cut. Source: v6/24.
blocks: "You've got the week," Bram said. It wasn't a question. He had the folder and he hadn't opened it, and he was looking at the man at the table the way he looked at the index on a Monday: fondly, and for a number.
"When?"

"I can't give you the night. I can give you the morning after it." He had his hands flat on the table. "Wednesday. He plays at seven, alone, with the old dog in the cart. I was on the terrace with a coffee. He didn't see me. On the sixth he stopped with the putter in his hand and stood there for about two minutes, looking at his hands. Both of them. Turning them over, like a man who's been given the wrong change."
"That's all?"

"He missed the putt and laughed. He's played that course for years and I've never seen him laugh at a putt. He talked to the dog all the way down the seventh. He didn't check the car park once, coming in." A pause. "He's not afraid."
"Of us?"
"Of us, yes. The way you'd be afraid of a car. The other thing's gone. You can see it. He stands differently."
Bram smiled. "Looking at his hands."
"That's the one I like. That's the one that goes in the file, if we kept that kind of file." Bram turned the folder a quarter turn. "And you'd know."
The man at the table didn't say anything.

"I'm not asking to be cruel, Julian. I'm asking because I've got six handlers who'd have sat on that terrace and seen a man miss a putt, and one who'd have seen what you saw, and I need to know I'm reading the right one." Bram folded his hands. "You'd know. You're the only one of mine who would."
"How long, for you?"
"Nine years."
"Leiden."

"The month after the transfer. Her kitchen. I'd been in and out with a clipboard for three weeks, and on the last day she gave me tea and didn't say anything for twenty minutes and neither did I." He looked at the table. "I didn't go looking for it. It was in the room. It went through me, and I drove to Zwolle, and I sat in the car, and I understood what the index was. Before anyone told me."
"And you reported it."
"I reported it."
"Your own."

"I'd been told what the right-hand column was for. I filed it, and I understood that I had become the only instrument you had that could see the thing it was measuring, and that there was a seat in that." He lifted his hands off the table and put them back. "So I asked for the seat."
Bram was quiet for a long moment.
"I've always thought that was the bravest thing anyone's done in this building," he said, eventually, and he meant it, and that was the problem with him too. "And the saddest. You know that."

"And now there's another one. In a kitchen. With a dog." Bram opened the folder, finally, and took out the sheet, and turned it to the light, and the right-hand column had a line on it that wasn't a number. It was a name. "I need the line, Julian. Hands, yes or no. In your words."
The man at the table looked at the sheet for a long time.
"James has hands," he said.
The first name. He heard himself use it and so did Bram, and neither of them remarked on it, and it sat on the table between them like a cup.

"Thank you." Bram wrote. One word, in the right-hand column, next to the name. "Then we do what we said we'd do. He reconciled the annex and signed it. He read the schedule and acknowledged it and didn't go to a newspaper. He's kept a dead man's appointment in his diary since the summer, and the head would like to make the offer himself; he enjoys it. Five seats. Him, the wife, three of his choosing. I'll authorize it today." He closed the folder. "The date stays where it is. And if it comes to visiting anybody, afterward, I'll go myself. I'd like you to hear that from me."
"Because of the dog."
"Was it you?"
Bram waited.

"He was at home every day. The car never left the drive, there was a camera on the front, and he'd made his arrangements around the date you gave me. I needed him out of the house at night for four hours and I got four hours. The item was on the kitchen table. The dog lived." He said it the way he read out yardages. "It was efficient."

Nobody had asked him for it, and they both knew that. The room had heard a great many things said quietly over a great many years, and it did not like this one. Bram looked at the table, and then at the window, and then he moved the folder two inches further from the man's hands.
"He'll know," Bram said.
"He knows."
"And he'll sit across a table from you again, if he's asked to?"
"He's polite." The man thought about it. "And he'll want to see if the dog was right."
Bram stood. He went to the door, and stopped, with his hand on it, and said, not turning round: "Nine years, and you've never once asked me whether I've got them. Hands."
"Why not?"
"Because you'd have told me," the man said. "You tell everyone everything. It's how you seat them."
Bram laughed, once, surprised, and went out.

chapters.title: Twenty minutes
chapters.what: The scene and its order are kept; the objects are now the ones he made or signed (captures, referral, annex, watcher printouts, Henk's words, the flask, photographs where the thin book was). Added: Ana names his tell and learns where he was at the grave; she asks about the next address and he says his rule. Corrected to canon: one employer, her mother's flat, no date moved by the floor, and she is coming home. Source: v6/25.
blocks: Ana's mother lives in a flat where every surface has a cloth on it, and I put the objects on the cloth, one at a time, in the order I'd decided on in the car, and Ana sat opposite with her arms folded and her mother in the bedroom with the television up loud on purpose, and Mora under the table with her chin on my foot, because it had been three weeks and in Mora's world that's a resurrection. Buddy was in the car downstairs with the window open a hand. Two flights.

"Twenty minutes," I said. "You can stop me. You can throw me out. I'm going to put things on the table and tell you what they are, and I'm not going to tell you what I think until the end, and then you can decide."

The two books. "This is a sentence that was changed in 1931, two years after the man who wrote it walked into some hills. They changed one line and left the typos so nobody'd check. I don't know who. I found it on our kitchen floor. That's the night you came down for water and I said I hadn't found anything weird."
"I remember."

A stack of photographs, where a book should have been. "These are pictures of a list of forty more. Kept by a dead man and his grandfather. I was handed it in a crate. The book itself was taken off our kitchen table the night Buddy was at the vet. Nothing else was. I don't know who took it. I know who'd walked the lane."

The three pages. "This is the style guide the edits were made from. His daughter found it in a dresser. It's got a section on what to do when someone like me notices, and the answer is: agree with him, and reclassify."

The captures. "This is a job that runs every night at the bank and sends forty kilobytes to a foundation. It's a list of staff numbers with two words beside each. I'm on it three times. Wrote (dealer). Asked (job). Posted (forum). After I asked what it was, it got a new name, an owner and a ticket. This screenshot is the only place the old name still exists. The bank pays for it per person. It's called a recall index. I don't know what they do with the number."
The referral, the yellow copy. "This is a form Pieter gave me in a car park at the golf day. Bereavement, sleep, preoccupation with historical documents. I signed it."
"You signed it?"
"On the hood of the car. It seemed polite. I kept the yellow one."

The annex. "This is a list of who gets a desk and a bed if the bank burns down, and their families. Forty-nine rows. Nine of them are people the bank has never employed. It says no pets. Those are my initials on all four pages, and that's Pieter's under them. I checked it for them."
The page from the schedule. She looked at it and didn't touch it. "You've seen that."
"Our address."
"Our address. The word in the box is the annex's word for Buddy. The visit was four nights early, round the back. Nobody came to the door. I don't know what a visit is supposed to be."

The watcher's printouts. "This is a thing I built the night of the barbecue. It copies the forum every night and shows me what changed. Three weeks of it. People who post a question get left alone. People who post what Henk said, more or less, in their own words, get a reply with bloodlines in it inside four days, and then they stop posting. Four of them so far. I don't know why. That's a label, not a theory."
"Who's Henk?"

My notebook, open. "A retired engineer in Zwolle. His address is on the schedule. He drove into a canal in October, three days after a nice man came about his pension. These are his words, from his widow. I wrote them down in her kitchen and she corrected me once."
Ana read them. She read them twice.
The flask. "And this is what the nice man left on her table. Julian carries one like it. So does half the country. I don't know that it's his."

The slip from Noor. "This is a number a woman in Leiden wrote from memory because I asked instead of argued. It's an item in the foundation's archive. She's gone quiet since. Not dead. Working. There's a difference, and it's my fault."

Page 212. "This is the tool Frank sent us a link about, with the skull. It's been told, out of the box, never to see the job. One boring sentence in the defaults, that only a role called vendor support can see. Revision four. It's got a review date on it, the thirty-first of December."
And then the last thing, which wasn't an object, so I put my hand flat on the cloth where it would have gone.

"And this is me. On the floor. Four nights. I can't put it on the table. I can tell you I've been afraid of dying since I was sixteen, in a corridor, and that I'm not anymore, and that it happened on the kitchen floor with the dog watching and the oven clock on. I got a hand. That's all. Somebody's hand, holding mine, somewhere cold. No words. Then my own hand went cold for a minute and I sat on it. I'm not glowing. I'm not going to make you do anything."
I took my hand off the cloth. "That's it. Nineteen minutes. What I think is on the table. You can throw it out."
<hr />
Ana didn't say anything for a long time. Her mother's television laughed at something.
Then she reached across and picked up the notebook, and read Henk's two lines again, and closed it, and put it down exactly where it had been, square to the cloth, the way her grandmother would have.
"You sit on your hand," she said.
"I just told you that."

"No. I'm telling you. You did it at the funeral. At the grave, after everyone had gone past. You let go of me and put your hand in your armpit like you'd burned it, and in the car park you were sitting on it. I thought it was your circulation. I nearly said something." She was looking at my right hand. "Where were you?"
So I told her. Cold mud, a low sky, a cracked hand reaching, for about as long as a camera flash, while a priest said amen. And then her face, and her question, and my yes.
"You were in mud," she said. "At Grandma's grave."
"For a second."
"And then you came back and told me she was okay."
"I said yes. It wasn't a very good yes."
"No," Ana said. "It wasn't. I took it anyway." She wiped her eye with the heel of her hand, angrily, like it had let her down.
Then she said, "I don't believe it."
"Okay."

"I want to say that, so you've heard it. I don't believe there's a them. I don't believe a bank in a wig has been paying for a machine that counts souls. I don't believe you've got a soul, or I do, but not like that, not like a thing that gets counted, that's insane, James, that's the most insane thing anyone's ever put on my mother's tablecloth." She wasn't crying. She was doing the other thing, the clear thing. "And I've been sitting here for nineteen minutes watching you put it there, and you did it the way you do the toaster. In order. Boring. With the bits you couldn't prove labeled. You said I don't know six times. I counted. You've never said I don't know six times in a year."
"I've stopped pretending."

"I can see that. That's what I can't get past." She unfolded her arms. "You look different. You've looked different since the phone call. You stand like somebody who's put something heavy down, and I've been married to you for eleven years and I've never once seen you without it, and I didn't know it was there until it wasn't."
"So what do you believe?"

"You." She said it like a slap and a kiss at once, the way she says most things that matter. "I believe you. I don't believe it and I believe you and I don't know what to do with that, so I'm going to sit here until I do."
<hr />
What she did, in the end, was ask for the plan. Not the memoir. That's her. Twenty minutes of what, and then: so what are you going to do about it, Mulder.

"I don't have a plan. I've got a problem. Here's the problem." I moved the schedule next to the captures. "Everything I do to find out what it is gets written down. I asked about the job and I got a row. I wrote to a dealer and I got a row. Then I tried shutting up at work, and what I got for that was a friend who comes to barbecues. I can't ask and I can't stop."
She put her finger on the schedule. Not on our line. Lower.
"This one hasn't happened yet."
"No. Hengelo. A woman on her own. Nine days."
"So what are you doing about her?"
"Nothing."
"Nothing."

"I have a rule. I tell nobody until I know what they were told and can put their own paper in front of them. I don't know what she's been told. I've got nothing of hers. If I knock on her door with this, I'm a stranger with a bank's list and a story, and that's all I am."
"You made that up. The rule."
"When?"
"After the last time I told somebody. At work. She wrote a kind note about my sleep."
She looked at me for a while. "And if something happens to her, in nine days, while you're keeping a rule you made up."
"Then it happened while I kept it. I know that."
She didn't tell me it was all right. I'd have liked her to. She took her finger off the page.
"What do they want? With you."
"To buy me, I think. They put me on the program the week I asked. The annex is seats. There's room on it."
"They'd offer you me," Ana said.
"And the dogs."
"No. It says so. I initialed it."

She stood up. She went to the kettle, which is what her family does instead of deciding, and she filled it, and she didn't turn it on, and she stood with her back to me, and Mora's chin stayed on my foot.
"I'm coming home," she said. "Tonight. Mora's eaten a cushion and Mum's stopped pretending she hasn't noticed."
"Ana, the address is still—"

"The address is still on a list, yes, I can read. And you've just told me the list runs to the end of the year, and I'm not spending it in my mother's spare room waiting for whoever they send to turn up at our house and offer you a desk while I'm here. If they want to offer you a desk they can offer it with me in the room." She turned round. "That's the plan. That's the whole plan. I don't believe it and I believe you, and the four of us are going to sit in our own kitchen, and if somebody comes to the door, I'll open it. Because I'm not in. Whatever that means. I'm not on any list of yours or theirs, and I'm the only one of us who can say that, and I'd like to see what happens to whoever they send when the wife answers the door and offers him tea."

I looked at my wife, standing by a cold kettle in her mother's kitchen with her arms folded, and understood that she'd just done the thing I do, the thing I'm supposedly good at, which is to look at a system from outside and work out what it can't handle, and that she'd done it in four minutes.
"Okay," I said.
"Good. Where's the hat?"
"In the car. With Buddy."
"Then it's coming home too."
It looked ridiculous on the back seat, next to an old dog, and Ana looked at it through the window, and for the first time since the pub she almost laughed.
Almost. We're not there yet. But I saw it go across her face, and I'd have signed for forty more years of almost.

chapters.title: Frank, loose
chapters.what: "The band" is folded in: James brings the foundation's published accounts and the invoice and says nothing, and Frank finds the grants in the cold years himself, plus one cold year with no grant that neither can explain. The watcher reports the eighth address at 02:14, and James says what it cost. The simulation talk, the stand-up Frank can't remember and Kalder at the glass are cut. Source: v7/43 and v6/26.
blocks: Frank came round on a Saturday because I asked him to, which I'd never done, and he knew it, and he brought beer anyway, which is how I knew he was worried.

Ana was home. She'd been home a week and a half, with Mora, who had eaten a cushion at her mother's and shown no remorse, and the house had gone back to being a house: two dogs, a kettle, somebody upstairs. I'd forgotten how much of my thinking I do against the sound of another person in a building.

Frank sat at the kitchen table. Buddy went and lay under it, across his feet, which he does to people he's decided about, and Frank said, "Oh, hello," and went very still the way people do, and I thought, good, that'll keep him here.
"So," Frank said. "You've got the face."
"I don't have a face."
"You've had the face since about April. Pieter's noticed. Pieter thinks you're job-hunting." He opened a beer. "I told him you don't job-hunt. You'd have to talk to people."
"Thank you."
"So what is it. And if it's the Egyptians, I'm going home."
<hr />

I'd thought for a long time about how to do this. For Ana I'd put every object on a tablecloth, because Ana needed to see that I'd labeled what I couldn't prove. Frank needed the opposite. Frank needed almost nothing, and no story, and to be left alone with it.

There was a reason for that, and it was his. In his kitchen in the summer he'd put the thin book in the wrong column in under a minute: anything from a market is a story with paper attached. He was right. Most of what I had, somebody had handed me. So I'd spent a week making a pile of the things nobody had. And before I carried that pile into a room in December, I wanted to know whether paper like that could move the most stubborn man I know when I wasn't there to help it.
So I put two things on the table and kept my mouth shut.

The first was a sheet I'd made myself. Thirty-one years of quarterly invoices from a foundation to the bank, pulled from our own ledgers one evening, a line per quarter: Continuity reconciliation (recall index). Per flagged person, with the number of persons, the rate, the total, and the same two initials approving every one.

The second was a stack. The same foundation's annual accounts, which it has to publish, like any charity. Thirty-one of them. I'd downloaded them from the register for nothing. Income on one page, grants made on another.
"What am I looking at."
"Money."
"I can see it's money. Whose?"
"The top one's ours. The bank pays that, every quarter, and has since 1994. The stack is theirs, the people we pay. It's public. Anyone can get it."
"And what am I looking for?"
"I'm not going to say."
"James."
"If I tell you, you'll find it to be nice, or you'll not find it to be right. I want to know what's there if nobody tells you. Kill it. Like the screenshot."
He looked at me. Then he looked at the stack, the way he looks at a log file somebody says is clean. "Have you got a pen?"
<hr />
It took him three hours and I'm not going to pretend I enjoyed them.

He started with the invoice, because it was one page. He's good with numbers; it's why he's good at the job. He found the steps on his own in about four minutes. Six of them in thirty-one years, the count going up by clean amounts and never coming back down.
"Per flagged person," he said. "Flagged how?"
"I don't know how. I know what the list looks like. It's the honeypot."
He put the pen down. "The what?"
"The job Pieter told you lot was a honeypot, the week I was out. That's what it sends. Staff numbers and two words. It's billed per head, to these people."

"That's not what a honeypot—" He stopped. He looked at the last step on the sheet, and at the date beside it, and I watched him work out which week in June that was. He didn't say it. He picked the pen up again.

Then the accounts. He checked the income first, which I hadn't expected and should have. The foundation's income from reconciliation services stepped in the same six years as my sheet. Their books and ours, kept by different people in different buildings, with the same staircase in them.
"So your sheet's real," he said. "Fine. A bank pays a charity. It's dull, but it's real."

Then he read the grants. All thirty-one years. Heritage. Conservation. Digitization. A great deal of roof. I made coffee. Ana came down, looked at Frank, looked at me, and went back up without a word, which is the nicest thing she's ever done for him. Buddy slept on his feet.
Around midnight he started writing years in two columns on the back of an envelope.
"This is stupid," he said.
"Okay."

"No, it's stupid. Look." He turned the envelope round. "Most years they give money to roofs. Some years they give it to something else. A production company, 2003, enough to make a documentary. A publisher, 2011. A retreat center, 2014, with a name like a yogurt. A festival. Something that calls itself a channel. Five of those. Six, if you count the second payment to the yogurt."

"And I got bored and wrote down the years where your head count dips. Inside a step. It goes down some years, did you know that? Not much. Fewer people flagged." He tapped the left column, then the right. "They're the same years."
I didn't say anything. I'd promised myself.

"Every time your number's low, these people pay somebody to make a film about pyramids." He sat back. "That's the wrong way round, James. If you were hiding something you'd pay for the nonsense when people got close. When the number's high. This is paying for nonsense when nobody's asking at all."
"Why would you do that?"
"I don't know. To keep them asking? Badly?" He heard himself. "Oh, you bastards," he said, to the envelope. And then, to me: "You knew."
"I had the two piles. I hadn't put them together. I wanted to see if you would."
"That's a horrible thing to do to a guest."
"You got beer."
He went back down the columns with the pen, because he's Frank and a pattern that neat offends him. And that's where he found the other thing.
"2007," he said. "It's cold. Coldest on the sheet. And there's nothing. No film, no yogurt. Roofs."
I looked. He was right. I hadn't seen it.
"Maybe it's in a different line."
"I've read every line. I've read the notes." He turned the page toward me. "It doesn't fit."
"So what was different in 2007?"
"I don't know."
"Good," Frank said. "I'd have left if you did."
<hr />
"Now," he said. "What's wrong with it."

He told me. He was thorough. He said five grants in thirty-one years is a small number, and a man with a pen can find five of anything. He said foundations are badly run and bill in round figures because somebody's nephew does the accounts. He said flagged is a word consultants use for everything, that the job could still be what Pieter said it was, and that my number turning up on a list the night after I'd asked about the list was the most ordinary thing a security tool could do.

"And the book thing," he said. "The sentence. I believe you found it. I think it's a dead scholar's second thoughts, and I think you've built a cathedral on it because you needed somewhere to put what you felt at that funeral. I say that as your friend, and as someone who's watched you do it with smaller things for three years."
I didn't argue. I'd heard it all before, in my own head, in my own voice, which is better at it than Frank's.
"So I don't believe it," he said.
"Okay."
"I don't believe any of the story." He put his finger on my sheet, on the last step. "I believe the invoice."
I looked at him.

"That's the bit I can't do anything with. I've sat here all night trying to make that be something boring, and I can't. Their books match yours. Nobody steps a contract up by one clean unit in the week a monitoring engineer opens his mouth at stand-up, unless the unit is the engineer." He took his finger off. "And I found the film thing myself. That's what annoys me. If you'd told me, I'd have had it in the dead column by ten."
"I know. That's why I didn't. The memo's the table."
"Don't quote me at me."
<hr />
It was nearly a quarter past two when he stood up, and I know that because my phone buzzed on the counter while he was looking for his coat.
It has a sound for this. I'd heard it once before.
1 new listing. Match: Hengelo.

I opened it standing up. A terraced house, photographed that week. Three bedrooms, a long garden, somebody's reading glasses still on a windowsill. For sale owing to the owner's move into residential care. Available immediately. Thursday had been the date on the schedule. It was Sunday morning now, by fourteen minutes.
"What's that?" Frank said.
"A house has gone up for sale."
"Whose?"

"A woman I've never met. I knew her address and I knew the date, for more than two weeks, and I didn't go, because I've got a rule about not telling people things until I can prove them." I put the phone face down. "She's in a home now. That's what the rule cost, and it wasn't me who paid."
Frank looked at me for a long moment. I saw him decide not to ask, and I was grateful. He's better at that than anyone who's only met him at a barbecue would guess.
"Is that on one of your sheets?" he said. "Her. The house."
"It's in the paper. It's public."
"Then put it with the others," he said, and found his coat.
At the door he said, "What are you doing with it. The pile."
"Taking it to a meeting on Monday."
"With who?"
"The people in the stack."
He nodded slowly. He looked back into the kitchen, where Buddy had got up from under the table and was standing at the window in the dark, watching the street.
"He does that," Frank said.
"He does that."
"I still don't believe it," Frank said, and went out to his car, and sat in it for a minute before he drove away.
Ana came down. "Well?"
"He believes the invoice."
"Is that good?"
"It's Frank," I said. "It's the best he's got. It's better than I had."

I cleared the table. The photographs of the thin book and Els's folder went back in the drawer. They were true and they'd been handed to me. What went in the bag for Monday was the other pile. Two copies of a book I'd compared myself. Captures I'd taken. A sheet of invoices I'd pulled. Accounts anyone can download, and an envelope in Frank's handwriting. Five weeks of a forum, copied nightly. Ten addresses, checked, with one more line to add.
I added it.

chapters.title: Leiden, 1931
chapters.what: Unchanged apart from the title and American spelling; it sits directly before the ledger is read, so the reader knows what the struck line is when James does not. Source: v6/27.
blocks: The visitor had a good coat and did not take it off, and he stood in the composing room with the smell of ink and hot metal around him as though it were a smell he'd known all his life, which the printer, whose name was Van der Hoeven and whose father's name had been on the door before his, took to be a courtesy and later understood to be a method.
"One line," the visitor said. "Page one hundred and eighteen. I have it written out."
He had. On a card, in a hand that had been taught to be legible, with the old words on the left and the new words on the right, and a vertical rule between them, drawn with a straightedge.

Van der Hoeven read it twice. He was a careful man. His father had been a careful man and had gone bankrupt being one, and the son had learned that care was a thing you did with your hands and not with your opinions, and so he read the card with his hands, holding it to the lamp, and then he said, "It's not a correction."

"The old line is not wrong. I don't read English well. But I read enough. The old line is a scholar's sentence. The new line is also a scholar's sentence. They say different things, and neither of them is a mistake."
"That's right."
"Then I don't understand what you're paying me for."
The visitor looked, for a moment, almost pleased. "You're the fourth printer I've asked," he said. "The first three understood immediately. I'd rather it was you."

He explained. Not why; never why. What. The plate for page 118 was to be opened. The one line was to be re-set, exactly, with the spacing adjusted so that the justification would hold and the line count would not change. Nothing else on the plate was to be touched. There were two misprints on that page, and a flaw in the top margin where the metal had pitted, and they were to stay. The copyright page was to say second impression and nothing more. No corrected. No revised. The book was to go out under the same words on the title page, to the same continental trade, at the same price, and the author, who had walked into some hills in Anatolia two years before and had not walked out, was not to be mentioned, because there was no one to mention him to.
"A reader will see it," Van der Hoeven said. "Someone. Eventually. Somebody will have both."

"Somebody will. In fifty years, or a hundred. And when he does, he'll find two typos left in and a flaw in the margin, and he'll think: they didn't even clean the plate. Who would go to the trouble of changing one line and fix nothing else? And he'll decide that it must have been the author, before he went. Or a lazy compositor. Or nothing." The visitor put the card down on the stone. "The misprints aren't an oversight, Mr. Van der Hoeven. They're the reason he'll stop looking. A clean plate is a confession. A dirty one is just a printer."
Van der Hoeven looked at the card on the stone for a long time.
"My father would have refused."
"Your father went bankrupt."

"I'm not threatening you. I want to be clear about that. I don't do that. I'm telling you that there is a foundation, in this city, that is about to take an interest in the Leiden printing trade, and that it will be placing work for forty years, and that the houses it places work with will be the houses that are still here in forty years. That's all. I've told the other three the same thing. I'd rather it was you, because you asked what you were being paid for, and in my experience the man who asks that is the man who'll do it properly and then never think about it again." He buttoned his coat, which had never been unbuttoned. "You have two sons."
"They'll be looked after. Not because of this. Because of the forty years. This is one line." He went to the door. "I'll come back on Thursday for the proof. Leave the flaw."

Van der Hoeven set the line himself. He did it at night, when the apprentices had gone, because he found that he didn't want to be watched doing it, and he noticed himself not wanting that, and did it anyway. He set it with the spacing adjusted so that the justification held. He left the two misprints. He left the pit in the margin, and when he inked the proof and pulled it and held it to the lamp, the page was perfect, and identical, and said something else, and he stood in his father's shop with it in his hands and felt, he would have said, if there had been anyone to say it to, like a man who has been asked to move a chair in a room and has done so and the room is the same room and will never be the same room again.
On the Thursday the visitor came, and read the proof with his hands, and nodded, and paid, in cash, and did not haggle.
"It's very good," he said. "You'll never see me again."

He did not. The foundation placed work with the house for forty-one years. The two sons took it over in 1958 and sold it in 1972 to a firm that became a firm that became a firm, and the plates were melted in a war, and the books went out, every copy, under the same words on the title page, to every library and every dealer and every scan, wearing the first impression's clothes.

Van der Hoeven kept the card. He never knew why. His grandson found it in a drawer in 1994, with a straightedge rule down the middle, and threw it away, because it was in English, and it was one line.

chapters.title: The reading room, continued
chapters.what: He asks first: the reference on a slip, on the table, and Aylin is told to mark it "in conservation". He then collates both impressions against the 1931 ledger in pencil and lays down only paper he made or pulled himself. The old man thanks him for the annex and reads the referral aloud for Anneke. Five seats, no dogs; no; he leaves the lower door shut. The method speech, the hearings and the "what I loved" ending are cut. Source: v7/45.
blocks: The generator stopped.

I don't know how long it ran. Long enough for the tray to stop shivering against the table; I'd been watching the ledger shake on its wedges. The old man had waited for it to finish the way you wait for a truck to pass before you go on with a sentence. The woman by the window hadn't moved at all.
"Tests," he said. "They test it on Mondays. I've asked them not to and they tell me it has to be Mondays. One doesn't argue with engineers." He smiled at me. "Does one."

I'd practiced a first sentence at two sets of traffic lights. It went: I'd like to ask for an item. It wasn't a sentence I needed. There'd been a pad of request slips on Aylin's desk downstairs, next to the visitor book, the kind every reading room has, and I'd taken one while she was turning the big book toward me, because I was a reader and that's what readers do.

I filled it in on my knee under the table, in pencil, in capitals, so there'd be no argument about my handwriting. A letter, four digits, a slash, two more. My name. The date. I didn't look at my phone to check it. I'd checked it against Noor's slip in her hall, one character at a time, and I'd had it by heart for three weeks.
Then I put it on the table, square to the edge, on his side of the tray, and took my hand away.
He didn't pick it up. He read it where it lay, upside down, which is a thing I'm used to watching people do, and he looked, for a moment, almost pleased.
"He asked too," he said.
He didn't say who. He didn't have to.

"Two pages of argument and four lines of request. We answer requests. He was given this day, and he didn't come, and then you did, carrying his date around like a man who's inherited a dentist." He turned the slip round with one finger so that it faced me. "Nobody else has, you know. In nine years. People write to us about their rights. They write to us about Sumerians. You've written down a shelfmark and asked for it, at the desk, on the day. It's very nearly moving."
"Can I see it?"
He lifted his voice very slightly, not turning his head. "Aylin."
She'd been in the doorway. I don't know for how long. She came to the table with her glasses on their cord and he slid the slip toward her with the same finger.
"Mark it, would you. In conservation."

She looked at the slip. Then she looked at him, and it was the second time I'd seen her face move. She knew the shelfmark. You could see her know it: a woman who knows where every item in her building is, and that this one was on its shelf, sound, twenty meters from where she stood.
"In conservation," she said.
"If you would."

She wrote it, in ink, in a neat hand, across the bottom of my slip where the status goes, and initialed it, and the ink was still wet when she put it back on the table in front of me, and she went back to the doorway without looking at anybody.

So: I'd asked. I'd done the one thing a dead man wrote at the bottom of a page and a woman in Leiden told me to do before anything else. And what I'd got for it was a piece of paper that said the item I'd asked for was unavailable, in somebody else's handwriting, which, if you think about it, is the only thing they ever give anyone.
"Thank you," I said, and put it in my pocket. It had her initials on it.
<hr />
"You've got a bag," the old man said.
"I've got a bag."
"Everyone who gets this far has a bag." He folded his hands. "Go on, then."
I'd thought about the order for three weeks, and in the end I did it the way I'd do it at work, which is: start with the thing on their screen.

I took out the two green books. Tresidder, 1926. The professor's, first impression, and mine, second. I opened them both at 118 and put one on either side of the tray, so that the ledger lay between them, open at its page with the one line struck through and the other written beside it.
Then I got a pencil out and did what I do.

I'm going to describe it, because the thing itself is dull and the dullness is the point. The ledger entry was a printer's job line, in Dutch, in a hand with no interest in being read: a customer, a title, a quantity, a page number. One hundred and eighteen. Beside the struck line somebody had written in a smaller hand, in English, eight words. I read them against the professor's copy, left to right, with the pencil. They matched the first impression, word for word: appear to have been transmitted to the early settled. The struck line. Then I read the line written beside it against my copy. Appear to have arisen among the first settled. The second impression. Letter for letter.
