I ticked each word in both books, lightly, in pencil, the way a proofreader does. Nobody stopped me. I'm a reader and they were my books.

"You've put the two impressions either side of your own order book," I said. "The struck line is the first printing. The line beside it is the second. The second says it's the first. I found the difference on my kitchen floor in April, and I've found what ordered it on your tray, and I've just checked them against each other with a pencil. Those are three copies that agree. In my work that's not an argument. That's a finding."
"It's very tidy," the old man said. He was looking at the pencil ticks, not at me. "I've always liked tidy."
I put the rest down. Not fast. Each one where I could reach it.

The captures: a list of staff numbers and two words each, printed, with three rows circled in my own pen. Wrote (dealer). Asked (job). Posted (forum). "This is what runs at the bank at fourteen minutes past two. I caught it myself. It's called bc-recon-nightly now, with an owner and a ticket. This is the only place the old name still exists."
The invoice sheet. Thirty-one years, one line per quarter, pulled from the bank's own ledgers one evening. "Reconciliation, per flagged person. Six steps. The last one was the week I asked."

For the first time, the woman by the window turned her head. A few degrees. Enough that I saw her face properly: a face from a photograph on an intranet page. Anneke de Wit, head of risk, whose department had approved that invoice, or whose signature had, thirty-odd times, sitting in a reading room on a Monday in December watching an engineer from her own bank put it on a table.
She didn't speak. But she looked at the sheet, and she kept looking at it, and the old man noticed that.

The accounts. Thirty-one of them, downloaded from the register for nothing, with an envelope on top in Frank's handwriting: two columns of years. "Your own grants. Films, a publisher, a retreat center, in the years the count was low. A friend of mine found that on his own, at my kitchen table, with a pen. Twenty-oh-seven's cold and there's nothing. We don't know why."
The old man looked at the envelope a little longer than at the others. "We fund a great many things," he said. "Some of them are embarrassing. That's philanthropy."

The watcher. Five weeks of printouts, a page a night. "I copy the forum at 02:14 and show what changed. Questions get left alone. Anyone who describes a last minute, a place and a hand, gets dressed up inside four days and then stops. Four so far. My own post, which I deleted for a woman in Leiden, has been put back six times, a sentence longer each time."
"You're very thorough," he said.

The schedule page, with my acknowledgment on it, and in the margin, in my hand, what had happened at eight of the eleven addresses. Canal. Sold. Care. Quiet. Quiet. Quiet. Quiet. And the eighth, added on Sunday morning: Care. House listed. Beside our own line, one word, and then: Nobody came to the door. Round the back, four nights early. Dog lived.
And last, because it was the only thing on the table I hadn't made or pulled, Henk Boersma's words in my notebook, and next to them a steel flask.

He read it all. He took longer over my handwriting than the typed parts. He read Henk's two lines twice. Then he put everything square on the tray, beside the ledger, and he sat back and did something I hadn't expected, which was laugh.
Not at me. A small, delighted sound, the laugh of an old man who's been shown a card trick and seen how it's done and likes it more for that.
"Oh, this is very good," he said. "Anneke, isn't this good?"
She didn't answer.

"They all come in here with the old things. The pyramids. The flood. The thing in Turkey. They sit where you're sitting and tell me about Sumerians, and I listen, because it's polite, and it's never once been interesting, because the old things are a result. You've brought me the thing being done. With a pencil." He said pencil like a vintage. "And I'll tell you what I liked best, since you've earned it. Annex C."
"The annex isn't on the table."

"No. It's in a file at your bank with your initials on it, and it's the cleanest reconciliation that program has had in years. Forty-nine rows, every name checked against a record. Nine vendor allocations signed for. Four pages initialed, and your manager under each. The pets clause read, I'm told, and initialed anyway." He inclined his head. "Thank you for that. Genuinely. It saved somebody a week."
I'd known that was coming, in some form, since Pieter's office. It still landed.
"You haven't said one of them's wrong," I said.

"Mr. Klippe." He folded his hands. "I'm going to do you the courtesy of not insulting you, and I'd ask the same. You've put nine things on this table and asked me, in effect, to confirm each one, and I'm not going to, because I don't need to, and because each of them could be explained in a court by a bored man in an hour. A printer's correction. A vendor's job with an owner and a ticket. A charity's grants. A forum. An invoice for a service you don't understand. Some sad things that happened in the east of the country in an autumn." He tilted his head. "You know what they are. I know what they are. What they are in a room is nothing."
"Then why am I in one?"

He didn't answer that. He reached, instead, into the inside pocket of his jacket, and took out a single folded sheet, and unfolded it, and I knew the form before he'd got it flat, because I'd signed it on the hood of a car.

"Anneke," he said, "you should hear this. It's from Mr. Klippe's own employer. A wellbeing referral, from September." He read it in a kind voice, like a man reading a reference. "Wellbeing referral, line manager. Recent bereavement, family. Disturbed sleep. Preoccupation with historical documents. Signed by his manager." He paused. "And countersigned by Mr. Klippe. On the same day. Which I thought was very honest of him."
He folded it and put it back in his pocket.

That's what the room was for. I understood it the way you understand a dashboard that's been built for somebody else. It wasn't for me. Nothing I'd put on the tray had been read by the man across from me; it had been watched being read by the woman at the window, who approved an invoice thirty times a year and had come to see what kind of person complained about it. And now she'd heard: a man who'd lost somebody, who didn't sleep, who was preoccupied with old documents, which, to be fair, was exactly what she was looking at.
The woman by the window had turned back to the window.
<hr />
"Now," he said, and he unfolded his hands. "You've put your papers on my table. Let me put mine."
He didn't put anything down.

"There are seats in the building below us. You've sat in one. Forty of them belong to your employer, under a contract you've read, with an annex you've reconciled. The people on that annex are not being rewarded. They're being kept. Because somebody will need to do the payroll on the Wednesday, Mr. Klippe. That's all continuity ever is."
"And the offer."

"Five seats." He said it flatly, like a price. "You. Your wife. Her mother, if you like; I'm told they're close. Two more, your choice. A friend, a colleague, the man who sells curtains, I don't care. Five names on Annex C, dependents per allocation, in a building you've already got a desk in."
I waited.
"No dogs," he said. "I'm sorry. You've read the clause. You initialed it. I'm told it's a question of air."
<hr />

I'd like to tell you I thought about it. I didn't, and that's not courage. I'd already thought about it, for three weeks, on a kitchen floor, with the dog in question asleep across my feet, and I'd found there was a sentence underneath all the other sentences, and the sentence was Ana's, at four in the morning, and it was run where, I've got a Doberman.
"No," I said.
He nodded, as if I'd confirmed a delivery time.
"May I ask why? Not to persuade you. I'm curious. Most people, at this table, take a day."
I looked at the tray. The ledger. My two books with their pencil ticks. Nine things I'd made. A thin book was not among them, and I'd looked for it, on every shelf behind him, since I sat down.
"There's a clause on the annex I read and initialed anyway," I said. "I'd like that back. That's the whole reason."
I stood up. I picked up my two books and the notebook and the flask. I left the rest. They were copies. I'd kept the originals the way I keep everything, which is twice.
"Mr. Klippe," he said, as I got to the door. "You'll be back. Not for the seat. You've got the face of a man who's asked for an item."
"It's in conservation," I said. "I've got the slip."
<hr />
Aylin didn't look up as I passed her desk. The visitor book was open. I didn't sign out. Nobody had asked me to.

The stairs down go past a door on the landing, gray, with a reader beside it, the same reader as every door in the lower floor, and my lanyard was in my coat pocket because I'd come straight from a drill brief and I'm untidy. I know what my badge opens. I'd sat at desk forty behind that door with a sandwich.

I stood on the landing for about as long as it takes to decide not to, and then I went on down the stairs and out through the front, like a reader, into a car park where it had started, very lightly, to snow.

Buddy was in the car. He'd got up. He was standing on the back seat with his nose against the window, watching the door I'd come out of, and when he saw me his tail went, once, and he lay down again, with the grunt.

I sat in the driver's seat for a while before I started the engine. I'd asked, and been given a slip. I'd shown them what I'd made, and been read my own form. I'd said no to five seats, out loud, to their faces, in front of the woman who signed their invoice.
In my work you never tell a system what you're watching for, because it'll give you exactly that and nothing else, forever. I'd just told one. I'd told it the dog.
I drove home in the snow, with the slip in my pocket and her initials on it.

chapters.title: The dinner
chapters.what: This file held the v6 Bram scene ("The table"), which Structure 01 replaces: Kalder now comes uninvited as the answer to James's no, the talk is in code, Ana uses her mother's pills, and nobody touches the phone while he sleeps. Kalder wakes, does the sum aloud, unlocks it himself and pours from his own flask. Source: NEW from Structure 01 entry 6.1 and THE BOOK v8.2; Ana's pill speech reused from v7/47.
blocks: Ana had been home four days and I wanted one ordinary Friday.

That was the whole plan. Pasta, the kind with the jar. A series she'd watched half of at her mother's and would have to explain to me. Mora upside down on the kitchen floor, and Buddy on his blanket under the table with his chin on my foot, which he does more since the vet. On Monday I'd sat in a reading room and said no to five seats. Nothing had happened on Tuesday, or Wednesday, or Thursday. I'd started to think no might be a thing you could just say.
The bell went at ten past seven.
Buddy lifted his head. He didn't get up. He made a sound I hadn't heard from him in twelve years, low and steady, like a fridge that's about to die.
"Is that the dog?" Ana said.
"That's the dog."

She went to the door. I heard it open, and I heard her say "Julian!" in the voice she keeps for people she's delighted to see, and I stood at the cooker with a wooden spoon and understood what you get when you turn down an old man's offer. You get the friend.

She knew who he was. I'd told her all of it at her mother's, with objects on a tablecloth, including the name Noor gave me and what had been in the bowl by the gate. She'd had three weeks to decide what she'd do if he ever stood on our step again, and what she did was take his coat.
I've thought about that since. If she'd shut the door he'd have learned that we knew. She opened it wide and he learned nothing. It took her about a second. I'd have stood there with the spoon.

"I was passing," he said, coming down the hall. Nobody passes our street. It doesn't go anywhere. "I've been a terrible friend, Jim. Three weeks. I brought a bottle to apologize, and then I thought, that's not enough for three weeks, so I brought two."
He looked the way he always looked, like a man who'd slept well in a good hotel. And he had his clubs on his shoulder.
"You brought your golf bag to dinner," Ana said.

"I came from the range. I'm not leaving these in a car, no offense to your street." He stood the bag by the front door on its two little legs and patted it like a horse. "They were built for me by a man in Scotland who's dead now. There are three people in this country I'd let regrip them, and one of those I'm not sure about."

It was a tan leather bag with a brass tag on the strap, and I'd wondered about it since our first Wednesday. I'm bad at golf, but I know what things cost. I looked at it by my front door the way you look at a car you don't know parked outside your house.
Under the table Buddy was still going.
"He's got a new noise," Kalder said.
"He's had a rough month," said Ana.

"He's allowed." He didn't crouch down this time. He sat where Ana pointed, and put his phone face down by his plate the way he always did, so you could see he wasn't looking at it. Mora, who has no principles at all, went and lay on his foot.
<hr />

For twenty minutes he was just good company, and that was the hard part. He asked after Ana's mother by name. He told a story about a client in Antwerp who'd insured his wine cellar and not his wife. He ate the pasta from the jar and said it was exactly what he'd wanted, and I believed him, and Buddy growled through all of it at a volume you could talk over, like weather.
Then he turned his glass a quarter turn and said, "I hear you had a meeting on Monday."
"A short one."

"Short's fine. People think short means no." He smiled at Ana, to include her. "In my business nothing's a no until the renewal date. You'd be amazed how many clients say no in the first week of December and ring me on the thirtieth."
"What happens on the thirty-first?" I said.
"Allocation closes. After that it's whatever's left, and what's left is never by the window." He ate some pasta. "I'd hate that for you. You've got a nice desk."
"Is this golf?" Ana said.
"Work," we both said.
"Because it sounds like golf. It's got the same amount of nothing in it."
He laughed, properly, and topped up her glass. He's the only man I know who can pour for a woman and make it look like listening.

"The trouble with saying no in December," he said, "is the house. People don't think about the house. You've got an old place here, and it's lovely, but an old place in winter is a job. You can't leave it. Pipes. And you can't be in it every hour either, can you, not with work, not with the Wednesdays." He looked under the table, pleasantly. "Same with an old dog. You can't leave him and you can't watch him. They get into things."
Then he turned to Ana, and his whole face went kind.
"I hope Buddy's okay now," he said. "I should have asked that first."
Nobody in my house had told him Buddy was ill. I hadn't. Ana hadn't seen him since October. He knew that, and he knew I knew it, and he said it to my wife, gently, with her wine in his hand.
Ana didn't move a thing. "He's fine," she said. "He's eating like a horse. Do you want cheese on that?"
She got up for the cheese. On her way past the cupboard by the sink she stopped, for about as long as it takes to read a label, and went on.
<hr />
I'm not good at code. I'd had eight months of other people's, and I was tired, and I answered in the only language where I don't have to think.
"Can I tell you what I do all day, Julian? You've never really asked."
"You watch things."

"I get paid to detect a problem. Not to fix it after. Anyone can fix it after, there's a whole floor for that. So the rule is that the slightest doubt gets looked at. You don't wait for a second one, and you don't decide the first one's nothing because you like the system." I put my fork down. "I've had one since the pub. The book you said you'd read."
He didn't pause. He's too good to pause. He just stopped chewing a little early.
"The Quiet Presses," I said. "Van der Berg. I made it up at the bar and you'd read it. You said the chapter on the type foundries was the good bit."
"Did I."
"Dry as a biscuit, you said. You were very fair about it."
"What book?" Ana said.
"Doesn't matter. It doesn't exist." I turned to her, because I couldn't keep looking at him. "Have you ever seen Burn Notice?"
"Is that the one with the yogurt?"
"He eats a lot of yogurt, yes."
"I watched it with Mum. She fancied the old one." She put the cheese down. "Why?"

"I was thinking about how it starts. He's a spy, a good one, and one day somebody finds out who he is. And his own side doesn't rescue him. They burn him. That's the word. No job, no accounts, nobody picks up. It's nothing personal. A spy with his face known is just a cost."
"That's sad," Ana said.
"It runs seven seasons."
"I never saw it," Kalder said. He was looking at me with real interest, the way he'd looked at the forum man talking about the Sphinx. "Is it any good?"
"Dry as a biscuit. The second half's the good bit."
He laughed. I'll give him that. He laughed with his head back, and Mora thumped her tail against his shoe, and under the table Buddy went up a note.

And I thought: that's it, that's everything I've got. I've told a man who poisons dogs that I know what he is, in my own kitchen, with my wife three feet from him. I'd run out of code. So I did the other thing, the one I'd asked her for on this floor at four in the morning, after the barbecue.
She looked at me.
"You remember what I asked you. On the floor. I said one day I'd tell you, and you'd know it was the day." I kept my voice the way it had been that night. "It's today."
It sounded mad. I'd told her it would.

She held my eyes for about a second. Then she looked at the bottle and said, "That's finished. I'll open the other one," and picked up his glass, and hers, and went to the counter with her back to us.
She hadn't heard. Or she'd heard and decided I was being dramatic in front of a guest. I sat there with my heart going and thought, I asked for one thing. One thing, in fifteen years.
Kalder watched her go. "She's very good," he said quietly. "I've always thought so."
She came back with three glasses, poured in the kitchen, and put his in front of him.
"To Buddy," she said. "Being okay now."
"To Buddy," said Kalder, and drank.
<hr />

It took twenty-five minutes. He told another story. Partway through it he lost a word and went looking for it, and found it, and smiled at himself. He said the pasta had been perfect. He said, "That's a heavy red," and looked at the glass, and then at Ana, and I watched him get to the answer about four seconds too late to do anything with it.
"Oh," he said. "That's very good."
He put his head down on his arm, slowly, like a man listening to the table. His mouth came a little open. It made him look younger.

Buddy stopped growling. Just like that, mid-note. He came out from under the table, slower than he used to, and stood in the kitchen doorway looking at the sleeping man with an expression I can only call professional.
Ana was by the sink with her arms folded and her mother's pill bottle in her hand.
"How long?" I said.

"Mum takes one and she's out for seven hours. He's had two." She looked at the bottle. "I didn't plan it, James. He asked if Buddy was okay now, and I was standing at the cupboard, and Mum's bag was in there from Tuesday. And I thought, he's going to sit here being lovely until one of us says something we can't take back. I'd rather he slept."
"You improvised."
"I improvised." She put the bottle down very carefully. "Is that a crime?"
"Probably."

"Good," said Ana, and sat down, and put her face in her hands, and started to shake. Not crying. The other thing. I've seen it in people after an outage, when the system's back up and there's nothing left to do with the adrenaline.
I'd been paying for this in forms and initials. She'd just paid in something you can be arrested for, and it was my bill.
I got her up and into the hall, away from him. I don't know why. He couldn't hear anything.
"I told you to run," I said.
"I heard you."
"That was the sentence. That was the whole promise. You said okay."
"I said okay to believing you. I believed you. I never said I'd leave you in a kitchen with him." She wiped her nose on her sleeve. "And run where? He's got my Doberman on his foot."
We both looked. She was still there. She'd gone to sleep on a drugged man's shoe.
"She's a terrible dog," I said.
"She's a terrible dog."
<hr />
I took four photographs. It's what I do when something's in a state it won't be in again. I capture it first and work out what it's for later.

Him, from across the table, with the glass. His face, close. The whole kitchen from the doorway, so you could see it was a kitchen and whose. And one from the hall, which is the one that mattered, though I didn't know it yet: the front door, the tan bag standing beside it with the brass tag, and through the kitchen doorway behind it a man asleep at my table.
Then I sat down opposite him, and the phone was right there.
Face down by his plate. His right hand was on the cloth beside it, palm up, the thumb a little apart from the fingers.
"James," Ana said from the doorway. She'd seen where I was looking. "His thumb's right there."
"I know."

I've read a few hundred incident reports in eleven years and a lot of them start exactly here. Nobody breaks into a phone. They don't need to. People leave them face down on tables. They fall asleep next to them. Every report has a line near the top where someone borrowed something for a minute because it was right there, and that's the line the report is about.
"If I open it with his hand, I've got something I took off a drugged man," I said. "I can't put that in front of anybody. I can't put it in front of Pieter. I couldn't have put it in front of you."
"I'd have looked."
"You'd have looked, and then you'd have asked where I got it."
She thought about that. "I drugged a man for you," she said, "and you won't borrow his thumb."

"Unbelievable." She went and got the blanket off the couch. I thought it was for her. She put it over his shoulders, tucked it in at the neck, and looked at what she'd done with real disgust. "Don't," she said. "I know."

So we waited. That's all I did that night, for seven hours, and it's harder than it sounds. Ana slept on the couch in her clothes. Mora was eventually persuaded off his foot with ham. Buddy lay down in the doorway and didn't close his eyes, and I sat at my own table across from a man with his mouth open and a phone I wasn't going to touch, and drank cold tea, and kept not touching it.
At one point I turned it a few degrees with one finger, so it was square to his plate. Then I turned it back. I'm not proud of either.
<hr />
He woke at ten to five.

There was no start. His eyes opened, and he lay with his head on his arm and looked at what he could see from there. The glass. The clock on the oven. The blanket, which he touched. Ana sitting up on the couch. The bottle of pills on the counter, which she hadn't put away. My phone, on the table in front of me.
Then he sat up and rubbed his face with both hands.
"Zopiclone," he said. "It tastes like a coin. I thought it was the wine." He looked at Ana. "Your mother's?"
"I'd have bet on him." He nodded at me. "I'd have lost."
Nobody said anything. Buddy started up again from the doorway, quietly.
"How many did you take?" Kalder asked me.
"Four."
"Is the bag in any of them?"
"Sent anywhere?"

"Doesn't matter." He picked up his own phone, looked at where it was lying, and put it down in the same place. I think he could tell it hadn't been opened. I think that annoyed him more than the pills. "I'll do the sum out loud, Jim, since you like to see the working. Either I report tonight or I don't. If I report it, I'm the one who was put to sleep at a subject's table by the subject's wife, and photographed with his clubs by the door. If I don't, there's a seven-hour hole in my Friday, and in March that picture's on a widow's dresser in Zwolle and somebody asks me about the hole." He turned his hand over on the cloth. "For that photograph I'm retired. Either way. And we don't do a dinner and a clock."
"Burn Notice," Ana said.
"I told you, I never saw it." He almost smiled. "I'll take your word that it's dry."
He got up. He was steady, which I hadn't expected. He walked down the hall to the bag by the door, unzipped the long side pocket, and came back with a steel flask.

I knew it. The same make, the same dented shoulder where the cup screws on. The other one was on the shelf behind his chair, between the cookbooks, where it had been since Marijke pushed it at me in a doorway in Zwolle. He'd have seen it when he sat down.
He looked at it now, and then at me, and unscrewed his own.
"I never drink anyone's coffee," he said. "Old habit." He poured into the cup. It steamed. It had been in a golf bag for ten hours and it steamed, which told me what the flask cost too.
Then he turned his phone over, put his own thumb on it, typed something with his other hand, opened a gray folder with no name, and slid the phone across the tablecloth until it touched my cup.
"You've got as long as this lasts," he said. "It holds four cups, and I drink fast when I'm annoyed."
I didn't pick it up. "Why?"

"Not for you. Don't thank me, I'd find it embarrassing." He drank. "On Monday they have one problem, and it's me. If you're driving around the east of the country with what's on there, they've got two, and you're the loud one. I need about a week of them being slow."
"And you think I'll do that."
"You read things, Jim. You can't help it. It's the only reason any of us ever met you."
I looked at Ana. She was already coming back from the hall with my bag, the one with the annex in it.
He'd finished half the cup.

chapters.title: What was on the phone
chapters.what: Now a two-hander: Kalder awake across the table with his flask while James reads, and checks the gift against his own annex (desk twelve sold four times) and against what Frank, the dealer and the site manager told him. The thumb and the forty-minute clock are gone; "Compartments" (v7/48) survives as the last paragraph. Source: v7/47, with v7/48 folded in.
blocks: He drank with his left hand and watched me with the rest of him. I've been read by monitoring tools for eleven years and none of them ever did it that calmly.

"You're going to want to photograph everything," he said. "Don't. Your wife's phone is in the hall and mine logs the screen. Read it. You're a man who remembers paper. That's what they were worried about."
"Who's they?"
"Three cups and a bit, Jim."
I read.
<hr />
I'm going to give you the four things in the order they came, because the order is how I understood them, and because what I understood wasn't on any one screen.
No messages. That was the first thing. Not deleted; absent. The app was there and it was empty, the way a show house is empty. Whoever he talked to, he didn't talk to them here.
Then the gray folder. Three things that looked like spreadsheets and one that didn't.

The first was people. Not names. Codes: two letters and three digits, a region, a status, and beside each one a short note in the register I'd come to know from the schedule, the register of a man confirming a delivery. Active. Active. Reassigned. Active. Retired (natural). Forty-odd rows, and most of them for other regions, with a region code I didn't know. Ours had twelve. I didn't know what I was looking at until I found him: our region, active, and in the note column, the only one with anything personal in it, a single word.
Hands.
"That's me," he said, without looking. "Third from the bottom. You'll be looking for the 'Retired' column. There isn't one yet."

Handlers. The people who do the visiting. By code, by region, and I had a dozen of ours, and I didn't know a single name, and I understood that this was on purpose and that the purpose was that nobody, not even the man across the table, could give the names, because he'd never had them.
"You've met two of them," he said. "You wouldn't remember. One sold you the coffee at the drill."

The second sheet was the schedule. Next quarter's. The one after the one I'd acknowledged at work in October and carried in my bag since. Addresses, dates, a column headed Visit, a column of notes. I read it with my heart doing something I didn't like. Our address wasn't on it. I read it again. It wasn't. The addresses that had gone quiet were carried over, with new dates, and nine new ones, and beside three of them the word pension, and beside one the word companion.
I turned the phone so he could see it. "We're not on it."

"The dog lived and the book's back where it came from," he said. "The visit was about the book. They don't come back to a house for feelings." He drank. "Hengelo's still on it. I'd look at Hengelo if I were you, and I'm not."

The third was seats. Not ours. Four companies. Four annexes, laid out exactly like the one I'd reconciled in the autumn, with names and dependents per allocation and the line about animals. A shipping firm, a hospital group, an energy company and a university. The totals across the four, when I added the column in my head, were a number of people that would fill the recovery site in the business park three times over.
So there were other buildings. Of course there were.
<hr />
And then the fourth thing, and I want to go slowly here, because it was the thing I hadn't expected and it was the thing that told me how to win.
It was a list of helpers.

Not handlers. The others. The people who make the phone calls and close the tickets and sign the invoices and catalog the records and drive the vans. Hundreds of them in our region alone, and they weren't by code. They were by name, because nobody had ever thought a helper needed protecting. They weren't the ones who knew anything.

And beside each name, in a column with no heading, was a word. One word per person. When I'd read enough of them I realized the column had a heading after all, it just wasn't written down, and the heading was what we told them.

Now here's where I stopped reading like a man being given something and started reading like a man at work. Because a gift from this man was worth exactly nothing until I'd checked it against something I had made myself, and for once I had plenty.

Honeypot. That was Pieter, and a dozen more at the bank, and it meant they'd been told the nightly job was a security trap for leakers and that they were helping by leaving it alone. I didn't need the phone for that one. Frank had told me on his stairs, in the spring, with Mora under his table: Pieter told the team it's a honeypot. Match.

Conservation. That was the dealer in Groningen, and a woman in Deventer who turned out to be the professor's neighbor, and a records clerk in Apeldoorn. I'd driven to Groningen and the dealer had said the word to me himself, over a receipt from 2011 marked Second impression. Match.

Disaster recovery. The site manager at the recovery site, the bus driver, the people who stock the canteen. True, every word of it, which is the genius of it. And heritage, for the depot upstairs, which the site manager had said to me through a shut glass door with his hands in his jacket: different tenant, same generator. Match, and match.

Three reasons I'd been given by three people in person, in three different towns, with no phone in sight, and they were sitting on this sheet in the right column against the right names. I don't believe lists. I believe lists I can check three times against things I was there for.
"You're checking it," Kalder said. He sounded pleased, which I'd have paid not to hear. "Of course you are."
"It's what I do."
"I know. I've watched you check a scorecard you knew was right." He turned the cup. "Do the desks."
<hr />
I hadn't been going to. I did.
Our annex was in my bag, in Ana's hand, and she put it on the table beside the phone without being asked, open at the first page, with my initials at the foot of it.

Annex C. Forty-nine rows. Desk one, Anneke de Wit. Desk twelve, Pieter, dependents per allocation three. Desk forty, a man in Legal who'd been off sick since March. Nine vendor allocations with references beginning V, which Pieter had told me to leave, and I'd left, and signed.
The shipping firm's annex, on the phone. Desk twelve: a name I'd never heard of, in Rotterdam. Dependents per allocation, two.
The hospital group. Desk twelve: a consultant, Nijmegen. Four.
The energy company. Desk twelve: a woman with a double surname. Three.
I went back to ours. Desk twelve. Pieter. Lotte and Bas and Marieke, three.

I did it again for desk one. Four Annekes, in effect: four heads of something, each in the chair by the window. Then I did desk four, and desk twenty, and desk thirty-three, and stopped, because Ana had put her hand flat on the annex and I understood that I'd been saying the numbers out loud.
"It's one building," I said. "There's one floor of desks under the reading room. I've sat at one. I counted them at the drill. A hundred, maybe. And they've sold each desk to four companies."
"Four that I know of," Kalder said. "The university's new."
"So when it happens, whatever it is, four people turn up for Pieter's chair."

"Nobody turns up." He said it kindly, which was worse. "That's the part you're not getting yet, and I don't have the cups for it. The seats were never for sitting in. A seat is what you promise a man so that he'll leave a job alone for thirty years. You don't need a hundred desks for that. You need an annex, and a man like you to initial it."
"And the brewery."
"He's got a four in his column and he's in three annexes. He's the happiest man in the east of the country."
I sat back. Under the table Buddy had come in from the doorway at some point and put himself across my feet, and I hadn't noticed, which tells you something.

I'd signed that annex. I'd found nine names with no HR record and taken them to Pieter and been told leave it, and I'd written the exception in and initialed every page, because it was a real list of real desks in a real building and I'd eaten a sandwich at one of them. I'd thought the seats were the thing under everything. They were the lid. They were a lie with a floor plan, and I'd reconciled it.

That's where the lifeboat broke. Not on anything the old man said in December, not on anything this one said over coffee. On a desk number that appeared four times, in four documents, one of them with my initials on it.
<hr />
I went back to the helpers once more, because there was one thing I hadn't looked for.

The fifth column. Against every name, down the whole list like a watermark, the same word: Continuity. That was the promise. Not saving the world; nobody believes that. The thing that goes on. The payroll on Monday. And every one of them had heard that word and taken it to mean, without once examining it, you'll be all right.
I looked for them on the four annexes, and on ours. Pieter's honeypot dozen. The dealer. The site manager. The clerk in Apeldoorn. Aylin, who was on the list as heritage.

Not one of them. Hundreds of people who'd been told continuity and heard kept, and the lists of who was kept were in the next folder along, and not one of their names was on any of them. Except Pieter, who was on ours. At a desk sold to three other men.
He put the cup down. It rang on the table, empty.

"That's four," he said, and reached across and took the phone out of my hand. Not roughly. The way you take a glass from someone who's done with it. He thumbed the folder shut and put the phone in his inside pocket, and then he stood and screwed the cup back onto the flask.
"Too bad," he said. "I liked you."
He meant it. That was the thing about him, start to finish. He'd meant all of it, and it hadn't changed anything he did.
Ana got his coat. She held it out at arm's length, the way you'd hold out something a dog had been sick on. He took it the same way and said thank you.

At the door he shouldered the bag. The brass tag caught the hall light. "Don't ring me, Jim. The number's gone by lunchtime." He looked down the hall at Buddy in the kitchen doorway, who'd started again, very low. "He was always right about me, you know. First day. On the green. I liked that about him too."
Then he went down the path with the clubs, and got into his car, and that was the last time Julian Kalder sat at a table of mine.
<hr />
We stood at the door and watched his car go round the corner, and when it had gone Ana said, "I liked him," in the voice of someone identifying a body.

So I'd been given a gift by the man who poisoned my dog, and I'd checked it, and it was good. That's the cost of that chapter and I'd like it written down plainly. Everything I did for the next three weeks stood on four cups of his coffee.

I sat down at the table with the annex, which was mine, and the schedule, which was mine, and the three words I'd been given in Groningen and on Frank's stairs and through a glass door, which were mine, and what I'd read was already going where things go in my head when they've been checked. For a month I'd thought the thing I'd found was a machine, and you don't beat a machine, you go around it, you take the seat. It wasn't a machine. It was a few dozen people with codes, standing on a few hundred who'd each been told one small true-sounding thing and the word continuity, standing on everybody else. Each helper knew one task, and could tell a policeman the whole truth and it would come out as nothing, because it was nothing. That's not strength. It's width. And width only works as long as the people being stood on have never been shown the list they're not on. Nobody had ever put it in front of them. Nobody had ever needed to. They never asked.
"Say what you're going to do," Ana said. "Plainly. No systems."

"One page per person," I said. "What they were told. What they did, from their own records. What it was part of. And who's kept, with a space where their name should be." I looked at the kitchen clock, which said half past five on a Saturday morning in December. "And then I need a printer, and three weeks, and you're going to have to drive."
"Mora comes," said Ana, and went to look for the paper.

chapters.title: The sheets
chapters.what: The sheet gains its third box (your desk on three other lists); Saskia, Marijke, Els, Frank, Beard Man and James's own sheet are added; the brewery man now refuses ("I'm in") instead of being embarrassed; the half sentence goes to the forum and eleven strangers finish it; the thirteen days of the calendar replace three weeks; and he says once that everyone he tells is now counted. Pieter, the dealer, Anneke and Aylin kept from the draft. Source: v7/49.
blocks: A sheet looked like this. I'm going to show you one, because I made two hundred and ninety of them in thirteen days and they were all the same shape, and the shape is the argument.
At the top, a name. Then four short sections, with a line between each.

What you were told. One sentence, in the words from the phone. The nightly job is a security honeypot; leave it in place. Or: Certain editions are tracked for conservation; please telephone if asked for. Or: Your cellar holds heritage material; access is restricted for its protection.

What your own paper did. Their records, not mine. The ticket they'd closed, with its number and date. The call they'd logged. The invoice line they'd approved, with their initials. The access they'd granted. Taken from systems they had the right to look in and never had, and printed with the reference numbers, so they could check. Beside it, one line from the schedule, their line: the date their ticket closed or their call was made, set against the date on the schedule it had moved, and the address, and in my handwriting one word for what the public record said had happened there. Heart. Sold. Fire. Quiet.

Who is kept. The seat list, for the four companies and ours. Names, dependents per allocation, the line about animals. Printed small, two columns, a page and a half. And at the top of it the only sentence on the whole sheet that was mine:
Your name is not on this list. Please check.

Your desk. This box was empty on most sheets, because most people had no desk. For the ones who did, it had four lines. Our annex, their desk number, their name. The shipping firm's annex, the same desk number, somebody else's name. The hospital. The energy company. Desk twelve, four times.

That was it. No theory. Nothing about books or sentences or what happens when we die. I'd learned that from Frank in my own kitchen: don't give them the story, give them the invoice. A sheet made no claim they could argue with. Here is what you were told, here is what you did, here is who's kept, here is who else has your chair, and the space between the boxes was theirs to fall into.
Two hundred and ninety. Thirteen days, the seventh to the nineteenth of December. Ana drove.

One more thing, and I'll say it once because I said it to myself every morning. The job at 02:14 counts people who ask and people who are told. Every person I handed a sheet to was a row the next night, if they weren't one already. I was doing to two hundred and ninety people the thing that had been done to me in June, and I knew it, and I did it anyway, because the alternative was to leave them in the dark where the counting doesn't matter. I'd like that written down against my name as well.
<hr />
Pieter first, because he had to be, and because I owed it to him.

I did it at his desk on the Monday, after seven, when the floor was empty and the cleaners had gone through. He was still there because he's always still there; Pieter works late the way other men drink, steadily and without enjoyment. I put the sheet on his keyboard and sat down in the chair beside his desk, the one people sit in when they've come to resign, and I didn't say anything.

He read it. I watched him read the first box and recognize the sentence, because it was his, from a meeting I'd never been in, and I watched his ears go red. I watched him read the second and nod, because the ticket was mine, #41790, closed by him as a duplicate of #41822, which hadn't existed when I opened mine, and the date was right, and the closing note was his. He read the word in the margin, which for his line was fire.
Then he turned the page and found the list, and his own name was on it, which I'd left there on purpose, and I watched his face start to clear, and then I watched him read the number beside it.
Dependents per allocation: 3.
"I've got two," he said. It came out very quietly. "Two kids. Lotte and Bas. And Marieke. That's three." He looked up. "That's three with Marieke."
"So that's us. That's all of us. Why does it say three like it's a—" He couldn't find the word. I had it; I'd had it since the autumn. Allocation. I didn't give it to him. He'd get there.

He read the names around his. He knew most of them. Heads of department. Two board members. Anneke. The forty from the drill, and the people he reported to and the people they reported to, and nobody, not one person, from the floor he managed. Not Frank. Not the six in the glass box. Not the woman at the next desk who'd been at the bank twenty-two years.
"My team's not on it."
"No. You are. Because you said leave it. That's what the seat's for, Pieter. It's not a reward. It's a retainer."
Then he got to the last box, and I watched him read his own desk number four times.
"Who's this?" His finger was on the second line. "Rotterdam. Who's he?"
"Somebody who was told the same thing you were, by somebody with the same job as Julian."
"He's got my desk."
"You've got his. There's one floor. I've sat on it."

He sat there for a long time with his finger on the number three. Then he said, in a voice I'd never heard him use, "What do I do," and I said the thing I'd decided to say to all of them, because it was true and because it was the only instruction that couldn't be reported upward as a threat.
"Nothing. That's the point. Next time, don't."

I left him there. The next morning he said good morning to me in the glass box exactly as he always had, and I thought I'd lost him, and then, four days later, a ticket I'd opened against page 212 as a test came back not closed. Not actioned either. Just open. Sitting there. For the first time in eleven years Pieter had failed to tidy something, and I knew what it had cost him, and I said nothing, and neither did he.
<hr />
Saskia I did on the Tuesday, at her desk, in daylight, because she's a woman who distrusts anything that happens after six.

Her sheet was short. She'd been told nothing; she wasn't on the helper list at all. What she had was the grant log, which is hers the way the visitor book is Aylin's, and in it one line she hadn't written. My program role, ticked on the eighteenth of June, by a service account, three weeks before anybody had asked for me.
She'd told me about that line herself in the autumn, with a sigh, and then she'd filed it under the things that are wrong in a bank and don't matter. Now it was on a page beside a schedule.
"I didn't write this," she said.
"I know. That's why it's on your sheet. Everything else on there is something somebody did. This is the one thing nobody did."

She looked at it for a while. Saskia owns the access reviews; a grant she didn't make is, to her, a stain on a tablecloth. She'd already written me up once, in the summer, two words in her log, seemed tired, and I think she thought about doing it again. She'd been told the rule on page 212 cut down the noise, and nobody had ever said the word honeypot to her, which is why she wasn't on the list: they hadn't needed to tell her anything. She'd done her job. Then she turned to her screen and typed for a minute and wrote something on the back of my sheet and turned it round.

A service account name. The system it belonged to. The vendor whose address it was registered to, which was the address on the invoice, which was the address that had fixed my access in eleven minutes.
"That's who ticked you," she said. "I'd like it back when you're done with it. It's mine."
<hr />

The dealer in Groningen I did by post, because he'd earned the courtesy of not having me in his shop again. I put a note in with it. You asked who sent me. Nobody. This is what the number in your ledger does. Two weeks later a parcel came. It was the ledger, cloth spine, fourteen years of his handwriting, with the telephone number cut out of the back cover with a scalpel, cleanly, the way a conservator would do it, and a card that said, in the neat old hand, I find I no longer need it. The receipt from 2011 was still in it, marked Second impression, which he'd left for me to find.
The professor's neighbor in Deventer got hers through the door. I don't know how it landed. I know she didn't ring anyone, because the watcher would have told me what happened next, and nothing did.
<hr />
Marijke I took by hand, on the Wednesday, with Buddy, because she'd opened her door to a man with an old dog once and I wasn't going to send her an envelope.

Her sheet had almost nothing on it. She'd been told distracted, by a policeman and a minister, and that was in the first box in their words. The second box was one line from the schedule, her address, pension, and the date. And clipped to the sheet, the one photograph I'd printed for anyone: a man asleep at my kitchen table with his mouth a little open, a blanket over his shoulders, and on the shelf behind his head, between the cookbooks, a steel flask.
She looked at the photograph for a long time at her kitchen table, with Buddy under it, and the flask's twin not there, because she'd given it to me.
"That's him," she said. "He's younger than I thought. Henk said he was about fifty."
"He's forty-four."
"Henk always made people older." She put the photograph face down and then turned it back up again. "Is he asleep?"
"Did you do that?"
"My wife did."
She nodded, slowly, as if that was the correct answer. "Good," she said. "Tell her from me."
<hr />

Els had already turned, and I'd thought about not giving her one, and then I thought that the whole point of a sheet was that it was yours. So she got hers, in the curtain shop, between a customer and a delivery, and she read it standing up with her reading glasses on, and the first box said conservation, because the foundation had rung her in March about her father's papers, kindly, and she had let them photograph the notebook.
"I let them in," she said.
"Everybody let them in. That's what the word's for."

She folded it in four and put it in her apron. "He'd have liked this," she said. "A sheet. He'd have said it was the only honest thing anyone's done since." She looked at the list. "His name's not on it either."
"Good. He'd have hated the company."
<hr />
Frank's I gave him in his own kitchen, with Mora under the table, because Buddy can't do his stairs, and because it was the one sheet I was ashamed of.

He wasn't on any list. He'd done nothing. What he had was one word against his name in the honeypot dozen, because he'd been in the room when Pieter said it, and he'd repeated it to me on these stairs in the spring.
He read it and laughed. "I'm a helper."
"You're on the list."
"For saying honeypot on a staircase."
"For saying it to me. That's what a helper is, Frank. Somebody who passes a word along without checking it." I didn't enjoy saying it. "I did the same thing at a funeral once."
He looked at the seat list for a while, the way he looks at a dashboard he doesn't trust, top to bottom and then back up the right-hand side.
"Pieter's got three," he said. "Who's the third?"
"Marieke."
"They counted his wife?" He put the sheet down. "Okay. Fine. I still don't believe any of it. But that's an insane spreadsheet and I'd like a copy."
<hr />
Beard Man I did on the Sunday, at the stall, because that's where he is on Sundays and I wasn't going to ask for his address and ruin something.

He was mid-sentence. He's always mid-sentence. I put the sheet down on a box of Reader's Digest condensed books and he read it without stopping talking, which I've seen him do with a newspaper, and then he stopped talking, which I'd never seen.

The first box said conservation. The second was a telephone number in a ledger he'd never kept, because the polite man who came round in the spring had asked him to ring if anyone wanted a single title from the professor's lot, and he'd said he would, and he hadn't, because he'd sold the whole lot to me in two crates on a Sunday morning before the van came, to save himself the trouble.
"I was supposed to ring," he said.

"I never ring anyone. I've got a theory about that." He did. It took eleven minutes and had a comet in it. The short version was that the universe divides people into those who ring and those who get rung, and that the ones who get rung are the ones who've got something, and that he'd sold me everything at once because somewhere in him he'd known that a man who wanted a single title was a man who wanted it for someone else. "Nobody buys one book," he said. "Not off the ground. You buy the lot or you're working."

Ninety percent nonsense. I've said that before. But he'd sold me the thin book to avoid a phone call, and it was the only mistake they'd made in the whole east of the country, and he'd made it out of laziness, and I stood there in the market with the sheet on the condensed books and thought: that's the hole in it. That's the whole hole. A helper who couldn't be bothered.
"Did I do something?" he said.
"You didn't ring."
He thought about that. "I'll put that on my stone," he said, and went back to the comet.
<hr />
The brewery man went to them.
I knew somebody would. I'd told Ana one in ten would, and it was closer to one in twenty, and he was the first, and I want to describe him because he wasn't a bad man.

He had a family firm in a small town, four generations, with a cellar under the brewhouse that went back to the seventeenth century, and twenty years ago a foundation had come to him with a grant and a request: the cellar was heritage, it was dry and cool and stable, would he allow part of it to be used for the storage of archival material, under seal. He'd said yes. He'd have said yes to anyone with a grant and a kind word about his great-grandfather. His sheet said heritage, and his record was a key register with his signature on it four times a year, and his last box was the full one: five seats in our annex under a V-number, dependents four, and the same desk in three other annexes under three other names.

He read it standing in his own yard with the smell of malt coming off the brewhouse. He read it carefully, all of it. He read the last box twice. Then he looked up with an expression I'd expected to be anger and wasn't.
"You've got this wrong," he said.
"The desk number's from your annex. I reconciled it."

"I don't care about the desk number." He tapped the box. "These three. They've been told they're in. They're not in. I'm in." He said it the way you'd correct somebody's spelling. "I've met the people. I've been to the building. There was a dinner. You've been given a list by someone who wants you to think it's all the same, and you've believed him because you're the kind who believes paper. You don't get it. I'm in."
"Four people have been to that dinner."
"Then four people think they're in and one of them is." He folded the sheet and handed it back to me, which nobody else did. "Thank you for coming out. I'll let them know you've been."

He rang them that afternoon. I know because of what happened on the Friday. And I want to say this about him: he wasn't betraying me. He was doing what twenty years of heritage had taught him to do with something strange in his yard, which was ring the number. He was being a good helper, one last time. It was the last time, because the people he rang could not explain the sheet to him either, and he'd run a business for forty years and knew what it sounded like when somebody couldn't explain an invoice.
<hr />
Anneke de Wit I'd left till the Wednesday of the second week, because she was the one I was afraid of, and because her sheet was the longest.

Her record wasn't a ticket or a phone call. It was thirty quarterly approvals of a line that said continuity reconciliation (recall index), per flagged person, with her initials against each, going back to the day she'd got the job. Her sheet had all thirty, in a column. Beside the schedule's eleven addresses, what the public record said: the care home, the sale, the canal, the four that had gone quiet, checked by my own watcher against the family announcements and the house listings, nothing I'd been handed. And one more page nobody else got: seven nights of the reason column from the job at 02:14, one week in October, with the employee numbers blacked out and only the two words left standing in each row. Asked (job). Wrote (dealer). Posted (forum). Asked (job). Forty rows, so she could see what a flagged person was, and what kind of thing gets you flagged, and that it is nothing.

I asked for a meeting through her assistant, under the program's name, and I got twenty minutes, and I walked in and put the sheet on her desk and sat down, and she read it, and she did not say a word for eleven minutes. I counted. She read the invoice page, the one with her initials on it thirty times, and she turned it over and read the back, which was blank, and turned it back and read it again, and I understood that she was doing what I do. She was reading the middle. She was looking for the place where her own signature stopped being a formality and started being a thing.
Then she read the reason column, and something happened to her face that I didn't understand until a Monday morning on her step.
When she spoke, it was the first time I'd heard her voice.
"Thirty," she said.
"Thirty."
"I approved this thirty times." She looked at the red cell. "This is you."
"That's me. The week I opened a ticket."
She looked at me with the face from the reading room: not hostile, not frightened, assessing, the face of a woman whose job is to look at a thing and say what it will cost.
"You were in that room in December," she said. "He read your referral out loud. I thought that was for you. It was for me."

"I've been on the foundation's board for four years. I was asked to join because the bank funds it and someone from the bank should sit there. I've sat there. I've approved the minutes. I've never once been told what the reconciliation line reconciles." She stopped. "That's not an excuse. I'm head of risk. It's the opposite of an excuse."
"I'm not here for an excuse."
"What are you here for?"

"For you to read the rest. There's a schedule. There are four other companies and one floor of desks. There are two hundred and ninety people in this region who were each told one small thing and the word continuity, and not one of them is on the list you're on. I've given them their sheets. I've got eleven left, and they're the board. Yours." I looked at her. "I'd like you to read the rest before you sign next quarter's schedule, because I'd like you to know what a visit is before you sign for one."
She was quiet. Then: "Give me the rest."
"All of it?"
"All of it. Tonight. Here." She looked at the reason column one more time, and her hand went to the second page and stopped. "I've approved thirty of these without reading. I'm going to read one."
<hr />
And Aylin.

I'd nearly taken her off the list, because she was the one I liked and because her sheet was the thinnest: a woman who sat at a desk in a reading room and kept a card index and booked appointments for dead men. Her word was heritage. Her record was the catalog, and on the sheet I'd put the one line in it that was hers and recent: a request slip dated the second of December, in her handwriting, for a shelfmark I'd written out on the reading-room table, marked in conservation. I'd seen the item on its shelf through the glass door at the drill. So had she, every working day for nine years.
I gave it to her on the Thursday, the nineteenth, at the desk, when I came up the stairs for the appointment she'd booked me into without my asking.
She read it. She read it the way she did everything, calmly, like a woman who's seen a lot of paper. When she got to her own handwriting she stopped.

"He told me to write that," she said. "In front of you. He said it was in conservation and I wrote it, because he's the head, and I know exactly where it is, and it's sound." She looked at the slip. "I've never written a false status on a card in my life, Mr Klippe. Not one. I wrote that one with you watching."
I said I knew.

"No. You don't." She got up. She went to the card index, the wooden one, and she didn't open a drawer. She reached behind it and took out a book. A big one, bound, with a ribbon, and she brought it to the desk and opened it and turned it round to face me.

It was the visitor book. Every person who had ever sat at the long table, in her handwriting and the handwriting of whoever had kept it before her, going back, when I turned to the front, to 1931. Name. Date. Shelfmark requested. And in a final column, headed Outcome, a word.

I read down the page she'd opened it at. The professor was there, in March, with the shelfmark that was on the last page of his thin book, and the word in the last column was Deceased. Above him, a name I didn't know and the word Seated. Above that, Quiet. Quiet. Seated. Deceased. Declined. Quiet.
And at the bottom, in December, in Aylin's hand: my name. The date. The shelfmark, because I had asked for one. And in the outcome column, one word.
Pending.

"I keep the book," said Aylin. "That's what I conserve. I've kept it for nine years and I've never been told what the last column means and I've never asked, because I was told it was heritage, and because it's very old, and because somebody has to." She looked at the sheet, still on the desk. "You've just told me what it means."
"I didn't tell you anything. I gave you a list."

"You gave me a list I'm not on." She closed the visitor book. "Copy it. Not now. He's upstairs. Come at midnight on Sunday; the door's on my badge. Copy it and give it to whoever you're giving things to." She looked at the slip on my sheet, in her own hand. "And bring that. I'd like to correct a card."
<hr />
I'd made one sheet nobody would read but me.

My name at the top. What you were told: nothing, which is its own kind of word. What your own paper did: Annex C, forty-nine rows, nine exceptions noted, reconciled against HR and initialed on every page by J. Klippe; a wellbeing referral, signed on the hood of a car; a request slip. Who is kept: not me. Your desk: forty, a man in Legal's, white card. I put it in the folder with the others. It wasn't for anyone. It was so I couldn't say later that I'd only been handing them out.
<hr />
And the forum, which I did last, on the Thursday night, from the kitchen floor.
I didn't post a sheet. A sheet needs a name, and the forum is where people go not to have one. What I posted was a line. Half of one.
Looking for anyone who's ever heard this said, anywhere, by anyone. Not read it. Heard it. "Don't be afraid. Hold on to"
And nothing more. No question mark. I'd learned at least that much from a reading room: you don't argue, you ask.

I didn't think it would work. The forum doesn't finish sentences; it corrects them. By the morning there were two replies, one of which was about bloodlines, which I'd expected. By Friday night there were nine more, and I read them with Buddy's head on my foot and my own hand under my leg, which I noticed, and left there.

They finished it. Not all of them the same. Hold on to whoever's got your hand. Hold on to the one holding you. Hold on to whoever is holding your hand, twice, word for word. A man whose grandfather had said it in a hospital in Groningen in 1988. A woman whose mother was an archivist and had said it to her, once, drunk, and never again. A bridge. A beach. A corridor, which I read three times. A kitchen in Hengelo. Eleven people, in a week, who'd heard it said, by someone who was dying, to someone who wasn't, and had never found anyone else who had, and had filed it where you file that.

Henk's version was in my coat. Said not to be frightened, only to hold on. I put the notebook on the floor next to the laptop and read the two together, and then I read Els's father's line, which Beard Man had been improving for years. The ones who held on come out together. Three versions and eleven strangers, and none of them had met.

That's a challenge and a response. That's what you do at work when you think two systems are reading the same clock: you send half a thing to one and see if the other knows the end. I'd sent half a sentence to the internet and the internet had given me the rest, eleven times.

The watcher ran at 02:14. In the morning it showed me two of the eleven replies with a sentence added each, in a voice that wasn't theirs, about who really controls the hospitals. By Saturday one of the two had deleted his account.

So the eleven were counted now too. I'd done that. I sat on the floor and wrote down the eleven handles in the notebook under Henk, because a copy is the only thing I know how to make, and then I wrote the whole sentence out once, in full, and looked at it, and put the notebook back in my coat.

chapters.title: The leak
chapters.what: The calendar is now Friday 20 December, the review pulled from 31 December to Monday 23 (the second and last move); the man at Pieter's door is Bram, and Pieter hands him the sheet on his own, against James's advice, so Bram learns from a helper that the desks are oversold; Buddy goes to Frank's because the mother's flat has stairs. American spelling. Source: v7/50.
blocks: The brewery man rang them on the Wednesday afternoon, and by Friday night the date had moved, and I know that because of a calendar entry I'd had no business caring about.

The new schedule, the one I'd read on a phone with a flask ticking down beside it, had a date at the top: the day it came into force, the day Anneke was due to sign it. The thirty-first of December. The old man's review date, the one from the bottom of page 212, the one that had moved once already in the autumn, the week I signed a form and went quiet. And in our own systems, in the continuity program's own calendar, which I had every right to read, the thirty-first had an entry, blandly named, a quarterly meeting that had been in the calendar for eleven years and that I'd been invited to because I was on the program now.
On Friday night at eleven the meeting moved.

From the thirty-first to the twenty-third. Monday. This Monday. The entry changed the way entries do, with a little note that said rescheduled by organizer, and the organizer was a name I'd never heard of at an address that was the foundation's, and I was sitting at the kitchen table with eleven envelopes in a folder when my phone made the small sound that means a calendar has changed, and I looked, and I knew.

The review had come forward for the second time. Somebody had listened to a brewer, and somebody had looked at the number of helpers in the east of the country who'd stopped closing tickets that fortnight, which I imagine looked, on whatever they look at, like a dial being turned the wrong way, and somebody had done what I'd have done, which is pull the date in before the thing spreads.
Twice. The first time, in September, for a man going quiet. This time for a man being loud. There's no speed you can go at that they don't count.
She came down. She looked at my face.
"Monday," I said.
<hr />
I'm going to tell you what I thought in the next ten minutes, because it was the clearest I've ever thought and I don't expect to think that clearly again.

Monday was the schedule. Anneke signs, the quarter starts, the visits begin. I'd given Anneke everything on Wednesday night and I didn't know yet what she'd do with it; she'd said I'm going to read one, and she'd taken the folder, and that was all. If she signed, the addresses on the new schedule, Hengelo among them, plus whatever had been added since the brewer, got their visits, and I had a very good idea now what a visit was.

The board met on Monday too. Not about this. About the foundation's trustees, once a year, a formality, twelve people in a room approving a list of names they'd never met. That was the quarterly meeting in the calendar; that was what had moved. They'd pulled the foundation's annual confirmation forward to the same morning as the schedule, so that whatever the board did, the schedule would already be signed.
Twelve board members. I had eleven sheets left and they were theirs, and I'd been going to deliver them next week, calmly, one a day, the way I'd done the others.

I had two days. And they knew about me properly now, not as a man with papers in a reading room but as a man with two hundred and ninety sheets in the east of the country, because the brewer had rung and I'd been in his yard.
"They'll come here," Ana said.
"Tonight?"

"I don't think so." I looked at the window, where the dog had been standing every evening for two months and where he was standing now. "They don't like fingerprints. A visit to the house of the man who's been handing out sheets, the week he hands them out, is a fingerprint. They'll go round me."
"Round you how?"
My phone rang.
<hr />

It was Pieter. It was twenty past eleven on a Friday night and it was Pieter, who in eleven years had never once rung me outside working hours, and I could hear, before he spoke, that he was in his car.
"James."
"Pieter."
"There's a man at my door."
I put the phone on the table on speaker and Ana sat down across from me and we both looked at it.
"Tell me."

"I'm in the car. I was coming home. I'm at the end of my street and there's a car outside my house that isn't ours and there's a man on my step talking to Marieke." His voice was very steady, the steadiness of someone who's decided to be steady for the length of a phone call and will pay for it after. "He's got a folder. He's got the same kind of coat as the man at the drill. In the car park."
"Can you see his face?"

"No. He's turned away. Marieke's got the door on the chain. She does that. I told her to do that, years ago, I don't know why, she thought I was mad." A pause. "He's just standing there. He's not pushing. He's waiting."
Ana's hand had found mine on the table.
"Pieter, listen to me. I'm going to tell you what to do and I need you to do exactly this, and I'll explain afterwards, and you can be as angry as you want."
"Okay."

"Drive up to the house. Park where you always park. Get out. Walk up to him like it's nothing, because to him it is nothing; he doesn't know you've seen a sheet, and if he did he'd be surprised you were calm, so be calm. Say good evening. Say, can I help you."
"And then?"
"And then let him in."
Silence on the line.
"James."

"Let him in. Make him tea. Sit down with him in your kitchen with Marieke and the kids upstairs and listen to whatever he says. He'll have a reason. It'll be about the bank, or the program, or your access, or something about the migration. It'll be plausible. It'll be kind. He'll ask you things. He'll ask whether anyone's been in touch with you about your work, and whether anyone's given you anything."
"And I say—"
"You say nothing."
"I can't say nothing, he's—"

"You can. That's the one thing you can do. You answer every question with something true that isn't the answer. You've been busy. The program's a lot of lists. You don't really follow the politics. You're very happy to help. You let him talk, and you nod, and you make a second cup of tea, and you say nothing, and in forty minutes he'll leave, because he's not there to hurt you, Pieter. He's there to find out what you know. And if you give him nothing, then nothing is what he's got."
I could hear him breathing. I could hear the indicator ticking in his car.
"Why would he hurt me? I'm on the list. You showed me. I'm on it."
"You're on it because you said leave it. You stopped saying it on Monday. That's why he's on your step."
A long pause.
"Marieke's not on it," Pieter said. "Not separately. She's a number. She's one of my three."
"I know."
"And if I'd closed your ticket. Like always. He wouldn't be here."
"So this is you. This is because of your sheet."

"Yes," I said. "It is. And I'm sorry. And I'd do it again. And I need you to go and let him in and make him tea, because the alternative is that he waits on your step until he's been seen waiting, and then it's not a visit anymore, it's a thing with a fingerprint on it, and I don't know what they do about those and I don't want to find out at your house."
The indicator stopped. I heard the car move.
"He's turned round," Pieter said. "He's seen the headlights. He's—" A breath. "He's smiling. Jesus. He's waving."
"Wave back."
"James."
"Wave back, Pieter. Park the car. Say good evening. And ring me when he's gone, from the kitchen, with the kettle on, and I'll be here."

The line went quiet for a second, and then I heard a car door, and footsteps on gravel, and Pieter's voice, from a distance, saying "Evening. Can I help you?" in a tone I'd heard him use in a glass box for eleven years, the tone of a man who's never once lost his temper at work and has saved it all for somewhere, and then the call ended.
<hr />
He rang back at ten past midnight.
"He's gone."
"Tell me."

"He was from the foundation. Compliance. Routine, he said. A review of access on the program, everyone added since the summer, nothing to worry about. He asked if anyone had approached me about the program's data. I said the program was mostly lists. He liked that. He said he was a list man himself." Pieter stopped. "He asked about you. By name. Whether you were settling in. I said you liked lists too. He wrote that down. He had a little book."
"Good."
"He asked after the kids. Their names. He knew their names, James. He asked if Lotte was still doing the hockey."
I didn't say anything.
"And then I gave him the sheet."
Ana's hand closed on mine.
"Pieter."

"I know what you said. I'm not you. I can't sit in my own kitchen with a man asking about my daughter's hockey and say nothing. You can. That's what you've been doing for a year and I don't know how you stand it." He breathed. "It was in the drawer by the kettle. I got it out and I put it on the table in front of him and I said, this came to me, and I don't know what it is, and I'd like you to tell me."
"What did he do?"

"He read it." Pieter's voice had gone strange. "All of it. He read it the way you read things, with his finger on the line. He read his own word, the first box, and he nodded, like it was correctly spelled. He read the ticket. He read the list and found my name and I watched him look at the three. And then he got to the last box."
"The desks."

"He read desk twelve four times. He read it out loud. Rotterdam, Nijmegen, the woman with two names. And he stopped, and he looked at me, and he said, 'Where did you get this?' Not angry. Like a man who's found a page in his own file he's never seen. I said it came to me. He said, 'Four,' and he said it again, 'Four,' and then he asked me, very politely, whether I'd been to the building, and I said yes, every year, I sit at desk twelve for the drill, there's a card with my name on it. And he said, 'Yes. There would be.'"
"And then?"

"And then he folded it in three and put it in his folder, with his own papers, and he thanked Marieke for the tea and shook my hand and said if I thought of anything I should ring, and he gave me a card. The foundation's name and a number. It's the general number. The one with the music."
"I know the one."
"James, what the fuck is this."
"I'll tell you. Properly. Not tonight." I looked at Ana. "Tonight I need to know one thing. Did you see his face properly, in the kitchen? Was it Julian?"

"No." Pieter sounded surprised at the question. "Nothing like. Sixty, maybe. Gray. A good jumper, the kind a wife picks. Nice voice. He drank the tea. Both cups." A pause. "He didn't know, James. About the desks. I'd swear to it. He read it like it was news."
I closed my eyes.
"Okay," I said. "Thank you. Go to bed. Lock the door. You did it exactly wrong and I think it might have been better than right."

"I gave him the sheet," said Pieter, in a voice of wonder. "He was in my kitchen asking about my daughter's hockey and I gave him the sheet and he read it." And then, differently: "He had the same face you had. In the autumn. When you put the annex on my desk. Like he'd found a thing that didn't reconcile."
"Something like that."
"Is that good?"
"I don't know," I said. "I've got a dog," which wasn't an answer, and Pieter didn't understand it, and said goodnight.
<hr />
Ana took her hand off mine.
"Three addresses," she said. She'd been counting on her fingers; I'd seen her. "You said they'd go round you. Pieter's one."

"Pieter's one. There'll be two more tonight. People who got sheets and stopped. They're checking the ones nearest the top." I pulled the laptop over and opened the list, the two hundred and ninety, with ticks beside all of them and the eleven at the bottom with no ticks that were the board. "And on Monday Anneke signs the schedule, and the board confirms the trustees, and all of this goes back to being nothing."
"Unless."

"Unless the board doesn't confirm them. Unless twelve people walk into a room on Monday morning each holding a sheet that says what the foundation they're about to approve has been charging their bank, per flagged person, for thirty-one years. And who's kept. And who else has the chair."
"Eleven sheets."
"Eleven. Anneke's got hers."
"By Monday."
"By Sunday night. Monday morning's too late; they need to have read it."

Ana looked at the list. She looked at the dog at the window. She looked at the clock on the oven, which said twenty to one on a Saturday morning, and she did the thing she does, which is put the kettle on, and while it boiled she stood at the counter with her back to me and said, "Where are they? The eleven."
"All over. Two in the city. Three in The Hague. One past Woerden. One in Bunnik. The rest in between."
"That's a long night."
"About that."
The kettle clicked. She didn't move.

"Buddy goes to Frank's," she said. "Mum's is two flights and he can't, and I'm not leaving him in this house for a night with nobody in it. Mora comes with us; she's good in a car and she's a Doberman and I'd like a Doberman in the car. We leave Sunday after dark, because if they're watching the house they're watching it in daylight like normal people. We do the far ones first and work back. You read, I drive, and nobody reads me any signs about pumping stations."

"And on Monday morning you're not anywhere near that building, you're somewhere with a scorecard, because if this works I don't want you in the room when it does, and if it doesn't I want to know where you are."

I looked at my wife, in her dressing gown, at one in the morning, with a kettle behind her and a list of eleven strangers in front of her, planning a night's driving to deliver the only thing that could stop a machine she'd told a man to his face she didn't believe in.
"You don't believe any of this," I said.
"Not a word." She poured the tea. "Drink that. Then print the eleven again, the long version. Then sleep. I'll ring Frank."

Buddy got down from the window at last and came and lay across my feet, and I sat at the table and printed eleven sheets, one at a time, while my wife rang a man who'd never been responsible for anything that breathes, and the Doberman watched the door, and somewhere in the east of the country two more people were making tea for a nice man with a folder and saying nothing, because I'd told them to, and one man hadn't, and I didn't know yet which of them had done me the favor.

chapters.title: The night before
chapters.what: Buddy goes to Frank's because the mother's flat has stairs, not because her house is on the schedule; at midnight Aylin strikes "in conservation" from his slip and brings the item, Tresidder's 1929 letter, which he copies by hand and leaves; Anneke opens at six with her hand under her arm and one row of the reason column is hers. The wrong house stays a nobody; no handler's house by mistake. American spelling. Source: v8/51.
blocks: We left on Sunday after dark, with a Doberman in the back and twelve envelopes in a supermarket bag on my lap, and I'd like to say we had a plan. We had a list and a full tank. Ana had a thermos. I had a stomach that had stopped working on Friday and hadn't sent anyone to explain.

Ana drove. She's a better driver than me in every way you can measure, and in a few you can't, like how she doesn't take it personally when a Volkswagen cuts in. I only drive when she lets me, which is mostly when she wants to sleep. She drove the way she does anything she's decided on, both hands, radio off, and Mora's head between the seats breathing on the gearstick like a second engine.

Buddy was at Frank's. That had been its own negotiation. Ana's mother lives up two flights with no lift, and Buddy stopped doing stairs the year before, so that left Frank, who lives alone in a flat with a bike in the hallway and a fridge full of oat milk and had never once been responsible for anything that breathes.
"What does he eat?"
"His food. It's in the bag. Not your food."
"What if he wants my food?"
