"He'll want your food. He's a dog. Say no."

"I can't say no to that face, mate. Look at it." Buddy was looking at him from the bottom of the stairs to the flat, Frank's on the first floor, with the expression of an old man who has been told about the stairs and is filing a complaint. "Do I carry him?"
"You carry him."

He carried him. Twenty-eight kilos of gray dog up a narrow Rotterdam staircase, Frank going red and saying fuck on every third step, Buddy calm in his arms like a bishop being moved to a new diocese. At the top Frank put him down and said, "I still don't believe any of it, you know," and I said I knew, and he said, "Go on. Go. I've got the dog," and did the skull at me with his actual face, which I'd never seen him do without a phone.
<hr />

The list was twelve names. Twelve people who would sit in a room at nine on Monday morning and, at item four, confirm the trustees of a foundation that had been invoicing their bank per flagged person since 1994. Eleven of them had never heard my name. The twelfth was Anneke, who'd had her sheet since Wednesday and read it twice, which I'm told is a thing she does not do.

Each envelope had a sheet. For the board the last box said something different from the others. Their names weren't missing from the list; they were the list, practically. So it said: On Monday you will be asked to confirm these trustees. This is what the foundation charges, and for what. These are the people it keeps. These are your staff who are not kept. This is your desk, and the three other people who have been sold it. Please check before you vote.
Please check. I'd rewritten that line eleven times. Every version that sounded clever sounded crazy.
"Read me the first one," Ana said.
"Leiderdorp. A woman. Treasury, twenty years. Two kids, one horse."
"How do you know about the horse?"
"She's got a horse in her profile picture."
"That's not knowing about a horse, James. That's a picture."
She was right. I wrote horse? next to it, like a man doing something.
<hr />

Leiderdorp was a letterbox. A neat brick house with a light on downstairs and the blue flicker of a television, and I'd decided, we'd decided, at the kitchen table, with the kettle, not to knock. A man at your door at nine on a Sunday night with a document is a man you call the police about. A letter is a letter.

So I walked up the path with the envelope like it was a parcel of something alive, and I put it through the slot, and the slot had one of those brush things inside, and the envelope stuck. Half in, half out. I pushed. It folded. I pulled it back to straighten it and the brush took the corner off.
Inside, a dog started barking. A small one, the kind that barks with its whole body.
I stood there with half a sheet of evidence in my hand and the other half somewhere in a stranger's hallway, and the television went quiet.

I ran. I'm not proud of it. I ran back down the path and got in the car and said "Go, go, go," and Ana didn't go, because Ana doesn't go for anybody who says it three times. She looked at me, and at the torn corner in my hand, and said, "Did you just post half of it?"
"Most of it. Eighty percent. The important part."
"Which part's in your hand?"
I looked. The bottom right corner. The word check.
"Fuck," I said.

She laughed so hard she had to put her forehead on the wheel, and Mora barked once at nothing, in solidarity, and the hall light came on in the house and we drove away with our lights off for the first twenty meters like idiots in a film, and then turned them on because it's illegal.
"Good start," Ana said. "Very professional."
<hr />

After that I had a system. I'm good at systems. I folded each envelope once more, and I held the flap of the letterbox up with two fingers, and I fed the envelope in slowly, like you'd feed a pill to a dog, and I want it understood that this was the most competent I was all night.

The Hague, two, ten minutes apart. Both letterboxes, both fine, both in streets so quiet I could hear the canal. At the second one a cat watched me from a windowsill with the face of a cat who had seen men post things before and thought less of all of them.
Delft. Leidschendam. Wassenaar. At Wassenaar the house had a gate, and the gate had an intercom, and the letterbox was on the far side of the gate. We sat in the car for four minutes looking at it.
"Throw it over," Ana said.
"It's a bank document."
"It's an envelope. Throw it."

I threw it over. It went beautifully, a little spin on it, and landed face down on a wet gravel drive about a meter from the door, and I stood at the gate in the drizzle and thought about everything I'd ever read about the history of the world, the edits, the forty-one books, the hill in Turkey, the professor in his blue chair, and all of it came down to this: a man in a damp coat watching an envelope get rained on in Wassenaar.
A light went on in the porch. The door opened. A man in a sweater came out, looked at the envelope, looked at the gate, looked at me.
"Klippe?" he said.
I didn't say anything. My mouth wouldn't.

He bent and picked the envelope up and shook the water off it. "Anneke rang. Four of us, this afternoon. She said a man might come with an envelope and that I should read it and then ring her." He looked at the car behind me, at the Doberman's head in the back window, ears up, like a hood ornament. "She didn't say you'd throw it."
"There's a gate."
"There's a bell on the gate."
"I didn't want to ring the bell."
He nodded like that was a reasonable thing for a grown man to say. "I'll read it tonight." Then, because he was Dutch and it was raining: "Do you want a coffee?"

I said we had more to do. He said, "Then go," and went in, and I walked back to the car, and Ana said, "Well?" and I said, "Anneke's been ringing people," and Ana started the engine and said, "Good," in a voice that told me how scared she'd been and wasn't going to say.

So that was two already turned. That's the thing nobody tells you about doing something like this: halfway through, it stops being yours. Anneke had rung four. One of the four, in Voorschoten, met us at the door at half past eleven in a dressing gown with her own copy already printed, because Anneke had scanned hers and sent it, and she held out my envelope back to me and said, "I don't need two. Give it to someone who hasn't got one." It was the first time anyone had given me anything back in the whole year. I sat in the car afterwards and couldn't talk for about a minute, and Ana let me, and Mora put her nose in my ear, which is wet and enormous and didn't help at all, and helped.
<hr />
The wrong house was in Zoetermeer.

Number fourteen. I walked up to number fourteen, I fed the envelope in with my two-finger pill technique, and I was halfway back down the path when the door opened behind me and a very large man in boxer shorts said, "Hey."
I turned around. He had my envelope in his hand.
"This isn't me," he said.
"It's fourteen?"
"Fourteen B." He pointed. Next door. A second door I hadn't seen, round the side, with a second bell. He looked at the name on the envelope. "That's the guy upstairs. He's never in. He's got a boat."
"Okay."
"What is it?"

I have spent eleven years at a bank explaining things to people who don't want them explained, and in that moment, in Zoetermeer, at a quarter to midnight, with a stranger in boxer shorts holding the end of the world, the best I had was: "It's about his pension."
"At midnight?"
"It's urgent. For a pension."

He looked at me for a long time. Then he said, "Okay, man," and posted it through the B door himself, carefully, with two fingers, and went back inside. I'd like to think he went to bed and never thought about it again. I'd like to think a lot of things.
"Wrong house?" Ana said.
"Wrong house."
"Was it one of them?"
"It was a guy with a boat. Next door. His neighbor's got a boat."
"So it was nobody."
"It was a very large nobody in his underwear."
She nodded. "This is how they're going to make the film," she said. "The underwear guy. They'll cut everything else."
<hr />
The van picked us up after Zoetermeer, on the A12.

White, no windows in the back, the kind every plumber in the country drives. It came onto the motorway at a junction behind us and stayed there. Three cars back. Then two. Then three again. Ana saw it first. She said, "There's a van," in exactly the voice she'd use for there's a sign, and I turned round, and Mora, who'd been asleep across the back seat with her legs in the air like a dead insect, turned over and sat up and looked out the back window and went completely still. She never goes still. She's a Doberman. She was built still and then someone forgot to turn it on.
"What do we do?"
"Nothing." My voice came out about a third higher than normal. "We drive. If they're following us they're following us to a letterbox. That's a fingerprint. They don't do fingerprints."
"You don't know that."
"I've read their paperwork."
"You've read their paperwork," Ana said, and changed lanes, and the van didn't, and then it did.

Forty kilometers. I counted. I counted the way I count everything when I'm scared, which is out loud in my head: exits, kilometer markers, the number of times Mora's ears moved. I held the supermarket bag of envelopes on my lap with both arms like it was a child that might jump out. I thought about Henk Boersma in his canal. I thought about Noor's message, there's a van on my street, and then nothing. I thought, very clearly, if this is it, I'd like it to be after the next envelope, at least, so I've done eight.
At the junction for Gouda, the van indicated, politely, in plenty of time, and came off, and was gone.
Mora watched the empty road behind us for another minute. Then she lay back down with a groan and put her chin on my seat.
"That was a van," Ana said.
"That was a van."
"I've decided it was a van."
"Good decision."

We never talked about it again. I've thought about it plenty. I think it was a van, and I think those were the longest forty kilometers of my life, and I think both of those things are true, and that's what they do to you, in the end. You can never again just see a van.
<hr />
At midnight I was at the depot.
"I'm not coming in," Ana said, in the car park, with the engine running. "I'm sitting here with the dog. If you're not out by one, I'm coming in with the dog, and I'm not asking anyone's badge."
"That's—"
"That's not a negotiation."

The building looked the way it always looked, low and long and gray behind its car park, the foundation's name on the sign and a smaller name under it, and no lights on the desk floor where I'd eaten a sandwich at desk forty during the drill. One light upstairs, behind the glass door.

Aylin had propped the outer door open with a fire extinguisher. That's the detail I can't get over. In a year of watching her, the pencil, the cards squared to the edge of the desk, the visitor book in its own gray box, I'd never seen her let a single thing lean on anything. A fire extinguisher, against a door, at midnight. It was the loudest thing she ever said to me.

She walked me up without a word. Her badge said A. Pekcan, Keeper of Collections, and she'd clipped it on to come in at midnight for this, which I also can't get over. The reading room was lit by the one lamp on the long table. The visitor book was on it, open at 1931, and beside it a flat scanner, the kind libraries use, already warm.
"Forty minutes," she said. "He reads on Sunday nights. He comes at one."
"Okay."
"The slip."

I had it in my coat, with the notebook. My own capitals, the shelfmark, the date, and across the bottom in her neat ink, in conservation, and her initials. She took it to her desk and sat down and uncapped a pen, and drew one straight line through the two words, the way you'd strike a wrong figure in a ledger, so that it could still be read. Under it she wrote on shelf, and the date, and initialed that too.

"I've never corrected a status in nine years," she said. "There. Now I have." Then she got up and went through the door at the back, the one to the stacks, and I heard a drawer, and she came back with a gray folder and put it on the table at the far end from the scanner, and went to her desk and sat down with her back to me and picked up a card, and I understood the deal. She wouldn't watch. She wouldn't help. She wouldn't stop me. And she'd brought the item, because a request had been made in her reading room, and in her reading room requests are answered.

I did the book first, because the book was for Anneke. My hands were shaking so badly I put the first page in upside down. Then the second. Somewhere around page ten I got a rhythm, lift, flatten, lid, button, the little light crawling across, and I stopped reading the words, on purpose, because I had forty minutes and because I was afraid of whose names I'd see. You can't not see some. Seated. Quiet. Deceased. Quiet. The same few words for ninety-five years in a dozen different hands, and I turned the pages like a man stacking plates.
And under my feet, the whole time, the floor hummed.

I'd heard it at the drill and filed it under air conditioning. It wasn't. It was lower, steadier, a big thing kept running in a room under a room: a generator, for a hundred desks sold four times, running on a Sunday night for nobody. Mora would have hated it. She hates the dishwasher.

I finished the book at twenty to one. I put it back exactly how it had been, open at the front, and slid the memory card into the last envelope, the twelfth, Anneke's, and went down the table to the folder.
<hr />
I'd like to tell you what it was in order, because the order is how I understood it.

It was a letter. Three sheets of thin paper, folded once, the folds gone soft, in a hand I knew from the margins of a flood survey, because I'd spent a year with his sentence and a man's handwriting gets into you. At the top, Urfa, and a date in the summer of 1929. At the bottom, Tresidder. It was to his publisher in London. The folder's label was the shelfmark from the professor's last page, in a hand from before Aylin's, and a note in pencil: correspondence file, transferred Leiden.

Most of it was business. He was sorry about the delay with the corrections. He had been ill. He was staying in the house of a family outside the town, and the grandfather of the house had died in the week, and he had been in the room.
Then this. I copied it word for word, and I'll give it to you the way I copied it, because I'm not going to improve on him.

The old man had my hand. I do not think he knew whose it was. He said a thing to me in his own language, and the son, who has some English, gave it to me afterward at the door, and I set it down here while I have it exactly: "Don't be afraid. Hold on to whoever is holding your hand." I have heard this before. My aunt said it to me, in Devon, when I was nine and she was dying, and I have never told anyone, because a boy of nine does not know what he has heard and a man of fifty does not like to say. I have now heard it twice, from two people who could not have met, in two languages, both of them going. I do not know what it is. I propose to put the plain fact of it into the next impression, in a note to the chapter on the river peoples, with no more claim than that it was said. You will tell me the trade will not like it. I find I no longer mind what the trade likes.
Then he said he was going east for a fortnight, on foot, to look at some stones a shepherd had told him about, and would write from there.
He didn't write from there.

I sat at the long table with the professor's shelfmark in a dead man's folder and my notebook open beside it, and I read the sentence three times. Then I turned back a page in the notebook to Henk, in Marijke's kitchen, in my handwriting: said not to be frightened, only to hold on. And the eleven handles under it, with their endings. Hold on to whoever's got your hand. Hold on to the one holding you. Hold on to whoever is holding your hand, twice.

Two copies is evidence. I'd had the eleven and Henk, and that was two copies by anyone's count, and I'd still half believed I'd been reading too much into a forum. Here was paper. Ninety-six years old, in an archive, requested by a professor who never came, marked in conservation in front of me by a woman who knew it was on the shelf. The same words. Not the idea of them. The words.
And the next impression had come out in 1931, two years after he walked into the hills, and the note wasn't in it, and the chapter on the river peoples had lost a hand instead.

I copied the letter into the notebook. All three sheets, the business and the illness and the stones, not just the sentence, because a copy you've trimmed is a copy somebody can argue with. It took me twelve minutes and my hand hurt. Then I put the sheets back in the order they'd been, folded the way they'd been, closed the folder, and left it on the table where she'd put it.

I didn't take it. I want to say that plainly, because I could have, and the man who'd taken the thin book from my kitchen had taught me exactly how much good that does. It was hers. It was the archive's. A letter in a reading room is a thing anyone can be sent to see. A letter in my coat is a thing I say I've got.
"The last column," Aylin said, without turning around. "Next to you. What does it say now?"
I looked. December. My name, in her hand. One word.
"Pending."
"Good." She turned a card over. "When it changes, I'd like to be the one who writes it. I think I've earned that much." Then, still not turning: "You left it on the table."
"It's yours."

"It's the archive's." She capped her pen. "He'd have taken it. The professor. He argued for two pages. You asked for it on a slip and you've copied it and left it where it goes." She put the card in the drawer. "I'll put it back on the shelf myself. Nobody has asked for it in ninety years, and now two men have in one, and it's going to be where the card says it is when the next one does."
I went down through the dark floor and out past the fire extinguisher and Ana had the car moving before my door was closed.
"Well?"
"I've got the book. All of it."
I had the notebook in my hand. I hadn't put it away. "And it's written down," I said. "In 1929. The sentence. Somebody wrote it down and sent it to London, and then he walked into the hills."
She didn't ask what sentence. She knew. She'd heard the half of it I'd posted, read over my shoulder on the kitchen floor on Thursday. She drove for a bit.
"Henk's," she said.
"Henk's. And the eleven."
"Okay," said Ana, and that was all, and I think it was the second time in fifteen years I'd heard her say the word that way.
<hr />

Three more after that. Utrecht, a letterbox, no lights. Bunnik, a man who opened the door himself at two in the morning because he couldn't sleep, read the first paragraph standing in his socks under the hall light, said "Fuck" very quietly, then "Thank you," and closed the door. And one we couldn't do, a farmhouse past Woerden at the end of a dike road, no car, no lights, nobody. I put the envelope through the door anyway.
"He's away," Ana said. "That's one who votes without reading it."
"I know."
"Ring Anneke."
"It's three in the morning."
"Ring Anneke."
I rang Anneke. She answered on the second ring in a voice that had not been asleep, listened, said, "I'll try him. Thank you. Go to the next one," and hung up.
"I like her," Ana said.
"She approved the invoice thirty times."
"And then she read it."
<hr />
There was no next one. There was only Anneke's.

She lives in a terraced house in Rotterdam-Kralingen with a bike chained to the railing and a pot of something dead on the step. We got there at ten to six, in the first gray, and I sat in the car with the twelfth envelope for a while because I'd suddenly forgotten how to stand up. A year. Twelve envelopes. A torn corner in my coat pocket that said check.
I walked up the three steps. I lifted my hand to knock.
The door opened before I did.

She was dressed. Not in a dressing gown; properly dressed, for work, at ten to six on a Monday morning, shoes on, glasses on her head. She looked like she'd been standing in her hall for some time. Her right hand was tucked under her left arm, flat against her side, the way you'd hold a hand you'd shut in a door.
I knew it. I'd done it on my own kitchen floor. I'd seen Noor do it at her table and Marijke describe it in a doorway. I'd never thought I'd see it on the head of risk.
I held out the envelope. "The visitor book. All of it. Nineteen thirty-one to now."
She took it with her left hand. She didn't open it.

"I've read the sheet," she said. "All of it. Twice." She looked past me at the car, at Ana with her head back against the headrest, at the dog's ears in the back window. Then she looked at me, and her voice did something I hadn't heard it do.
"The page from the job. The reason column. You blacked the numbers out."
"They're employee numbers. They're not mine to give you."
"One of them is mine."
I didn't say anything.

"The fourth row. Asked (job). The week after yours. I asked my own director what the line reconciled, on the telephone, in October, because an engineer had put it on a table in front of me in a room I'd been told was about an archive. One question. And I'm a row." She took her hand out from under her arm and looked at it, and put it back. "It's been cold since I read that. That was Wednesday. It comes and goes."
"You know what this is." It wasn't a question. "Is it true? What the sentence says. What they count."
I'd been asked that once, by a widow in Zwolle, and I hadn't had an answer, and I didn't now, and I'd learned at least not to pretend.
"A hand, twice," I said. "On a kitchen floor, and at a grave. That's all I've had. I don't know."
She looked at me for a long moment. Then she nodded, once, the way you'd sign off a figure you'd checked yourself.
"Go home, Mr Klippe."
"The farmhouse. Woerden."
"I got him at four. He's driving back. He's not happy." She almost smiled. "Go home."
She closed the door. I stood on her step and looked at the dead plant for a while.
When I got back in the car, Ana didn't ask. She looked at me and I said, "Twelve," and she put her forehead down on the steering wheel, just for a second, and then lifted it and started the engine.
"Frank's," she said. "Buddy. Then bed. And then you're going to go and hit a ball with a stick and not be anywhere near any of this."
"It's Monday."
"Monday you hit a ball with a stick and keep your phone face down." She pulled out. "You've done your bit, Mulder. Now you just have to not be in the room."

I was asleep before Kralingen. The last thing I remember is Mora's chin landing on my shoulder, heavy and warm and smelling, I'm sorry to say, very strongly of whatever she'd found in Anneke's front garden.

chapters.title: Monday
chapters.what: Prose unchanged except Anneke's call, which gains the two lines Structure 01 names: the old man ran one region and they are all called the head; and the reason James lives, corrected (they have killed, rarely, each time somebody's mistake; now two hundred and ninety people hold their own names). Reading-room summons moved to Friday because the 26th is a holiday. American spelling. Source: v8/52.
blocks: The sixth green at seven in the morning in December is the loneliest place I know, and I went there on purpose.

Nobody plays in December. The course is open because the course is always open, and the greenkeeper waves at you from the shed with the face of a man who's seen your type before — the ones who come out in the frost because something at home is worse. I'd slept forty minutes in the car — Ana says thirty — and none at all in the forty hours before that. My eyes felt like someone had sanded them.

I'd rung ahead from Frank's to ask if I could take the dog in the cart, which is not allowed. The woman in the shop said, "Buddy? The old one? Go on," because they'd known him for years and because nobody was going to see.
Frank, handing him back at the door of the flat, had looked about as tired as me.
"He snores," he said.
"I know."

"Like a man. Like a fat man on a train." He crouched down and put his forehead against Buddy's forehead for a second, which I'd never seen him do with anything. "He ate a croissant. I didn't give it to him. He took it. Off the table. With his face."
"Did you say no?"
"I said no. He looked at me." Frank stood up. "Go. Text me. Don't text me. I don't know. Text me."
<hr />

Buddy rode beside me with a blanket over his back and his chin on the edge of the cart, watching the fairways go by like an old man revisiting a town he used to live in. He can't walk a hole anymore — hasn't since the vet. But he can ride, and he likes the air, and I think he likes being somewhere that smells of nothing but grass and cold and, faintly, the greenkeeper's diesel, which to him is probably perfume.

I put the phone face down on the bench by the sixth green. I'd promised Ana — face down, on silent, and I'd look at it when I'd finished the hole and not before. I'm a man who checks dashboards for a living. I check the weather app when I can see out of the window. Face down was a big ask, and she knew it, and she'd asked anyway.
Then I took the putter and three balls out onto the frost and started knocking them around, badly, while twenty kilometers away twelve people walked into a room with coffee.
<hr />

I wasn't in the room, and I'm glad. What I know about it I got later — from Anneke, on the phone, and from Pieter, who heard it from someone who heard it from someone, which is how the bank hears everything. The two versions agree, which at a bank almost never happens, so I'll trust it.

The foundation's annual confirmation was item four. After the quarterly numbers and a thing about the Antwerp office. It had been item four for as long as anyone could remember, and it usually took about ninety seconds: the chair reads the trustees' names, someone proposes, someone seconds, hands go up, next.
This year, when the chair finished the names, the man from Wassenaar said, "Before we vote," and put a sheet of paper on the table. Slightly wavy, Pieter's source said. Like it had been wet.
The woman from Voorschoten put hers next to it.

And then — this is Anneke's version, and she's not a woman who decorates — there was a silence of the kind she'd only heard in a boardroom twice, both times in 2008, and in it nine more sheets came out of nine more folders and went down on the table. Not slammed. Just put down, the way you put down a card when everybody's already seen the hand. Leiderdorp's had a corner missing.
The chair looked at them. He looked at Anneke, who had never in four years spoken before a vote.

She said she'd approved the foundation's invoice thirty times and would like to read the line into the minutes. She read it. Continuity reconciliation, per flagged person. She read the number of persons on the last invoice, and on the first one, in 1994. She said she'd asked the foundation's director, on Saturday, by phone, what the line reconciled, and he'd said heritage, and she'd asked him to define heritage, and he hadn't.
Then — and this is the part Pieter's source loved — she asked for a vote to withhold confirmation of the trustees pending an audit. Bunnik seconded before she'd finished the sentence.
Eleven to one.

The one was the farmer from Woerden, who'd driven back from his boat at four in the morning and walked in at five to nine with my envelope still sealed in his coat. He voted no, Anneke said, not because he disagreed, but because he hadn't read it, and he was the kind of man who wouldn't vote for anything he hadn't read. She said she respected that enormously. She said she'd given him her own copy at the coffee break and watched him read it, and that he'd gone a color she hadn't seen on him before, and asked if he could change his vote, and been told no, that's not how minutes work.
Then she proposed that, pending the audit, the bank use its right under the funding agreement to put in interim trustees. She had names. One of them was hers.
That carried too.

By half past nine the foundation that had been counting a four-hundred-year-old bank's questions for thirty-one years had new trustees and a new chair. The old ones had been thanked for their service. The old man had been, in the language of these things, invited to step back. The quarter's schedule, the one with eleven addresses on it and Ana's mother's house and the word Companion in that font, was sitting on Anneke's desk unsigned, and would stay unsigned, she said, until somebody could explain to her satisfaction what a visit was.
Nobody shouted. Nobody was arrested. The minutes ran to a page and a half, and you could read them start to finish and not know anything had happened at all.
<hr />

I'd holed out on the sixth by nine, in eleven strokes — a record, not a good one — and I'd sat down on the bench next to the phone and not turned it over. Buddy had gone to sleep in the cart. The sun had come round enough to start melting the frost in a line across the green, and I watched the line move, the way I used to watch progress bars when I was a junior and didn't know yet that they lie.

I did not pray. I'd like that known. I thought about it, though. I thought: if there is anybody, now would be a good time, and then I thought that if there was anybody they'd been watching this whole year and probably had opinions about the torn corner.

The phone buzzed against the bench at twenty to ten. It buzzed twice. I let it buzz a third time — I don't know why, some superstition about seeming calm in front of a phone — and then I turned it over.
"Mr Klippe."
"Mrs de Wit."

"It's done." Her voice was exactly the same as at six in the morning on her step. "Eleven to one. I'm the chair. The trustees are out. The schedule isn't signed and won't be." A pause. "I'm not going to give you the details. You weren't there, and I'd like that to stay true."
"Okay."
I couldn't say anything else. I was looking at the dog.

"He's asked to see you," she said. "The old one. Friday, in the reading room. I'll be there. He'd like to talk, he says, because it no longer matters." Another pause. "You should know what he was, before you sit down with him. He ran this region. One region, the east of one small country, and a building with a generator. He's called the head because they're all called the head. I've spoken to two others this morning, and they both answered to it." The faintest dryness. "I had thought we were dealing with something larger. We're dealing with a man who liked a chair. Bring nothing. I'll tell you the terms there. I don't like telephones."
"Can I ask you something?"
"Once."
"Why am I still here?" It came out smaller than I meant. "They've done it before. The canal. The blue chair. It worked. Why not me?"
She didn't answer straight away. I heard her close a door on her end.

"I asked that too," she said. "On Saturday. I'll give you the answer I was given, because I checked it against the files I've got, and it holds. They have killed. Rarely. I've found three in thirty-one years, in this region, and the canal is one. And each time it was somebody's mistake. A handler who got impatient, or frightened, or liked a car. Nobody above him asked for it, and each time it cost them a year of tidying, because a body is the one thing that can't be reclassified." A breath. "That's the method. Not that they won't. That they'd rather not, and they're very good at rather not. Before, you were one man at one address, with a plausible ending available. Now you've given two hundred and ninety people a page with their own name on it. Eleven of them sat in a room this morning holding one. If anything happened to you, two hundred and ninety people would know who did it, and they're the two hundred and ninety who do the work. A body would confirm every envelope." The dryness again. "You made yourself too expensive to be a mistake. I don't think you planned it."
"I didn't."
"No. I didn't think so." Then: "Go home. Sleep. There's frost."
She hung up.
<hr />

I said "fuck" — quietly, to the green, not angry, just to have said something out loud to somebody. Then I sat there a while longer. The greenkeeper came past on the mower and lifted a hand and I lifted one back. I texted Ana one word, which was eleven, and then I texted Frank the same word, and Frank sent back the skull and then, about a minute later, wait is that good, and then, ok it's good, I googled the board, which I still don't understand.

Then I rang my dad, which I hadn't planned and don't do on Mondays, and he asked if something was wrong, and I said no, and we talked about his gutters for six minutes. It was the best conversation we've had in years. He doesn't know why.
The line of melted frost reached the far edge of the green, and the whole thing went from gray to that green that looks freshly painted.

Buddy woke up. He looked at me. He looked at the course. He made the small grunt that means he'd like to get down, which he hadn't made on a golf course since the summer, and I lifted him down — carefully, all twenty-eight kilos, my back registering a formal complaint — and set him on the grass.

He stood there with his legs not quite trusting him and his nose up in the cold. Then he walked out onto the sixth green. Four steps. Slow. He stopped about a meter from the hole, right in the sun, and lay down on it, on the actual putting surface, which you are absolutely not allowed to do, and put his chin on his paws.
The greenkeeper, at the far end of the fairway, saw. He looked for a second. Then he turned the mower round and went to cut something else.

chapters.title: The final conversation
chapters.what: The table now has objects on it: Tresidder's letter, brought by Aylin because the request stands, and the thin book, returned. The old man leads with the only news (they do it on purpose, to come back), changes one word in James's pencil copy, and the film claims are short boasts. James gets to desk twelve first. Anneke's reason, the deal and the one last thing are kept from v8; the "it's not for staying" callback stays. No dog under this table. Source: v8/53.
blocks: Aylin booked it. That's the part I keep coming back to. The Friday after the vote I came up the stairs with nothing in my hands, because Anneke had said nothing and I'm a literal man, and Aylin looked up from her cards and said, "He's in. He's got the room till four. I've put you down," in exactly the voice she'd used on the second of December. Then she wrote something in the visitor book. I didn't look.

"Your request is still open," she said. "You asked for an item on the second and it was marked wrongly. I've corrected the card. The item's on the table." She squared a card to the edge of the desk. "That's how a reading room works, Mr Klippe. Whoever is sitting at it."

He was at the long table. Anneke was next to him, not by the window this time; next to him, with a notebook, like a lawyer sitting with a client who's agreed to talk. The lamp on. He looked, I'm sorry to say, extremely well. Better than me. I'd slept about nine hours since Sunday.

There were two things on the table. A gray folder, closed, with a shelfmark on the label that I'd carried in a dead man's handwriting for eight months. And next to it, square to the edge of the tray, thin, no title, a book that had been in my kitchen until a night in November when a dog went down at the gate.
There was no dog under the table. First table in a year. I noticed it the way you notice a tooth is gone.
"Mr Klippe. Sit. You've brought nothing."
"I was told."

"Good. People have been bringing things to this table for forty years. I never needed any of it." He put one finger on the thin book and pushed it an inch toward me. "This is yours. It was collected in error. I'm told the man who collected it is no longer with us, in the employment sense. Take it when you go."
I didn't touch it yet. I wanted to. I didn't want him to watch me want to.

"And that," he said, nodding at the folder, "you've already read. Mrs Pekcan tells me you copied it by hand and left it on the table. Hendrik argued for two pages and never got as far as the chair. You wrote four lines on a slip and came back twice." He folded his hands. "I've been retired. I'm to have an office and no keys. I find I don't mind. I'd like to talk, because I enjoy it, and because it no longer matters. Ask."
I'd made a list all week and thrown it away that morning in the car park.
"What's it for?"
He laughed, the small pleased sound from December. "Oh, that's the right one. Everybody asks what is it. Nobody asks what it's for." He tapped the table near Anneke's notebook. "Write that down."
"I'm not your secretary," Anneke said, and didn't write it down.
<hr />

"I'll give you the only news first," he said, "because you've earned it, and because the rest is decoration. You've got the sentence. You've got it from a widow, from eleven strangers, and from a dead Englishman in a folder. You think we took it out of the books because we didn't want people to have it."

"We have it. We've always had it. We use it." He said it like a man confirming a train time. "Some people, near the end, remember the last few minutes of the time before. You know this; you've had a hand. What almost nobody knows is that it can be done on purpose. Not the remembering. The going. If you go the right way, holding the right thing, you come back to where you were. Same work. Same room. A chair you know." He opened his hands. "That's what it's for, Mr Klippe. That's all it has ever been for. We come back. And a world full of people comparing what they remember over kitchen tables is a world where the chair isn't there when you get back to it. So we keep the number of people who compare inside a range where they can be laughed at. It's not cruelty. It's housekeeping."
The floor hummed. I thought of a hundred desks, four names each.
"Who's we?"

"Fewer than you'd like. More than you'd hope. In this region, me, and before me a man I remember being." He smiled. "You'll want to know how that works and I'm going to disappoint you. There's no machine. There's no physics. There's a method and a sentence, and the sentence is yours, nearly. May I see your copy?"

I had the notebook in my coat. I hadn't planned to show him anything. I put it on the table open at the page, because I wanted to see what he'd do, which is the same reason I'd invented a book in a pub.

He read it. He read all three sheets of Tresidder, the business and the illness and the stones, with one finger on the line the way Pieter had read his sheet, and when he got to the sentence he took a pencil out of his jacket, an ordinary one, and before I could move he put one line through a word and wrote another above it.
Don't be afraid. Hold on to whoever is holding your ~~hand~~ name.

"That's ours," he said, and put the pencil down. "One word. His aunt's version takes you wherever the hand goes, and hands go everywhere, that's the trouble with them. Ours takes you back to whoever has your name. A list. A card on a desk. A register in a room like this." He nodded at the visitor book on Aylin's desk through the door. "Somebody holds your name when you go, and you come back to it. It works. It's the only thing in this building that does."

I looked at my own handwriting with his pencil through it. One line, one word, the rest left alone. I'd seen that done to a plate in 1931 and to a forum post in the summer, and now it had been done to me, at the table, while I watched, and I understood why they'd never needed to clean anything. It's quick, and it's small, and the man who did it is pleased with himself.
"That's an edit," I said.
"That's a correction."
"You left the rest in."
"One always does."
<hr />
"The films," I said, because it was on the list I'd thrown away and I wanted to hear him do it.

He brightened. "Oh, you've had those from every crank in the country. I'll be brief. Men in Black: every man who finds the agency is now the man in the film. The moon as a collector of souls: that one was for fun. Dracula, so that we don't die belongs to a man in a cape. Walt."
"Walt Disney."
"Walt was our best customer. He never knew."
I laughed. I didn't mean to. It came out of me like a sneeze, a real laugh, in that room, with the lamp, and once it started I couldn't stop it, and I had to put my hand over my face.
"Something funny?"
"Walt fucking Disney," I said. "Sorry. You've just told me you come back from the dead by holding a list, and you've followed it with Walt Disney. Is he frozen? Is he downstairs?"
"Freezing," he said, quite seriously, "is meaningless."
"Course it is."
Anneke was looking at her notebook. I think, I'm not sure, the corner of her mouth moved.
"You don't believe the films," he said.

"I can't check them. I can check a plate. I can check a desk number." I looked at him. "You've told me three boasts in a row and I laughed at all three. That's the technique, isn't it. Say it next to something stupid."
"You see," he said to Anneke, "this is why I asked for him."
<hr />
"The seats," he said, and leaned in, not for secrecy, for pleasure. "You'll want to know about the seats."
"Desk twelve."
He stopped.

"Pieter's. And a man in Rotterdam, and a consultant in Nijmegen, and a woman with two surnames. Four names, one chair. There are a hundred desks on that floor and I counted them at the drill. They're not for sitting in. They never were. A seat is what you promise a man so he'll leave a job alone for thirty years, and you can promise the same chair to four men because none of them will ever sit in it." I sat back. "A man told me that over coffee. I checked it against my own initials. The lifeboat's a lie with a floor plan."
He looked at me for a moment with no face ready, the way he'd looked in December when I'd mentioned the dog.
"Yes," he said. "Well. You've saved me a paragraph."
"Why four?"
"Because three looked thin on the invoice."
Anneke wrote that one down.
<hr />
And then I said it, and I hadn't planned to, and it came up from a kitchen floor in November, the fourth night, and I said it the way you'd say it to a dog.
"It's not for staying."
He looked at me.

"The sentence. Your version holds the name and comes back to the chair. His version holds the hand." I put my finger on Tresidder's word, under his pencil line. "A man in a market told me a thing his dealer told him, which the dealer got from a professor, who said it when they buried a dog. We all go back in the one bucket. The ones who held on come out together. Together. Not back. You don't hold somebody's hand to come back to a room on your own. You hold it so you don't go on your own. That's the whole instruction, and you've been using it to go round and round the same building."
It was very quiet. Even the floor seemed to go quiet, which it didn't, I know it didn't.
"Yes," he said.

That was all, for a second. Then: "We chose the room. What would you have done? On one side, everything you've ever been afraid of, and whoever has your hand, and you don't get to pick. On the other, this room, these people, the work, a chair you know. We chose the chair. Every time it costs more. Every time there's less of us to bring back." He looked at his hands. "We don't know where the other way goes. We stopped wanting to know a long time ago. Hendrik wanted to know. That's why he wrote two pages and I gave him a date."
I wanted to feel sorry for him. I checked, the way you check a pocket. I didn't.
<hr />
"So tell it," I said. "If you're done. If it doesn't matter. Let it out."
"It can't come out," Anneke said.
We both looked at her. She hadn't spoken since I'm not your secretary, apart from writing down thin on the invoice.

"I've spent a week on this," she said. "Not his version. Mine. Suppose everybody knew, tomorrow, as a fact, that it goes on, and that you can hold on to somebody through it. What happens on Thursday? Nobody goes to work. The hospitals, the water, the grid, all of it runs on people who are more afraid of dying than of their jobs." She closed the notebook. "I don't know whether that's been built on purpose. He says it has. I've read the recovery plans and I can tell you what they assume. Take the fear out fast and you don't get a better world. You get a week with nobody at the water board. I'm head of risk. I'm not doing that to a country on the strength of one letter."
"So the deal's the same as it always was," I said.

"No. The deal's mine now." She opened the notebook again, to a page she'd already written. "The nightly job goes. Frank closes it, through a ticket, like a normal person. The line on the invoice steps down; not to nothing, there's a contract, but down, and I read it before I sign it. The annex gets rewritten by HR, with one name per desk, and the desks stop being sold. The schedule is not signed, this quarter or any other, until somebody can tell me what a visit is in a sentence I'd put in a board paper. Continuity stays. The seats stay, for the people who think they've got them, because taking them away is louder than leaving them. And you keep quiet." She looked up. "The bank, the names, the foundation. Nothing."
"And him?" I didn't say the name.
"Julian Kalder's contract is under review. He didn't come in Monday. He's not answering." She paused. "He's not the bank's problem anymore. He may be somebody's. I've chosen not to ask whose."
The old man smiled at the table. It was the only time I wanted to hit him.

"And you can write a book," Anneke said. "You asked me, the day you gave me my sheet, whether you'd ever be allowed to. Under your own name. It claims nothing and names nobody. If anyone asks, it's a novel."
"We've been publishing those for four hundred years," the old man said. "Nobody reads the middle."
"I read the middle," I said.
"Yes. Well. There's one of you."
"Agreed," I said. To her, not to him. "All of it."
"Good." She capped her pen. "Is there anything else?"
"One thing. It's small."
"Say it."

I didn't say it out loud. I leaned over and said it to her, low, close to her ear, like a man telling a secret at a wedding, and the old man watched us and didn't hear it, and I've never written it down and I'm not going to now. It wasn't about the bank. It was mine.
She sat back. She looked at me for a long moment.
"Yes," she said. "That I can do." And she wrote one line in the notebook, and turned the page so it was face down.
<hr />
He stood up. He was old and it took him a moment. Anneke didn't help and he didn't ask.
"Leave it," he said to me.
Two words. The ones Pieter had used. The ones the whole building was built on.

"Not as a threat. As advice from a man who's had the keys. You've bought a generation, perhaps, in this part of the world. Then it starts again somewhere else, under a different word. You'll be dead by then. So will I, for a while." He looked at the thin book. "When it's your turn, do what you did on the floor, and hold on to the hand. Go. Don't come back. I'd like one of us to have tried it."
He went out. Anneke stayed sitting with her hand flat on her notebook.
"Is he right?" I said. "Eighteen months and you're him?"

"I don't know." She stood. "I approved an invoice thirty times without reading it. I'm reading things now." She picked up her coat. "He's got the room till four. Stay, if you like. It's the only room in the building that doesn't hum."
That wasn't true. It hummed. But I stayed.

I picked up the thin book. Forty-one entries, in a hand I'd learned, and his sentence at eleven, and the last page with its shelfmark and its date and its one word. It was all there. Somebody had been careful with it. That was almost the worst thing.

Then I sat at the long table with a dead man's folder and my own notebook and went through what he'd said, one thing at a time, like a list of alerts at the end of a shift. The films I couldn't check and didn't try. The chair, the name, the coming back: I had his word for it and a pencil line, and I've spent my life not taking anyone's word for anything. Every piece fit the next one perfectly, one long clean line from a flood survey to the floor under my feet, and that's what bothered me. Real things don't fit like that. Real things have a torn corner somewhere. He'd done to me what they'd done to everybody: handed me a story so neat it was impossible to believe and impossible to throw away.

What I could check was on the table. A letter from 1929 with a sentence in it, and the same sentence from a widow and eleven strangers, and a pencil line through one word in my own handwriting, made in front of me, by the man who'd ordered the line through the plate. I'd watched him do what they do. That I could put in front of anybody.

I rubbed his word out. It took a while; he'd pressed. Then I wrote Tresidder's back in, in my own pencil, and under it, so I couldn't later pretend I hadn't seen it: Changed to "name" by the head of this region, in front of me, in the reading room. Changed back.
I decided I'd work out which parts I believed later. Somewhere with grass. Somewhere with a dog.

When I went down, Aylin didn't look up. But the visitor book was open on her desk, and next to December, next to my name, the word Pending had a neat pencil line through it, and nothing written beside it yet.

chapters.title: A market, Sunday
chapters.what: 🟡 v9 — Claude, 16 Nov 2026. [K + phone]. EDITED. Moved from a border town to Beard Man's market: Kalder is found by his bag, because James told them what he carries and the three men in the country he'd let touch it, and one has a stall there. The closing-in is the seat he asked for (a desk and a bed on the lower floor, no course, no dogs). James rings from across the square. He counts the clubs to fourteen. Source: v8/54.
blocks: The market was the one James went to, which Kalder knew, and which was the reason he had put it off for five weeks.

He'd been living in a rented room over a bicycle shop two towns east, under a name that was not his and not the last one either. He'd cut his hair. He'd let his beard come in, gray at the chin, which he hadn't expected and didn't mind. He paid cash. He ran in the mornings, along the water, not too far, not too fast. He had been careful in all the ways he had been trained to be careful, and in two or three he had invented, and he was good at it. He had always been good at things.

But the grips were going. He'd noticed it in the kitchen on the Friday, turning the seven iron in his hands the way other men turn a glass, and the leather had gone shiny under his right thumb where it always went first. There were three men in the country he'd let regrip them. One was dead. One had a shop in Amsterdam he couldn't go near. The third was an old man with a folding table at a Sunday market in the east, between a cheese van and a man who sold books off the ground, and he'd been going to him for nine years, and he'd said so, at a dinner, to a man who remembered paper.

He knew that. He went anyway. He told himself it was because the grips mattered, and that was true, and it was also true that he wanted to see the stall again, and the square, and possibly, from a distance, a gray dog in a cart.
He parked three streets away and walked in with the bag on his shoulder, because you don't leave those in a car.
<hr />

The old man with the folding table was glad to see him and didn't ask about the beard. He took the seven iron, turned it, ran his thumb where Kalder's thumb went, and said what he always said, which was that the leather was good leather and the problem was the owner. He said it would take an hour and Kalder said he'd walk.
He bought a coffee from the van and stood with it by the cheese, because from there he could see both ends of the square, and because the cheese man talked about the weather in a dialect he enjoyed.
He saw the first one at ten past eleven.

A man in a good coat at the flower stall, choosing tulips. Mid-fifties, a scarf, a face Kalder knew from a room in Leiden with a long table, nine years ago. A man who had once told him, kindly, that the hardest part of the work was the paperwork. The man did not look at him. The man was very interested in tulips.
Kalder turned, unhurried, the way you'd turn to check the time on the church, and saw the second.

A woman by the bakery van. Red hat. He'd sat next to her at a dinner in Antwerp, the one where the brewer had been so pleased. She had a paper bag in one hand and nothing in the other, and she was not looking at him either.
He finished his coffee.

There was a third by the church steps, and probably a fourth behind him where he couldn't see without making it obvious that he was looking, and he didn't look. He stood by the cheese and did the arithmetic, the way he'd been taught, and it came out the way it does when people who know the method use it on you. He'd said three men in the country at a table, and the man at the table had written everything down for a year. They hadn't found him. They'd found the bag. They'd waited at the three places the bag could go, and one of them was dead, and one was in Amsterdam, and here he was in the east with a coffee, exactly where a man who loved his clubs would be.
He almost admired it. He'd have done the same.

Across the square, at the far end, a man with a beard was mid-sentence at a stall of books on the ground, and in front of him, with a phone in his hand and an old gray dog sitting against his leg, was James.
Not coming over. Not hiding. Standing where Kalder could see him, which was a kindness, or a message, or both. The dog had seen him too. The dog had not stopped looking since.
His phone rang. The old one, the one he'd kept in the lining of the jacket for no reason he'd ever said out loud. He'd switched it on that morning to look at something. He hadn't told himself what.
He looked at the screen and almost laughed.
"James."
"Julian." The market behind the voice, the same market. "You can see them?"
"I can see three."

"I don't know how many there are. I didn't find you. I want you to know that. I'm not that guy. They asked me what you'd carry and I told them, and they asked where it could go and I told them that too. You said it at my table." A pause. "They're much better at it than me."
"They are." The tulip man had bought his tulips. He was standing with them by the fountain. "Why ring? You're forty meters away."
"Because I don't want to be near you. And I wanted to say one thing, and I wanted it to be me."
"Go on."
"You shouldn't have touched my dog."
The cheese man asked if he wanted the usual. He nodded and gave him a note and waved away the change.
"No," he said into the phone. "I shouldn't."

He meant it. Not as an apology; he had never in his life done anything as an apology. As an error. The one entry in nine years he would go back and change. Everything else had been necessary, or clever, or both. The dog had been quick. Quick was the mistake. A man doesn't forgive you a thing like that, and a man who doesn't forgive you remembers what you said about your clubs.
"Is he all right?"
"He lay down on the sixth green on the Monday. Right next to the hole."
Kalder smiled at the fountain. He couldn't help it. "They'll have hated that."
"The greenkeeper pretended not to see."
"Good man."
The red hat had moved. Not closer. Just to a place that was closer to where he would have to walk.
"I liked you," Kalder said. "I'd like that on whatever you're keeping. All of it was work. The golf, the barbecue, Ana. And I liked you anyway. That wasn't the plan."
"I know."
"Do you?"
"Yeah," James said. "That's why it was so fucking hard."
Kalder laughed then, properly, the one from the back nine, the one people turned round for. The cheese man glanced up. The tulip man did not.
"Tell Ana it was very good. The pills. I'd have bet on you."
"I'll tell her."
"And James—"

But the line had gone. He looked at the phone. James had hung up on him. Across the square the man put the phone in his pocket and put his hand on the dog's head, and the man with the beard went on talking as if nobody had stopped listening, which perhaps nobody had.
<hr />
The woman in the red hat reached him first. She said his name, the real one, quite warmly, as if they'd run into each other by chance.
"Hello," Kalder said. "Isn't it a beautiful day."
"It is." She looked at the folding table, where the old man was wrapping the seven iron. "We'll wait for those. There's no hurry."
"There isn't?"

"You asked for a seat," she said. "Nine years ago, in a kitchen. It's been kept. A desk on the lower floor, with your name on the card, and a bed. You'll have the generator for company." She smiled. "You'll be the first person who ever actually sat in one. They're quite excited about it upstairs."
He thought about that. A hundred desks, under a reading room, humming.
"Is there a course?"
"Dogs?"
"Companion animals are not accommodated," she said, and he could tell she'd been looking forward to saying it.
The old man held out the parcel. Kalder took it and gave him a note and waved away the change, and the old man said the leather was good leather, and Kalder said he knew.

He slid the seven iron into the bag, in its place, between the six and the eight. Then he did what he'd done at the start of every round of his life, which was count. Driver. Three wood. Hybrid. Four through nine. Wedges, three. Putter. He touched each head as he went, the way you'd touch the back of a chair in a dark room.
Fourteen. The legal maximum. All there.

He shouldered the bag. The tulip man had come up on his other side, and the third one from the church steps was behind him now, close enough that he could hear him breathing, and across the square an old dog was still watching him go.
"Right," Kalder said. "Lead on."

chapters.title: Leave it
chapters.what: Prose left alone apart from the three additions Structure 01 names: he switches the watcher off, Pieter asks whether he is still on the list (nobody is kept, the ones on it included), and the book gets a last page of real, checkable things with their sources. The ticket now names the renamed job bc-recon-nightly; the invoice step is tied to stand-up, not the forum. Source: v8/55.
blocks: Nothing happened.

I want to say that first, because I'd been waiting for something for a year, and I think anyone who's listened to me this long has too. The thirty-first of December, the date at the bottom of page 212, the one they'd pulled to a Monday and then not needed, came and went like any other. On the Wednesday I went to the course at seven with the dogs. The retirees were on the third. The dew was on everything. Nobody was standing on any green with a flask. The world didn't end. It never once has, as far as I can tell, which is the main argument against it.

Ana's mother came back from Gouda with a cake and a list of things her sister had said about her. The hat went back on its own hook. Mora checked every room for the postman, twice, then ate a sock. Buddy went to his blankets by the radiator and lay down with that long sigh that sounds like a man getting into a bath, and I stood in the hall and thought: this is enough. Then I thought, don't go looking. And then I laughed out loud in my own hall, alone, because I'd thought that exact sentence once before on the seventh tee in April, and look how that went.
Ana heard me from the kitchen.
"What?"
"Nothing."
"You laughed at nothing in the hall."
"I'm fine."
"You're laughing at nothing in the hall, Mulder. That's not fine. That's a symptom." She came and looked at me. "Is it over?"
I thought about it properly. I owed her that.
"I don't know," I said. "I think it's smaller."
"Smaller's good." She went back to the kettle. "I'll take smaller."
<hr />

The invoice came on the first working day of January, like it always did. I didn't go looking for it. That's not true — I had a filter on it from October and it popped up on my second screen at 08:51 with a little blue dot, and I sat there for a while with my coffee and didn't click it.
Then I clicked it.

Continuity reconciliation. Same post box. Same font. Same everything, except the number, which for the first time since 1994 had gone down. Not to nothing — there's a contract, Anneke had said, and contracts at a bank die slower than people. One step down. A clean amount, the kind a committee agrees on. In the corner of the PDF, a set of initials in blue ink that hadn't been there in thirty years of scans: A. de W.
Thirty-one years of steps going up. Six of them. One of them the week I'd said eleven words at a stand-up in front of nine people. And now one going the other way.
I printed it. I don't print things. I folded it in four and put it in my wallet behind my driving license, where it still is, getting soft at the corners.
<hr />
The job took a month.

Anneke had said it would be boring, and she'd meant it as a term, and it was. That was the whole beauty of it. There was no midnight. Nobody pulled a cable. On the second Monday in January I opened a ticket like a normal person, in the normal queue, with the normal template.
Summary: Scheduled job bc-recon-nightly (02:14 daily), owner Business Continuity Program. No documented business purpose. Outbound transfer to external address. Request review and decommission.
Priority: Low.
That was Frank's idea. "Low," he said, leaning over my shoulder with a sandwich. "You put High, someone reads it. You put Low, it goes through on a Friday."
"That's horrible."
"That's the bank, mate." He chewed. "Assign it to me."
"You can't assign things to yourself."
"I can if you assign it to me." He pointed at the screen with the sandwich and dropped a piece of tomato on my keyboard. "Go on."
I assigned it to him.

It sat in the queue for nine days, which is normal. Someone from change management asked for a business justification and Frank wrote owner consulted; no business purpose identified and nothing else, which, it turns out, is the most powerful sentence in a four-hundred-year-old bank. The owner was the program. The program, as of the first, was me. Someone from security asked if the outbound address was known, and Frank wrote no, and someone from security wrote ok and approved it. Pieter signed the change. He looked at the ticket number on his screen for a second longer than you look at a ticket number, and clicked, and then he did ask me something, which he hadn't since the night he made a man tea.
"Am I still on it? The list."
I'd thought about how to answer that for a month, and in the end I gave him the plain version, because he'd earned it.

"There isn't a kept, Pieter. There never was. Not for the people who weren't on it, and not for the ones who were. Desk twelve's got four names on it. The man who sold it to you is sleeping in it." I shrugged. "Nobody's kept. You're on a list. That's all a list ever was."
He thought about that for a while. "Marieke will be relieved," he said. "She never liked being a three."
Then he went back to his screen, and that was the last time either of us mentioned it at work.
On the last Thursday in January, at 02:14, nothing ran.

I know because I was up. Of course I was up. I was on the kitchen floor with Buddy, who had decided that three in the morning was the time for a drink and then a long conversation about it, and I had the laptop open on the tiles and the dashboard up, and at 02:14 the line where the job had been for thirty-one years just wasn't. No error. No alert. A little gap in a graph, the way a tooth goes.
I sat there and watched the gap for about four minutes. Buddy put his chin on my foot.
"That's it," I told him.
He didn't care. He was right not to.

I switched the watcher off that morning. Not deleted; switched off, the way you'd leave a lamp in a room you've stopped using. It had run every night since a barbecue in October, copying my own threads and the forum's public pages and eleven addresses' worth of family announcements, and showing me in the morning what had changed. Nothing had changed for three weeks. The forum was the forum. The addresses were quiet in the ordinary way, the way streets are. I opened the config and changed one line and it didn't run at 02:14 either, and there was no gap in any graph because I'd never put it on one. It was mine. Nobody was counting it.

Frank closed the ticket at 09:03 the next morning with the comment Decommissioned. No impact observed. and sent me the skull, and then a second message: No impact observed lol. And then, a minute later, a third: still don't believe any of it btw. And then: but I believe the invoice.

We filed one more, the same week. A dull one. Against the new tools — the ones I'd read all four hundred pages of, the defaults — asking that the rule on page 212 be reviewed as possibly over-broad, suppresses legitimate unowned-job detection. Priority low. Frank's name. It went to the vendor's queue, wherever that is, which is where things go to die.
"They'll never touch it," Frank said.
"Probably not."
"Then why'd we file it?"
"Because it's wrong," I said, "and you write it down when something's wrong."
He thought about that. "That's the least cool thing you've ever said."
"Thank you."
<hr />

A parcel came in February. Not for me — for Ana. A Leiden postmark, no return address, a conservator's careful handwriting on the label. Inside, flat between two boards, a page from something very old that had been torn once and wasn't anymore. You had to hold it up to the window to find the join.
No note.
Ana held it up to the window for a long time.
"Who's this from?"
"A woman who repairs paper."
"Is she okay?"
"She's quiet."
Ana lowered the page. "That's not the same thing."
"No," I said. "She's okay."

She looked at me to see if I was lying, which she can do from across a room, and then she put the page back between the boards and put the boards on the shelf next to her grandmother's photo, where they still are. Mora sniffed the shelf and was told no.
<hr />
I started writing in March.

I'd been allowed to, under my own name, a book that claims nothing and names nobody — and the second I sat down to do it I found out that claiming nothing is really hard. Every page I wrote wanted to accuse someone. I'd write a sentence and look at it and think based on what? and delete it. I deleted a lot. Some nights all I kept was the dogs.
Ana read the first chapter over my shoulder, which I hate.
"You made me sound mean."
"You are mean."
"I'm right. That's different." She read a bit more. "You can't put fuck that many times."
"I counted. It's less than you say in a day."
"I'm not a book." She kissed the top of my head. "It's good. It's weird. Your weird is —"
"I know."
"Don't let them make it normal."

The last page I wrote first, and it's the only one that didn't want to accuse anybody. It's a list. Real things, each with where you can go and check it, because a book that claims nothing still ought to point. That Darwin changed a sentence about where life came from between the first and second editions of his book, in 1859 and 1860, and added a hand where my printer took one out; it's in any variorum, look up "Creator." That five scientists met in Washington for four days in January 1953 and recommended that the public be taught to find a certain subject ridiculous; the report is declassified, the phrase is theirs. That a Dutch publisher's archive, moved to Leiden, exists and can be requested on a slip. That a German archaeologist climbed a hill the farmers called Potbelly in 1994 and found that people had built in stone before they farmed. That a Mexican neuroscientist disappeared in 1994 and has not been found, and that this book connects that to nothing. That a Greek wrote a joke about Pythagoras recognizing a friend in a dog, in the sixth century before Christ, and it's the oldest surviving mention of the idea. That you may bury a dog in your own garden in this country if the hole is deep enough, and I've checked the depth.
None of it proves anything. That's the point of the page. It's what I could put in front of a stranger. The rest is what I saw, and I've said which is which.

On the Wednesday after that I took Buddy to the course in the cart, early, and played the seventh. My drive went in the trees. Obviously. I stood at the edge of the rough looking for the ball, and Buddy, from the cart, did the thing he does — stared at a spot in the long grass with total confidence, which is wrong about half the time.
It was there.
"Okay," I said. "Show-off."
He thumped his tail on the seat twice. I chipped out sideways, like I always do, and we went on.

chapters.title: Epilogue
chapters.what: He now holds Buddy's paw and says the sentence, once, before the phrase at the grave; his hope is the meeting (he will know the hand), not the method for leaving; Ana's half-asleep line about cracked knuckles is added and goes into the thin book as a forty-second entry he tells nobody about. Page 212 and Ida kept. American spelling. Source: v8/56.
blocks: Buddy died four years later, on a Tuesday in April, at home, on his blankets by the radiator, at a quarter past two in the morning.

We were both on the floor. That's where he was, so that's where we were. He'd been slowing down for a long time — the back legs first, then the appetite, then the thing in his eyes that used to follow me round a room — and the vet had said, a week before, kindly, that it would be soon and that he didn't think it would be hard. He was right, for once. I'd have preferred him wrong.

Buddy's head was on my knee. Ana was on the other side of him with her hand flat on his chest, the way she does, counting without counting. Mora was in the doorway, gray in the muzzle herself now, not letting anyone in or out, which at a quarter past two meant nobody. At some point his breathing changed. Then it got slower.

I had his front paw in my hand. I'd taken it without thinking, the way you do, the pad rough and the nails too long because we'd stopped cutting them when it started to hurt him. And I said it. Once, quietly, to a dog, in a kitchen, the thing I'd carried in a notebook for four years and never said aloud to anyone.
"Don't be afraid. Hold on to whoever is holding your hand."

Ana didn't look up. She knew the words; she'd read them over my shoulder on this floor. He didn't do anything. He was a dog, and he was nearly gone, and I don't know what he heard. His paw stayed in my hand because I was holding it.
Then there was a breath, and we waited for the next one, the way you wait for a ball to drop on the far side of a hill, and it didn't come.
Neither of us said anything for a long time. The fridge hummed. Mora lay down in the doorway with a groan.

Then Ana said, "Well. That's that, old man," in a perfectly steady voice, and started crying the real way, the way with no shape, and I held her, and the dog was between us and still warm, and I kept my hand on his ear because it was soft and I didn't want to stop.
<hr />

Frank came in the morning with beer, at nine, which is a crime, and sat on the kitchen floor where the blankets had been. He's thirty-three now and has a girlfriend who does yoga and he's started saying we about weekends. He didn't say anything for a while. Then he said, "Fuck," and then, "He was a good foreman," and then nothing, which was exactly right.

We buried him in the garden that afternoon, by the gate, where his water bowl used to be — the gate a man once walked up to at night with a bowl of his own. I'd checked the rules years ago. You can, here, if the garden's yours and the hole's deep enough. I made it deep enough. It took me most of the afternoon because there's a root, and I swore at the root the whole time, and Ana brought me tea and stood at the edge and didn't help, and Ida — I'll get to Ida — kept trying to get in the hole with me.
I put him in on his blanket. The gray one.
Then I stood there with the spade and the sky doing nothing in particular, and I said it.
"He's in a better place. I'll see him soon."

Ana looked at me. She'd heard me say a version of those words once before, at a grave, in a voice that was about eighty-five percent yes and fifteen percent question. She knew the difference. She's always known the difference.
"You said it," she said.
"I know."
"You meant it."
"I know what it means now."

I can't explain that better than that, and I've tried, in a lot of drafts. It's not that I'm sure. I'm a man who checks things for a living and I can't check this one. It's that I know what I'm going to do with it. When it's my turn, and it's coming, it's coming for everybody, that's the one thing in this whole story nobody disputes, I'm going to do what I did on the kitchen floor four nights in November, which is nothing, and not be afraid, and hold on to whoever has my hand. Not to come back. I've seen where coming back gets you: a chair, and a generator for company. To go with somebody. And I've been told twice, in mud, that there'll be a hand, and I think I'll know it. That's all I've got, and I said it at a grave with a spade, and this time it was a hundred percent of whatever it was.
Ana put her hand on my back.
"Okay," she said. "Come inside. You're filthy."
<hr />

Frank sent me a link a month later, with the skull. The new release of the monitoring tools — the AI ones, the defaults, version seven. He reads them now; that's my fault. Page 212 was gone — not rewritten, just gone. The rule that told the watcher never to see a job like the one I'd found — removed, no note, no reason, the section numbers just closing over it like water.
Somebody read our ticket lol, he wrote.
Nobody reads tickets, I wrote back.
Somebody read the middle, he wrote, and I didn't answer that, because I don't know, and I've stopped pretending I know things I don't.
<hr />
Ana said something that week, half asleep, which I'm going to put here and nowhere else.

It was a Thursday night, three days after. She'd gone to bed first and I came up late, and when I got in beside her she turned over without really waking and said, in the voice she uses for the shopping, "His hands were cracked. At the knuckles. I knew them." And then she was asleep.

I lay there a long time. I didn't wake her. In the morning she didn't remember and I didn't ask, and I've never asked since, because I know what she'd say, and I know what I'd do with it, and I've learned which questions you don't put to the one person you can't afford to be wrong about.

Cracked at the knuckles. I'd written that once, in a notebook, about a hand in the mud at her grandmother's grave. She'd never read that page. I'd kept it from her for a year and then it hadn't seemed to matter.

I went downstairs and took the thin book off the shelf, the professor's, with its forty-one entries in his hand and the last page with its shelfmark and its date and the word Ask. I'd never written in it. It wasn't mine to write in. I turned past the last page to the blank one after, and I wrote the date, and under it, in pencil, in capitals so there'd be no argument about the handwriting: Ana, in her sleep, three days after Buddy: "His hands were cracked. At the knuckles. I knew them." Nothing before it to say what it answered. Nothing after it to say what it meant. A forty-second entry, with no plate and no printer, from a woman who doesn't believe a word of it.
It's the only matched pair in this whole book. I've told nobody. I'm telling you because it's the last page and you've come this far, and because a copy is the only thing I know how to make.

Ida came that summer, from a woman near Deventer with a litter and a card in a bakery window. Brown, all feet, ears that hadn't decided yet. Not a replacement; Ana was very clear, and Mora was clearer — she took one look at the puppy and went to lie in the bathroom for three days. We called her Ida. There was no argument about the name, which in our house was a first.
One night in October I went up to bed and got to the top of the stairs and turned round, the way you do.
Ida was sitting at the bottom step.

Not following. Sitting. Looking up at me. She was six months old, made of springs, she could have been up those stairs in two seconds, and she'd never seen Buddy do anything in her life, and nobody had taught her. She just sat there at the bottom with her head a little on one side and watched me go, with that patience.
I stood at the top for a long time.
Then I went back down, and sat on the bottom step next to her, and she climbed into my lap, all elbows, and licked my ear and then sneezed in it.
"Okay," I said. "Okay. I see you."
Ana called from upstairs to ask what the fuck I was doing on the stairs at midnight.
"Nothing," I said. "Checking something."
